div.head: PRACTICAL POULTRY
div.p: PRACTICAL POULTRY
FARMING.
[BY REDCAP.]
MARKETING EGGS.

Now that eggs are getting a little more plentiful a few words on grading, &c., will be useful. If a little trouble is bestowed in this direction it certainly pays. Condition and uniformity are the two essentials to be observed. All the dirty ones should be care- fully washed, then pick out all the smallest and also any that are abnormally large and use them for home c. m•umption. Cleanliness is very important and poultry keepers would save themselves a good deal of trouble in washing the eggs, if greater attention was given to the

NEST BOXES. I have seen some nest boxes caked with dirt. Generally speaking the good old orange box is used as a nest box. I have no complaint to find with the device at all, if you will only be sure to place a rib of wood on the upper side, to prevent the dirt from dropping through the open spaces which are always found in the sides of these boxes. As I have said, if attention is given to the nest boxes a good deal of trouble is caved. You should thoroughly clean them out, at least once a week placing therein a fresh supply of clean straw.

div.head: COLOUR.
div.p: COLOUR.

Although the colour of the egg has nothing what- ever to do with the quality, a good many people prefer the brown shelled cries. It is a good plan to separate the broens from the whites, and for those who are fastidious, well, let them pay a little higher rate. Not only for this purpose is it advisable to do so, but also for the sake of making a pleasing show. Nicely graded eggs with the colours separated look -very well when staged, and for the extra trouble you are sure to attract new custcmers. PACKING.

The question of packing need not worry those adjacent to a market town, but, where one's produce has to travel fur any ccnsiderable distance, then it is advisable to pack them carefully. The cleanest and safest way to pack eggs is with hay. Place a good thick layer on the bottom of the box or basket about six inches deep, this forms a good "spring' mattress' and obviates the necesity of the succeedin4 layers being so thick. Some people use sawdust, others use bran, but neither is so good or safe as hay. Of the two latter materials you are bound to lose large quantities in unpacking, whereas the hay ia more easily retained and if kept dry will last again and again for quite a reasonable time. MARKETING OLD STOCK BIRDS.

As the breeding pens and surp'us stock birds are disposed of, care should be taken not to mislead your customers. I have scanned the stalls of many a market town, but I have never yet seen poultry laid out in a business-like fashion. What you generally see is a few baskets of eggs laid about here and there, and a few lots of desd poultry with no sign whatever to indicate their purpose and price. Customers come by, and maybe purchase a good-looking fowl for a roast, only to find, after being cooked, that it is as tough as leather, the nett result often being "No more for me." That is why I say that in building up a connection care should be used not to mislead pros- pective customers. Therefore, in the disposal of surplus stock und old birds you should distinctly state the condition. Sell them as " boilets " and not as " roasters." You should never forget that every pur- chaser is a propective customer and when the time comes round for the sale of your spring chickens these people will come again. A good deal depends on how you set out your goods as to whether you will make good sales or not. A poultry and egg stall should be set out after the manner of api ovieion dealer's shop. Each article of produce should be distinguished by some mark, arranged in order and ticketed as to price. The buying public are often too shy to ask, and the smallest indication to attract attention wceld assist you in the intioduction with passers-by. Besides, it is more businesslike and up-to-date. CHICKEN CHIPS.

You must keep the chickens en the move now. As the mornings get warmer see that they get out in the early morning. It is still true that "The early bird gots the worm." Before the morning dew leaves the grass there are lots of insects which later on in the day disappear. The chicks would get these if liberated in the eel-4. morn. Move the coops abcut as often as space will allow Fresh ground is a great essential to the health of young growing stock. A morming's meal of bread and milk will work wonders. In fact there is nothing to equal it for keeping young chick on the move. Don't let them sleep on a boarded floor. It gives cramp and creates leg weakness. If the coops are wooden bottomed ones, cut a good thick sod and plsce therein. Keep a sharp look-cut for vermin. If there are rst holes about, fill them e ith broken bottles and tar. The rodentudon't like these and generally find fresh lodgings when so treated. If it is convenient for the broody hen to have her freedom, let her by all means. She will find more for the chicks than they can find for themselves. ifABOUT COMBS. is hardly necessary to point out that a fowl's comb is its head gear.' There are several different kinds of combs and it may prove of some interest if I name and describe them. The flat erect comb is the most common, such es are seen with the Minorca. The rosecornb is a sort of double comb, wide at the base, flat on top except for a !ember of coral-like small spikes such as are seen in Redcaps and Homburgs. A Pea ;.omb is seen with breeds like Malays and Brahmas. It almost resembles a cluster of boiled peas, thus the term pea-comb. The rest of a fowl's headgear comes under the term cf wattles, these are the red appendages which hang underneath the bottom mandible or beak. There are also the lobes, these are most conspicuous in breeds like the Minorca and Black Hamburg, because, of course, of their size and colour, which should be white. In utility stock, head points do hot count for eomuch as they do in exhibition varieties. This subject, however, will be more fully ,dealt with when I write on exhibition poultry a little later on in the season.

div.head: QUERIES.
div.p: QUERIES.

"SMALLHOLDER, "asks for the treatment of a male stock bird. She says that he has become generally , weak, and inasmuch as he is a valuable stock bird she does not want to loose him. Certainly not, this bird should be separated at once from the rest, and placed in a spare coop or shed, feed him liberally with hot bread and milk and a little lean meat daily. Green food in some form should, of course, be given* After a period of two weeks under this treatment he should be right again. Perhaps he has been fighting with other stock birds? I often find this tlie case where fowls are left to run together and breed at will. If you have some special purpose for this one, then mate him off in a separate pen with the hens. You will never get good results from your breeding opera- tions if the stock birds are allowed to fight. " NOVICE" Tells me that he has got some mis- marked Andaulusian hens, they are good layers of large eggs and he is anxious to keep the strain crossed with some other variety. He wants me to tell him which is the best variety to cross his hens with ? For the production of a first rate non-sitting cross I should use a Iloudan Cockerel. Another use- ful cross would be produced by mating your hens with a Rhode Island Red ccckerel. Thanks for your recommendation to other poultry keepers; every ltttle helps dcesn't it?

div.head: RELIGIOUS e-SOC
div.p: RELIGIOUS e-SOC
Easter Services.

The greatest festival of the Church's year was rnf.rl‘ed by services of an appropriately joyous character at: the Anglican and Roman Catholic Churches which had been beautifully decorated for the occasion. At the Pf.,rish Church at Evensong the choir Ilt3g the anthem "God hath appointed a day" and after the Blessing an inspir- ing rendering of the Hallelujah Chorus was given.

Wycliffe P.S A. Society. There was a fair attendance at the meeting of the above society on Sunday last. Mr W Beswick (vice- president) occupied the chair. Mr David Owen, of Warrington, gave a thoughtful address, hearing on ',lie Resurrection of our Lord and Master, and he urged all present to possess an awakening of dieir:own souls, if they would parteke of the full benefits of the futuro Resurrection in Citrist.—Miss Jones rendered the solos "He was Despised" and "The Lord is mindful of His own" in a very creditable manner. Mr J Owen ircal the lesson and Mr Beswick led the prayer. Mr "if /IL Wallington presided at the organ.

would lesult in much larger attendances at the ;ISM' services of the church and in a great increase of com- municants. He earnestly wisheo to see a considerable increase of men communicants, as well as of women. The communicants on Easter Day numbered 895, as against 953 last year. He did not know why there should be a decrease, and he hoped the number would reach 1,000, without any pressure, next year. The Rector then cordially acknowledged the help of all the assistant clergy and said that of late years he had found it a great advantage to reverse his former arrange- ments and have the senior curate at the Parish Church _ .

and the younger clergy at the missions. Referring to the vacancy to be created by the Rev A J Bratt's departure, the Rector said he was in touch with a clergyman who had had considerable experience as assistant diocesan missioner in the diocese of -.Torwich, with a view to his appointment to the curacy. That gentleman had already visited the parish and appeared to he pleased with all he had seml. If he decided to come to Warrington he would endeavour to arrange to take up his duties at the beginning of May. Having returned thanks for the Easter offering, the Rector concluded with the intimation that he attained his seventieth year last year, and that he completed twenty-five years as Rector of Warrington on Good Friday. (Applause). ST BARNABAS' CHURCH. The Rev 3 G Hollingworth presided at the vestry meeting on Thursday evening aad nominated Mr J E Morgan to serve as his warden. Mr W Boyle was re-elected people's warden and the other officers were elected as follows :—Sidesmen, Messrs W E Cotterill B Diruelow, T Evans, jen.. W Hind, J Houghton' T A Jones, F Kimberley, H V Mayhew,W IVlinards, TOxley, W Turner and E Wakefield ; lay representatives, Messrs J J Siddeli nod C Skinner. The statement of accounts showed that the balance brought forward from the previous year amounted to £1 is 4d. Tee receipts totalled £l5l 16s and 2d and included : Collections for church expenses, £66 -17 s 93 ; special collections, £42 2s id. After making grants of £3O to the curacy fund, £5 to the church painting and decoration fund, and £5 to the schools, there was a balance in hand of £ll 18s 6d. The usual votes of thanks were accorded to the church officers and workers.

div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Church.
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Church.

Preaching at St John's on Sunday evening the Rev W Reid contrasted the glory which overspread Moses, the dispenser of Law, with that which attended Him by whom came Grace. The one though subtly husbanded, faded, the other was seen in the laying of it aside, and was eternal. To the Apostle Paul, in his letter to the Church at Corinth, it was the spirit of the resurrected and glorified Christ which proved to be the power whereby we were to be transformed into his image. Two thinszs were e,sential, the true mirror and the unveiled face. The gospel, which truly portrayed Christ, Bed the soul attitude which wig sincera.

div.head: Bold street Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bold street Wesleyan Church.

" Rest in the Lord, and wait patiently JOE. Him," was the text chosen by the Rev H Williamson, 8.A., at Bold-street on Sunday evening. The words are familiar to all, and fall as it benediction to many a troubled soul; and yet they are w.trds born in tempest and trial. The modern problems that present themselves to mankind are in many respects different from those that erose in the Psalmist's day, but it behoves us still to preserve in the face of them a hopeful patience. This lesson can be learned from the slow corning of sprint, and the myriad years taken in the creation of our planet. Again, in the Jewish hope of the Messianic coming, long delayed, yet accomplished at last, may be rsad the same lesson. Our social evils, so appallingly awful and spch A mockery of our boasted civilization, demand of us the spirit of hopeful patience. Headway seems so little, and workers who have given A life-time to their solution feel that all is vain. and all failure. It takes years to effect a single reform. Yet after the efforts of a century the desi-e of many has arrived. In our religions difficulties, when times of questioning and doubt press heavily, it is useless and impossible to solve the problem by a violent endeavour to believe. The troubled soul must simply wait for the light, and in God's own time the difficulty will be removed. Similarly in dealing with the apparent lack of growth in Christian character, when after years of striving there seems but little result, the same hopeful spirit must prevail, and having fought the good fight of faith, the victory will surpas. all our hopes. In all things cultivate the habit of living in God's bright future, in the blessed happy years that lie ahead. " Rest. in the Lord, wait patiently for Him, and ye shall find rest unto your souls."

div.head: EASTER VESTRY MEETINGS.
div.p: EASTER VESTRY MEETINGS.

A spirit of concord and goodwill has characterised the Easter vestry meetings in connection with the churches of Warrington and district which have been held during the past week. Time was when these gathetings were, in some cases, characterized by lively scenes but now-a-days the meetings are hum-drum and uneventful. Occasion is, of course, taken to review the progress of Church life during the twelve months and the general feeling has been one of satisfaction.

WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH. The authorities of the Warrington Parish Church this year reverted to the c ustom, which has been broken for a few years past, of holding the vestry meeting in the evening, and the result was seen in a much largar attendance than usual at the gathering in the Fairfield .chools on Thursday evening. The Rector (Rev Canon Willis) presided and among those present were : The Revs A J Bratt, T Vickers and J M Buckmaster, Councillor Craik and Mr E Isherwood (wardens), and Mr E A White (vestry clerk).

THE ACCOUNTS. Mr B Isherwood (peopie's warden) presented the accounts, which were particularly gratifying, inasmuch as they showed a credit balance of £l5 133 6d. The ' year began with an adverse balance of £3 14s rid. The total amount received from all sources was £674 5s 9d, which included—collections for Church expenses, £305 3s ld ; collections for special purposes, £277 6s Id ; income from other sources, £9l 163 74. Mr G A Brown moved the adoption of the accounts and coupled with it an expression of thanks Ito Mr Isherwood for his efficient work. .

Councillor S Taylor seconded and expressed satis- faction that they had a substantial credit balance. During his (the speaker's) term of office as warden, it was a struggle to keep the eccounts on the right side, and it was evident that Mr Isherwood had carried out his duties with great zeal. The accounts were passed. ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

The Rector, in again nominating Councillor J G Craik to serve as his warden said he was sure that appointment was as acceptable to the people as to himself. (Hear, hear). Councillor Locker proposed the re-election of Mr Isherwood as people's warden. Few men occupying a position of that kind showed the same amount of zeal and energy as Mr Isherwood, and his term of office would be remembered by several great improvements which he had initiated. Mr W Watson seconded and the proposition, which was supported by Mr W Dennett,was heartily agreed to. Councillor Craik, in returning thanks to the Rector for his appointment, mentioned that this was the seven- teenth time he had been chosen for the office of Rector's warden. During that period he had seen many changes at the old church. When he first took office they were faced with a deficit on the churchwarden's accounts of £323, but they were fortunately able to wipe it off by means of a bazaar and, with very few exceptions, they had been able to keep practically straight from that time onwards. Councillor Craik nominated Councillor Locker as his sidesman and Mr Isherwood nominated Councillor Taylor. Belore the election of sidesmen by the vestry was proaeedz.l with, Mr Brown said the vestry clerk had in the past ruled that sidesmen must be elected at the minuet vestry meeting by show of hands. In the past there had been twelve and thirteen candidates for eight positions, and the method of election was very unsatis- factors, some people having given their votes for the whole ef the candidates. He asked for the vestry clerk's ruling as to whether it would be possible for the sides- men to be elected after the vestry meeting was closed. He did not see that sidesmen had any legal standing in the church. The Vestry Clerk ruled that sidesmen could only be elected at the vestry meeting. The only methods which could be adopted were a show of hands or a ballot but, in the latter event, those who were selected by ballot would afterwards have to be elected in open meeting. Any ratepayer who took exception to the result would be entitled to call for a show of hands. Mr Brown proposed and Mr Holbrook seconded that the vote should be taken by ballot. Mr R T Harding said he did not see why there should be any secrecy. Mr W L Williams: The argument for the ballot is not so much to ensure secrecy as to prevent people voting for more than eight candidates. It was decided to take a ballot and also to increase

the number of sidesmen to ten. Thirteen candidates were nominated and the follow- ing were elected :—Messrs J T Whittle, J Hill, KW Autwiss, K T Harding, GI E Knott, 11 Taylor, E H Coates, T Chidlaw, R Lee and J T Hopkins. Other officers were elected as follows :—Representa- tive sidesruen, St George's Mission Mr Robert Sumner; St Clement's Mission, Mr .1 H Mission, • auditors, Messrs P C Price and J T Whittle ; vestry clerk, Mr E A White ; lay representatives, Messrs T. 3 Hopkins and H Coates.

div.head: RECTOR'S REVIEW.
div.p: THE RECTOR'S REVIEW.

The Rector, atter announcing that the Archdeacon would hold his visitation at the Pasish Church on Wed- nesday, April 16th, referred to several outstand- ing features of the year's work. He said it was the first time for many sears that they had such a large balance as £l5 in band and they had every reason to be grateful. With regard to the repair fund, they had in hand and promised about £6OO, but they would need £7OO for the new vestry Of course, if they could not raise it in any other way, he supposed they would have to allot £l6O out of the proceeds of the next sale of work, so that they would not be in debt. The insurance on the Parish Church and other parochial buildings amounted to £50,000 £30,000 on the church and £20,000 on the schools and missions. The various parochial accounts were in a very satisfactory condition. The Rector expressed his thankfulness for the large attendances at the services during Lent and Eastertide. They bad had the very beat preachers who could be obtained to speak to the congregations of men and women on the Fridays in Lent and he hoped those services would not begin and end in themselves but,

div.head: ST. LUKE'S CHURCH.
div.p: ST. LUKE'S CHURCH.

The Easter vestry meeting was held on Thursday, th Rev H RWild (cutate-in-ch,irge presiding. There weir, also present Messrs Ja-,kson and Oldfleld (wardens), Messrs T Sutcliffe, R Armstrong, Toff, Dean, J Warburton, juts, Taylor and W J Forshaw:(vestry clerk). —The accounts which showed that the year had been a successful one were passed. Messrs Oldfield and Taylor were appointed church wardens and Mr Oldfield was elected treasurer. Mr Oldfield appointed Mr Jacl; son as his sidesman and Mr Dean will act as sidesrnan to Mr Taylor. The other sidesmen are Messrs T Ellison, T Cawley, J Warburton, R Armstrong, A Hewitt, J Mather, C H Massey, Merrington, Warburton and Tomlinson. Messrs H H Ashcroft and Horrabin were appointed auditors. Mr W J Forshaw was reappointed vestry clerk. A vote of thanks was accorded the vestry clerk, wardens,sidesmen, choir and Sunday school teachers. Tie Vicar was also thanked for presiding at that meeting.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.

The annual vestry meeting was held on Thursday evening. There was a very good attendance of the members of the congregation. The Vicar presided. Mr A C Rinks (people's warden) presented the balance sheet for the year, which showed that the collections in the church during the year had amounted to £374 16s and that the expenditure had been £383 12s sd, showing a debit balance of £8 16s sd. Mr Binks explained that this could be accounted for by the exceptional expenses during the year. The Vicar nominated as his warden Mr .1 H Smethurst who, he said, was one of the very best, and the vestry unani- mously appointed Mr A C Binks as their warden. The following sidesmen were appointed :—The ground floor Messrs H Broadhurst, S Bailey, G H Ingram, H Flood, W Cank, H F Greenough, T Locker, S A H Mackey, T Seed, J H J Hampson, H Collin, Frenk -Lindley, 3 Lawton,James Houghton, 3 W Parker, W Hosker, E White, It, G S Finney, G Newburn, S Lawton, 'l' Atherton, T Armstrong, J Hankinson, J Wainwright, W T Flood. Gallery: Messrs H J Clarke W H Thompson, W Woodcock, .1 Hayes, W Behbington, A Bowning, 3 Fern, B Warburton, G Goodwyn. The Vicar thanked his two colleagues for their loyal support during the year, the choir and organist, Sunday school teachers, and all the voluntary workers in the parish, and also those who had joined the free- will offering scheme. During his eleven years' ministry among them, be had been sup- ported by loyal and faithful workers, and they had always worked so harmoniously together, which fact accounted in no small measure for their great success at St Paul's. A vote of thanks to Mr Jeans, the vestry clerk, and to the Vicar for presi4ing, brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: ST. PETER'S CHURCH.
div.p: ST. PETER'S CHURCH.

--•- -- The vestry meeting was held on Wednesday, the Rev J H Garnett presiding. Among those present were Mr T S Steel and Councillor F T Lashford, the retiring wardens. The Chairman said they were all sorry that the vicar (Rev B Percival) could not be with them, but he was going to Torquay the following day, the doctor thinking that the change of air might restore him to health. He knew they all hoped that would be so. Mr Steel then presented the churchwardens' accounts which showed that the year was commenced with a balance in hand of £9 2s 11d. The contribution from the sale of work was £32 ; grant from parochial tea, £7 ; collections during the year for special objects, 18619 s 6d and for church expenses /GS Os 111,d. The expenses included £25 2s 2d for asphalting the church walks and the balance they had to carry forward was £lO 9s 103 d. Th,9 Vicar's Easter offertory came to £9 Os 4d. The accounts were passed. The Chairman ' said the Vicar had great pleasure in re-appointing Ali- Steel as his warden for the ensuing year.— Mr J 3 Hands said that Councillor Lashford had seen fit to resign his position as people's warden and they had now to appoint another in his stead. lie thought it was very unwise and very unjust for certain clergy of the Church of England to attempt to cram down the throats of the people Roman doctrines to which they had not been accustomed and which they did not want. They had to he very careful whom they appointed as people's warden and be had great pleasure in moving that Mr T Reddish fill that office. They would have a good representative in that gentleman. (Hear, hear).— Mr James Taylor seconded and the proposition was carried unanimously.—Mr Reddish briefly replying. Messrs 3 13arnforth and 3 W Kay were appointed lay representatives.—The following were appointed

div.p: WE PUT NO DROPS OR DRUGS IN THE EYES
The Examiner, Saturday, March 29, 1913.

vicars' sidesmen :—Messrs David Armitage, R Knight, J J Hands, J Taylor, Ernest Clayton, .1 W Kay, G .1 McQuillan and T Ince.—Mr Steel thanked the vicar for his confidence in re-appointing him as his warden, For health reasons he had decided to live in the coun- try during the week-ends, and although he might not be able to attend St Peters as regularly as he would like, his interest in the church would be none the less. He appointed Mr Bamtorth to act as his sidesma.n and Mr Reddish appointed Mr E Clayton as his sidesman.—The following were appointed sidesmen by the vestry : Messrs R Bennett, George E Greaves. R Granville, Browe, W Pinson and W Dickens. ST. JOHN'S CHURCH, WALTON. The vestry was held on Easter Monday, the Vicar (the Rev L J T Darwall), presiding. Mr Cooper pre- sented the wardens' accounts which showed total receipts of £lOl 19s 5 1 and total payments of £B6 18s 51, leaving £l5 Is in hand. An increase in both the general and special collections was reported. In addition to these accounts it was explained that Sir Gilbert Greenall had paid certain salaries and bills amounting to £174 is sd. The Vicar re-nominated Sir Gilbert Greeaall, Bart., as his warden, I and Mr John Cooper was unanimously re-elected people's warden. To fill the vacancy caused by the death of Mr Basrett, Mr John Parsons was elected a sidesman. Mr Wm Weir and Mr John Cooper were elected lay delegates to the Diocesan Conference. The various ciiicials were cordally thanked for their services Special mention being made of the efficient work of the organist and choir. A resolution against the Welsh Diseetablishment Bill was unanimously passer]. ST. ANN'S CHURCH. Held under the presidency of the Vicar, the Rev James Davies on Tuesday evening. Messrs 1' H Corbett and T S Jolley (wardens) and 57r G Armstrong (vestry clerk) were among those present. In thanking all those who had helped in the work of the church during the year the Vicar said special thanks were due to those workers in connection with the sale of work, which would be commenced on the following day. They would all agree that during the year they had accomplished a great deal of work from which he hoped beneficial results would accrue. The Vicar then nominated Mr T H Corbett as hiasswpaerodpeine,asndwathrdaetng.enrtrlheemapnropproospiotsioend Mrwas liiiertjil;llceayrried and the following gentlemen were re-elected sidesmen :—Messrs 0 Armstrong, A Brad- shaw, C Brad,havv, II H Bretherton, a Boswell, Hall, J E Harrison, CA Lea, A Owen, G Stringer, F Taylor and W Thomas. Messrs G Armstrong and T S Jolley wore appointed lay representatives. A resolution protesting against the dismemberment of the Cnurch in Wales was proposed by the Vicar, who said it was an injustice and an immoral proceeding to take from religious purposes and apply to secular pur- poses, money, which in days gone by, had been given for God's work. (Hear, hear.) Arising out of the protest lest year they canvassed their district and obtained over 2,500 signatures to the petition, which was sent up to London.—Mr Armstrong intimated that the resolution of the previous year had been acknowledged by Mr Boner Law and the Member.—The resolu- tion was seconded by Mr Corbett, and carried unanimously.—lt was decided to send a copy of the resolution to Mr Asquith, Mr Boner Law, Mr Harold Smith, ALP., and Lord Wolmer.— Cn the proposition of the Vicar a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr Armstrong for his work as vestry clerk. The sale of work they were having was for the purpose of raising funds for the renovation of the church, the introduction of a new communion table and memorial reredos. He felt greatly indebted to Messrs Peter Walker and Sons, and especially to Mr Mercer, who had supervised the erection of the various stalls. Mr Jolley presented the balance sheet, which showed a balance in hand at the beginning of the year £8 us 3ed. Receipts from general offertories were £55 is lid and from special offertories £35 7s sd. The cash in hand, after paying expenses, was 5s Old. ORFORD CHURCH. The annual Easter vestry meeting for the parish of Orford, was held in the Church vestry on Tuesday evening. The Vicar presided over a fair attendance.— The treasurer, Mr C Woods then presented the accounts which showed a falling oti in collections to the extent of about £lO. Collections for church expenses, £5l 4s 7d, compared with £49 4s tid last year; collections for sick and general fund, £9 7e (Id ; for Sunday school, £3 Is 101 ; choir fund, £1 Os 5d • special offertories. £5 13s sd; outside charitable Objects, £l2 les 8d ; '1 making a total of £B3 2s sd, compared with £B3 2s 9d ' the previous year. There was also a loan from a parochial fund, of £4 towards special repairs. The expenditure showed a balance owing to treasurer of £4 10s last year ; general church expenses, £4l ls 7d; sundry repairs, £8 8s ; making a debit balance of £1 15e, but there were accounts due amounting to over £5, which would make the debit balance almost £7. The treasurer made an appeal to the congregation, through the meeting, to try and raise their contribu- tions slightly. The collections averaged about lA per head per service, and if each one increased his or her offertory by a halfpenny per service it, would make a difference of £2O, and a great deal could be done with that amount. The accounts were passed on the proposition of Mr G Simcock, seconded by Mr Brown- bill. The Vicar again nominated Mr J Swinton, sen., as his warden. They had always worked together very well, and he did not think he could choose a better. Mr C Woods was re-elected people's warden on the proposition of Mr J Swinton, seconded by Mr H Williams. There were eleven nominations for sides- men, the following being declared electei :—Messrs Monks, L Cross, .1 Povey, E Brownbill, W Povey and R G Brandreth. Messrs L Cross and W H Houghton were re-elected rureedecanal representatives for the ensuing year. Messrs F White and G Simcock were elected auditors. A resolution was proposed by Mr J Swinton, seconded by Mr L Cross, and carried, welcoming Lord Ronaldshay's Bill to relieve Easter offerings of income tax. A resolution was proposed by Sir Brownbill and seconded by Mr eV Povey pledging themselves to fight against the disestablishment of the church in Wales.—The Vicar made a short speech in which he thanhed all the workers who had backed him up so splendidly all through the year. He also made reference to the Vicarage fund. He said he hati promised to have £lOO collected by the end of the month and he was glad to say that this would be accompli shed, and then they would have to start to raise the last £lOO. ST. THOMAS', STOCKTON HEATH. A SUGGESTED INNOVATION WHICH MIGHT GIVE OFFENCE. The vestry meeting in connection with St. Thomas' Church, Stockton Heath, was held-at noon, on Tuesday, the Vicar (Rev James Collins), presiding over a fair attendance. The statement of accounts showed that the year began with a balance in hand of £8 188 91 and closed with a balance due to the wardens of I:4 17s 4d. The general offertories (including harvest festivals) amounted to £212 Is 3d, as against £230 17s Id list year, but it was pointed out that there were fewer Sundays in the period under review. The clergy's ehare of the offertories was £lO7 12s 6d. Special offertories amounted to £6l 19s 3d, as against £BO 78.— The balance sheet was adopted on the proposition of Mr F Rose, seconded by Mr A .1 Willett.—The Vicar again nominated Mr Henry Greenall as his warden.—Mr F Pearson proposed the re-election of Mr T J Lee as people's warden, observing that his services in that capacity for several years were a guarantee that he would successfully dischirge the duties in the future. They all appreciated the hard work he had done for the Church.—The proposition was agreed to.—The following sidemen were elected : Messrs Arthur Down, T R Westbrook, W Richardson, W Mclntyre, A Melbourne, A J Willett, el II Brady, A Worrell, T Jackson, J Swinton, S McDowell, J Richard- son, jun , F Pearson, A Broady, F Gandy and F Warburtou.—Messrs F' Pearson and W Mclntyre were elected lay representatives. The Vicar pointed out that the question of Church finance had been under considerntieu and the Rural Dean would, as soon as possible, cell a meeting of church- wardens and lay representatives to discuss it. Mr Pearson said the scheme which had been suggested would, he believe, act very well in the diocese The Vicar said it was practically the freewill offering scheme on a large scale. In proposing a vote of thanks to the church cfficers, organist and choir and other workers, the Vicar expressed his gratification at the interest which was being taken in the free-will offering scheme. There were already 293 subscribers, which was exceedingly good, considering that the scheme was started only a few months ago. Mr Greenall seconded and the vote was heartily passed. Mr Jackson suggested that the church furniture should be completed by the introduction of a Litany desk. lhe Vicar said some people might regard such an innovation its a piece of priestly ritual. 111 r Rose said he had heard the Litany desk mentioned as a likely bone of contention. Mr Jackson : I. is very unfortunate. Mr Rose : 1. think it is the proper thing. Mr Greenall also expressed approval of the provision of a Litany desk. The Vicar said he would not like to adopt anything that would send one person away Irons Chu' ch. Some people were very touchy. Mr Pearson said the suggestion required careful con- sideration, as it would be a drastic alteration for that parish. The matter dropped without any definite proposition being brought forward.

A suggestion that the church officers should remain standing at the altar rails during the presentation of the alms appeared to meet with the approval of the meet- ing, but it was thought offence might be given in some quarters, Mr Rose remarking that anything new seemed to give offence in Stockton Heath. The change will, however, probably be tried as an experiment. CHRIST CHURCH, CROFT. The Rector (Rev H I Wadeson) presided at the' vestry meeting on Monday. The wardens' accourit6. showed the receipts to have been £69 9s sd. and the , expenditure £62 16a. Mr Joshua Ball was re-elected 85- Rector's warden, Mr P Ingham parishioners' warden, and Messrs W Priestner, S H Sankey and J EigbY. sidesmen. _

div.head: ST WILFRID'S GRAPPENHALL.
div.p: ST WILFRID'S GRAPPENHALL.

The vestry meeting was held on Tuesday, the Rector,. (the Rev H V Pigot) presiding. The churchwardens accounts, showing a credit balance of .C 7 3s. 3d. were passed. The Rector nominated Mr Henry Standish Leyland as churchwarden, and the vestry elected Mr Oswal,4 Lofthouse as the other churchwarden. Tile Rector nominated Mr Reginald W,Wilde as sidesrnanr and the vestry elected Messrs .1 E Ashcroft, T Brierley, W W Diminolow, A Evans, J Leigh, W Lomas, H N Morrey, II 1' Nicholls, W Peacock, N Smith, H A Thompson, J Williams, and W Winstanley as the other sidesmen. Mr 0 Lofthouse and Mr A Evans wers elected lay representatives for diocesan and ruridecanak conferences. A vote of thanks was given to Mr Arthur Down for his services as organist on Sunday aftern, ons and on many other occasions. The Rector rdporuct that the church had been supplied with 114 Prsyer Books and 132 hymn books for the use of the congrega" don, the cost 13 4s. being defrayed from the protit9 from the parochial tea party. HOLY TRINITY CHURCH. THIRTY-FOUR YEARS AS VICAR.

The remarkably early date of Easter this year was the subject of comment at the Easter vestry rueeting in connection with Holy Trinity Church which was held on Tuesday evening under the presidency of the Vicar (Rev E C E Carleton).—Mr W Gill (Vicar's warden) presented the accounts, which allowed that the year war commenced with a balance in hand of £1 9s ltd. Tbe special offertories were £B9 8s 10d, or 9s Id less than last year ; the general offertories £169 6s 7d, against £167 15s ld last year ; offertories for the poor,. £lB 5s Id against £l4 19s 2d last year ;and amount from all sources £266 13s 2d, as ncainst £984 16s 8d last, year. After paying accoun' s and putting £25 to the Curscy Fund and £2O to the Renovation Fund, there was a balance in hand of 18s ila- The wardens thought that statement was yell satisfactory whea they took in consideration the great number of wet Sundays, and, as they were aware, Easter was very early this year. It was 57 years since it was EO early, and would be many years before ib would be on the same date again. The earliest possible ' date for Easter Sunday was March 22ed, and if hie information was correct, it was only on four occasion that it had fallen on that date during the last four hundred years and would not occur again until the year 2286. No churchwardeu4 for generations to come would see an earlier. Easter Sunday than this year. The accounts; having been passed, the officers were appointed aa follows :—Vicar's warden, Mr W Gill ; people's warde2 Mr John Hesketh ; sidesmen, Messrs J Hignett, Welsby, James Haraing, James Bowcock, E Dyke, \S'll,3 Gandy. H Ferguson, G Gill, Joseph Hesketh, T Hun" H Milling, J Pickles, E Rose, Abe Walsh, T Emmett. L R Rowson, W W Leigh, W D Jeans, 'rhos Domville, H Turner, F Taylor and T D Amoa. lay representatives Messrs W D Jeans, jun., sad ,r) Rose ; vestry clerk, Mr Geo F F White ; auditor, 'Mr H W Naylor. The choir and church workers haviel been thanked, Mr John Hesketh, in proposing a vote 0 thanks to the Chairman, said that Mr Carleton was the best chairman in England. (Hear, hear.) Mr T Welsby seconded, and said it was a pleasure t°:.6 them all to know that Mr Carleton's health contiutlev good. (Hear, bear.) The motion was heartily agreed to. The Vicar, in reply, said he had now been vicar ' the parish for 31 years. He had bad a very happy tiol in Warrington, thanks to the loyal support he receivr: from the wardens, sidesmen and all connected with tu_v church. They had, of course, their small trials freiT time to time, but they bad pulled through very we a The year had been an eventful one in many ways, a% be did not think he ought to allow that occasion to p.% asi.tbout meetioeiog the ireirrt.nt development syn. had taken place in the opening of the Patten Hall (t ; gift of the Hon. Misses Wilson-Patten), which o.ac.; likely to be of great service to the parish in varieti' ways. (Hear, hear.)

Warrington v. Coventry. The return match between Warrington and Coventry was played at Warrington on Saturday, in a deluge of rain. Accurate football was out of the question arid the referee very properly stopped the game after GO minutes had been played. Only about 1,000 spectators put in an appearance, the receipts being £lB, as com- pared with £l9O the day before. Teams : Warrington: Jolley.back ; Brookes, Tranter, Renwick and Bradshaw, three-quarter backs ' • Dainteth and Nicholas, half-backs ; G Thomas, Naylor, Cheaters, Skelhorn, R Thomas and Cox, forwards. Coventry : Parkinson, back; Littlewood, Battersby, Phil Thomas and Young, threequarter backs ; Ruddick and Carter, half backs; Warwick, Bro Nn, Steel,Wright, Tomes and Naylor, forwards. Referee, R H Jackson, St Helens. The ground was a quagmire right from the start. Warrington were early aggressive, but combination was almost impossible and the Coventry men defended pluckily. The half was well advanced before a score accrued, and then Jclley put in a long dribble which led up to Brookes scoring. Renwick added the goal. Turning round, Coventry again showed up pluckily, the backs handling the ball better than the Wirepullers. Eventually Bradshaw broke away and beat the Coventry defence. The visitors rallied, aud Bradshaw failing to I kick dead, Warwick scored. Result :—Warrington, 11 goal 2 tries (8 points) ; Coventry, 1 try (3 points).

Warrington.—Jolley, back ; Waywell, Renwick, Tranter and Jordan, threequarter-backs ; Brooks and Nicholas, half-backs; G Thomas, R Thomas, Skelhorne, Cheaters, Cox and Arnold, forwards. Referee, C Platt, Swinton. Touch judges, J R Lawton, Oldbara, and E J Hannaford, St Helens. The Hornets had the advantage in the opening stages of the game and Paddon opened the scoring with a good penalty goal. Then Jones made a flee break-away run to the full back and passed inside for Woods to romp over. Padden failed at the goal kick. The Hornets continued to press, and Dearden was only pulled down a few yards short of the line from a pass by Jones. Before the interval Paddon kicked another grand penalty goal, the ball striking the crossbar before going over. Renwick and G Thomas missed easy penalty kicks for Warrington, and at half-time the Hornets led by seven points to nothing. Soon after the resumption Jones started another fine passing movement, which Carter completed by racing over with a good try. Paddon converted. From a cross kick by Renwick, Jordan secured and scored at the corner, Renwick failing at goal. Jones and Prudence were carried off hurt, and right on time Renwick scored again for Warrington, after a good round of passing. G Thomas failed at the goal kick. Result : Rochdale Hornets, 3 goals, 2 tries (12 points) ; Warrington, 2 tries (6 points).

WARRINGTON "A " V WIGAN ITIGHFIELD.—The Warrington " A "team was well represented at Wigan on Saturday, but quite failed to hold the Highfield team who won byl2 goals, 3 tries (13 points) to nil, and thus avenged the heavy defeat sustained at Warrington earlier in the season. WARRINGTON " A " V ROCHDALE "A."—Played at Warrington on Monday before a good attendance. The home team was short of Jordan, Waywell, and Dicken- son, but this was no excuse for the poor display given. Th-, forwards were very weak, and the backs seemed to have no ides. of combination. Rochdale showed got:d form and after gaining a lead of 2 points in the first half, they added 8 points in the second, and won 10-0.

MANCHESTER AND DISTRICT LEAGUE. RYLANDS' RECS. V EGERTON. For this match on Good Friday the Rylands' men travelled to Manchester, the home 103 m failing to put in an appearance. Rylands claimed the match.

RYLAND'S' RECS. V BARTON. , This return match was played at Barton in a perfect deluge of rain on Saturday, Rylands winning the toss and electing to play with the wind. The winning of this match, which had a bearing on the championship, made both sides play very keen, the rushing and kick- ing tactics of the Barton team spoiling the game. From a charge down Stretford scored a good try for the Recs.,Leah failing at goal. Half-time: Ry lands', 1 try ; Barton, nil. _

The second half saw a battle royal between both seta of forwards, both sides attacking in turn. A pass by Stretford to Carter saw that player romp under the posts for a try, which Morris failed to convert. The game now was very rough, one of the Barton players being given marching orders. Rylandi from now defended their charge well, Bramhall being at the top of his form. Rylands won by two tries (6 points) to Barton nil.

div.head: SHUNTING FATALITY.
div.p: SHUNTING FATALITY.

A fatal accident at the St. Helens Goods Station was investigated by Mr FA Jones,on TuesrLy when an inquest was held on the bony of Samuel Mainwaring, b 2, of 96, Lingholme-read, an assistant foreman.—Oswald Travis, a shunter, said that on Thursday, March 13, a goods train was being marshalled, and two of the waggons being shunted stopped short. The deceased went to the waggons and began to unfasten the tarpaulin sheets. The witney, who was about fifty yards away, saw Main- waring hopping away from the waggons, ana he waved his hand to witsess. When he got to him he was seated on a box, and had pulled his right bo,t off, showing that his toes had been crushed.—John Middleburst, the chief foreman, said the assistant told him he was untying sheet strings, and was stanoing with one foot in the six-foot, and one loot in the folr-foot, when another waggon came down iho shunt and struck him on the shoulder. He was knocked down and both wheels passed over his right foot.—The Coroner: He should not have been standing in that position ?—Witness I think it has been a little bit of absent-mindeduess.—Tne jury said that death was accidental.
SHOCKING ST HELENS CASE. COLLIER AND WOMAN sENr TO PRISON.

At St Helens, on Tuesday, John Miles, collier' and Sarah Davis, of 13, Liverpool-street, were charged with cruelty to two children. Mr Garner prosecuted. He said tbat the circum- stances of the case were very revolting. Miles was a married man, with a wife and family living near Wrexham, but for nearly three years he had been living with Davis, who was a single woman with two children, of whom Miles admitted he was the father. Mr Garner alleged that in a room eight feet by eight feet and seven feet high eight people frequently lived, and slept on a. filthy bed and in a poisonous atmosphere. Davis said that there were never more that Biz persons living in this room. Acting-sergeant Adams and Constable Smith said that the room was used as a boozing den. Dr Doran said that the child of two and a half years old was a stone under weight, and, like the seven- months-old child, bad been badly neglected. Both prisoners were sent to gaol for six months.

There are 'certain women who want to drive away the one man who has stood by them," said Mr. Keir Hardie as he faced, on Sunday, the hubbub caused by the militants. The remark was quite true. No one has been more resolute than Mr. Hardie in defence of the extreme gang. He has gone to great lengths for them. Probably he is not sur- prised to find that the moment he does any- thing of which they disapprove they turn on him with marvellous vehemence. That is always the way in which fanatics treat their war nest friends. The trouble of the militants, as Mr. Hardie confessed in a a candid moment, is that they have not the women of the nation behind them.

* " Last Saturday about twenty climbers of .rsthe Rucksack Club reached the summit of -116 en Nevis, where they encountered some- what severe climatic conditions. Snow lay to a depth of about fifteen feet, both the ,observatory and hotel being entirely covered. The surface was hard and the going fairly easy, but the faces were too highly ice-glazed to permit of the more prominent climbs being undertaken. The temperature varied from 15deg. to 20deg., and the strong wind which Prevailed whirled the fine, powdery snow in Freat crowds high over the summit. Very ittle Climbing could be accomplished on the tower and castle ridges, and it was found out of the question to venture at all on to the north-east buttress, which was one mass of snow and ice. This is the first occasion on which an English mountaineering club has l'isited Ben Nevis man official capacity.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, MARCH 29, 1913.
The fall of Adrianople, STOP THE WAR. no less than the intima-

tion of the Powers that the time has come when in their view hostilities should cease, brings the end of the great Balkan war at last within measur- able distance. Of the fall of the great Turkish fortress, at the close of the most remarkable defence in the whole story of the campaign, there is little to be said. It is as well that it has fallen into the hands of Bulgaria before the day for settlement came. It will make Turkey's task in accepting the terms which she has been offered as the basis of peace all the easier, and it satisfies the determinatiozi ef the Allies to prove the !completeness of their victory by a last dramatic triumph. The brave defenders of the fortress have the world's admiration. They withstood the ceaseless attacks of their overwhelming enemies to the last possible minute, and gave up only at the very end having provided, one feature of the war which will stand out" gloriously from the back- ground of disaster and retreat in which the story of Turkey's adventure is written. But with Adrianople down, and insistence upon an end of hostilities in the new autonomous Albania by the Powers, there is no reason why there should be any further bloodshed.

The words of Sir EDWARD GREY in the House of Commons on Tuesday were very plain. Their meaning canot be mistaken, nor can their demand be ignored, for the 3RITISH FOREIGN SECRETARY spoke not merely for a united House of Commons, with the full authority of a united British people, but for the,Powers of Europe. Convinced that nothing is to be gained by further conflict,•that more bloodshed would, indeed, be simply useless, purposeless, and criminal folly, the great Powers are determined to stop the war. That is, in a nutshell, the meaning of Sir EDWARD GREY'S important statement in the House of Commons, welcomed by the LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION, and endorsed by the PRIME MINISTER. With the settlement of the main frontiers of the new autonomous Albania the greatest point of danger in the negotia- tions of the Power has been passed, and a plain warning that any disputihg of the Powers' decision on this point will be ' met with the pressure of the Concert of Europe will ensure the cessation of hostilities within Albania without delay. Nor is there any reason why the high hopes entertained that the war will stop altogether, on the basis of peace suggested by the Powers, should not be realised. Adrianople having fallen there is nothing more to be accomplished by force of arms. If there were, and KING FERDINA.ND marched into Constantinople at the head of

the remnants of the brave armies of the. Allies, nothing would be gained. Such a dramatic develepment would but mean the ' kindling of 'a new fire which it would be almost impossible to prevent spreading through Europe. That, of course, is not to be thought of There is only one thing, to be done now. Common sense and humanity both demand it. The war must end without further delay on the terms suggested by the Powers, both sides being assured that in the settlement of outstanding points there will be absolute equity and impartiality. In some quarters) there seems to be a sense of grievance over the limits which the Powers seek to put to the spoils of victory which the allies are to be allowed to claim. Here and there the conditions suggested may be open to some such objection; but on broad issues there is very little less in the suggested basis of peace than Bulgaria and her Allies claimed. And, after all, it is futile at this hour to commence haggling over trifles. The Powers have shown in their whole dealing with the crisis the most remarkable moderation, and in several cases a self- sacrifice which the world had scarcely the right to demand. They had the right at this juncture to take a hand in 'clearing up the battlefields. Their desire is unanimous, and it must be obeyed. By resisting their wishes Turkey or the Allies will but court disaster. The whole future depends upon their retention of the world's goodwill. For ourselves, we are content to echo the courageous words of the PRIME MINISTER. He spoke for all of us. It is the considered judgment of this country that the time has come when this terrible war, with all its catastrophe and devastation and waste, should come to an end.

Colonel Seely announced PROFESSIONAL last week a scheme SOLDIERS. which will open to the private, access to pro- motion to commissioned rank which had been closed by the impossibility of a subaltern's living on his pay. Sir Henry Craik on Monday congratulated the Secretary for War on having for the first time in the history of the War Office made an attempt ,to put the pay of army officers on a footing which would make the Army a career for the pro- fessional soldier instead of an appanage of the idle rich. Colonel Seely had also given an agreeable surprise to all but those opponents who are disappointed when they find that the Government is not letting " the Service go to the dogs" by proving that the War Office has made much more progress with the development of military aviation. On Monday he amplified his statement, and pointed out that by May 21st we shall have 148 aeroplanes, of which at least 130 will come up to the necessary standard of efficiency laid down.

The nation's drink bill THE NATIONAL is declining, notwith- DIUNIC BILL, standing the abounding prosperity of the country. This is the gratifying fact gathered from a letter published in "The Times" of last Saturday from Mr. George B. Wilson, 8.A., secretary of the United King- dom Alliance. He says : I estimate the total expenditure of the Un-ited kingdom on alcoholic liquors during 1912 at ...,161,553 330, as compared with £162.797,229' in 1911, being a decrease of £1,243,899. Spirits show a decrease of £252,858 on an apparently decreased consumption of 160,545 gallons, and beer a decrease of .11,000,368, on a decrease of 333,456 standard barrels. Wine, on the other hand, shows a slight increase of £9,327 on an increased consumption of 10,368 gallons. It mast, however, be borne in mind that the conditions under which the wine and spirit trades have been cirried on during the past three years have not been normal. The spirit trade has been dislocated by the increase of the spirit duty, and there have been considerable with- drawals from duty-paid stocks of wine. It is, therefore, probable that the decrease in spirits is apparent rather than real, and the increase in the consumption of wine recorded here less than the actual increase. The decline in beer consumption is, however, actual. In 1912 the average expendi- ture per head was £3 10s. 9d., and per family of five :,17 13s. 10d., as compared with £3 us. 10d.1 per head and £l7 -19 s 3d. per family in 1911. These figures include both children and abstainers, and do not, therefore, lindicate what is spent by the adult population which consumes intoxicants.

The Final Report of the THE CENSUS OF First Census of Produc- PRODUCTION. tion of the United Kingdom (1907) pro- vides a great deal of useful information con- cerning the broad facts of the manufacturing industries of the country. It is true that some of its findings are limited by certain qualifications, such as were only to be expected in summarising a work of such magnitude, carried out as it has been for the first time and with somewhat limited powers of collecting information. Among the broad facts which emerge are the following (1) The total amount of the various British industries covered by the enquiry was in 1907 about 1,240 millions, which does not include the output of agriculture and fisheries (210 millions and 12 millions respectively) (2) The exports of the United Kingdom in 1907 amounted in value to about one-third of its total output. (3) he net imports of the "finished produce of industry" into this country in 1907 were only 7 per cent. of the United Kingdom output of similar goods. (4) The total cost to consumers of goods con- sumed in this country in 1907 was about 1,750 millions. (5) The total income of the United Kingdom in 1907 was "between 1,918 millions and 2,158 The revelation of the proportion that the imports of finished products of industry bear to our total output is one that Tariff I Reformers will find especially arresting.

The election of a Tory A DOUBLE-FACED candidate who has been MILESTONE? repudiated by the Tory Headquarters, and who stood as a Free Trader, has produced a strange clash of views in the Opposition Press as to what the Tory policy really is to-day. A correspondent of the" Spectator" whose standpoint receives the editorial approval, has taken up a ground on which Colonel Weston would be an ideal candidate. The " Spectator " endorses this representation of the official Tory programme : " The Free Trader is not asked to commit him- self to Tariff Reform; the Tariff Reformer is not asked to subscribe to Free Trade. The issues at the next election will be the simplest that have ever been known in modern days. The Unionist leader asks solely for support in his struggle against Home Rule, Welsh Disestablishment, the wreck of the Constitution, and the scandalous neglect of the Government to provide for our national security. On the other hand, the "Times " sees things at quite a different angle. The Free Tiader is to be asked to commit himself to Tariff Reform as far as a tax on manufactures is concerned, and the Tariff Reformer is to be
aNEK

asked—for the next General Election only-- to subscribe to Free Trade, as far as repudiation of food-taxes is concerned : t " While food-taxes are not to be an issne.s_ the next General Election, I eing for that &one: dropped, the rest of the tariff policy is the par% policy, and n attempt to treat this as an le question will be recognised in future contests. h 8 After Mr. Bonar Law's "milestones," t plain man is almost tempted to sigh for gr' Balfour's " half-sheet of note paper."

In addition one postal order and one cheque were give' This return does not represent the whole oui the offerings, no record having been kept 0" the amount received at the early celebry tions. Fire at a Firewood Factory. • At noon on Wednesday an outbreak, of fire occured at the fit ewood factory of Mr Rigby, Brackley-street, off Howley-lane, owing to the boiling over of some pitch. The flames spread. very rapidly and in a short time the whole place was involved, the adjoining house and stable property also being in danger. A telephone message was sent to the fire station and in the meantime the Firth 'Mattress Company's fire brigade got a line of hose at work and succceeded in keeping the flames in check until the arrival of the Borough brigade, in charge of the deputy- superintendent, Mr Frank Turner, junior. In half an hour the flames were extinguished, but not before considerable damage (which is not covered by insurance) had been done to the factory. The adjoin- ing property was saved. Any ladies wishing to see copies of the simple cooking recipes are requested to write to the Health Depariment in Sankey-street, Dr J Coote Hibbert or Mr W J Rowland, hon. secretaries of the Health Week Celebration Committee. The recipes, which will shortly be printed, are intended specially for circula- tion among working women in homes where economy is essential to physical welfare.—The Officer has again promised to give a public lecture on the evening of Tnursday, 10th kpril. Motor Accident. A Bank Holiday motor accident is reported from Chester. Miss Dora Whip, of Parkgate-road, Chester, ITas riding her bicycle from Black Diamond-street into Brook-street at 11.10 a,m. on Monday. The constable at that point put up his hand to stop her. , Meanwhile a motor car belonging to Mr Caldwell, of Lower Walton, Warrington, and driven by Mr. George Davies, of 110, Ellesmere-road, Stockton Heath, came along from the direction of Hoole, and caught the back wheel of Miss Whip's bicycle and knocked her over. Thomas Cooper, of 86, Trafford-street, Chester, and P.C. Owen picked her up, and the girl, who was dazed, bad a cut at the back of her bead. Her hand, also, was bruised.

A Warrington athlete scored a success in the Lancashire Walking Clubs' handicap which was decided on Monday, the distance being seven miles along the high road. The start took place from the c!ub's headquarters, Sherwood Hotel, Fallowfield, the route being through Withington and Didsbury to a point near Cheadle Railway Bridge, and thence hack over the same course, the tini-h being at Fallowfield Station. It was originally intended to return by Parr's Wood, Burnage, and finish down Balmoral-road, and five of the competitors made the mistake of taking this Course. There were 21 entries, of whom 14 com- peted. The handicap was framed from R Bridge, the amateur champion, and the limit ran out to 26 minutes. The virtual scratch man was J T Mulhall,of Warrington, with an allowance of smin 45 sec. The last-named eventually won somewhat easily, walking in brilliant style. Royal Theatre of Varieties.

By hpecial arrangement with Mr Montague Beaudyn, Mr Manville Morton, the energetic manager of the Royal Theatre of Varieties, secured the great Russian drama "The beantiful fiend " for the week ending to-day. The story is a thrilling one and each incident is well enacted by the Royal Stock Company. There is a pleasing element of comedy which tends to relieve to an appreciable extent the heavier aspects of the piece. The audience were delighted with the acting of the following artistes who are so popular with the Scotland-road house patrons Mr Val Vousden, Mr Mr C Vivian Charles, Mr Ed win McKenzie, Mr C E Warne, Miss Elsie Giddings, and Miss Hazel Head Miss . Phyllis Morton who successfully solicits the sympathy of the audience in the role of Nadini Strogoff, the heiress, and Mr Clvaering Craig, who is a capital Fedor Karateff, hre welootne additions to the Company. - For next week the Royal Stock Company will play in the great drama "Women of London."

Warrington Philomathic Society. On Wednesday evening last, Dr Hodgkinson was to have lectured to the members of the Warrington Philomathic Society and their friends on" The North American Aborigines," but unfortunate circumstances prevented him from being present. At the eleventh hour, Mr Fledley H Taylor, L.D S., readily undertook to fill the doctor's place by giving a lecture on "The life-history of a planet." Mr Taylor was a very acceptable substitute. His lecture, which was illustrated with an interesting series of lantern slides, traversed the career of the planet on which we live, from its gaseous birth to its present-day maturity, and offered some subtle hints as to its future. Mr Taylor showed that, when the earth was in a molten, liquid state, the moon was thrown off ; that its liquid state was followed by a process of hardening, the earth's crust thickening as the ages moved slowly by. He went on to speak of the theories concerning the earth's past which had resulted from geological observation, and dealt especially with those regarding the gradual appearance on our planet of vegetable and animal life, and ultimately of man. An interesting feature of the lecture was a comparison drawn by Mr Taylor, between the order of creation as expounded in modern scientific teaching and that set forth in Holy Scripture Incidentally he dealt with the movements of the planets, the evolution of nebulae, the action of volcanoes, and the vagaries and composition of comets. From amongst acknowledged theories regarding his subject, the lecturer merely presented those which to him appeared the most reasonable. A brief discussion ensued, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr and Mrs Taylor' the latter having very adeptly manipulated the lantern. There was a good attendance.

Crosflelds' Band Successes. Crosfields' Band opened its contesting season I with two first prizes on Monday last. heaving Bank Quay Station 11 30 Sunday night the members travelled 330 miles, played in competitions at Mountain Ash and Abergavenny, 24 miles apart and arrived back in Warrington 9 p.m. Monday, being exactly 211 hours away from borne. The band has been rehearsing continuously for these two competitions and every effort as put forward to win if possible. At Mountain Ash twelve bands ccmpeted and Mr Angus Holden(the judge)awarded Crosfitilds' the premier prize away then to Abergavenny, which place was reached at about 3.20 p.m. Time would not allow even a few minutes rehearsal. The band must do its level best without, Foden's Band could be heard rehearsing, but they had time at their disposal, only being drawn No 4in the competition, and could reach home by, a later train. Crosfields played No. 1 and gave a magnificent rendering of Wagner's " Lohengrin " being awarded first prize, the second place falling to Foden's Band. The successes augur well for the coming season, the band certainiy being in very fine trim. Engagements are being hooked up, but the dates of all the principal contests are being kept open to enable the band to attend.

div.head: GROUP OF COMMITTEE MEN,
div.p: A GROUP OF COMMITTEE MEN,

The Warrington Branch of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants held a successful social in Friars' Green schoolroom on Good Friday Railwaymen generally make a special point on Good Friday of promoting an effort to augment the funds of the Widows and Orphans, and this year was no exception to the rule. The tea tables were beautifully decorated with flowers &c, and •poke well for those of the committee who had the arrangements in hand. Over 450 sat down to tea, which was followed by a concert. Alderman James Evans presided and was supported by several of the committee. The Chairman at this interval .aid he was pleasA to he there mt such a gathering and for such a worthy cause. He gave his blessing to the railwaymen of Warringt in in taking such an interest for the benefit of those who were deprived of their breadwinner. The pro.zramote was a good ope and the artistes included some of the best local talent, who gave excellent satisfaction. The arrangements were in the hands of a capable committee consisting of the railway men and their wives.

div.head: CHURCH LADS' BRIGADE EASTER MANCEU-VRES AT STRETTON.
div.p: CHURCH LADS' BRIGADE EASTER MANCEU-VRES AT STRETTON.

The Easter holiday is always turned to good account by the memb-rs of the Church Lads' Brigade and on Monday last the members cf the 2ed (Liverpool) Cadet Battalion engaged in interesting marneuvres at Stretton. The fine weather enabled the plan of opera- tions to be successfully carried out in every detail, and the lads entered into the work with the utmost zest. Lieut-Col. Appleton, C.L B , assisted by his Adjutant (Captain Sankey) had um& excellent arrangements to test the general capabilities and smartness of the battalion.

--Cheshire was supposed to have declared war on Lancashire, and the cadets were concerned in the mobilisation of the Lancashire force at Appleton Park. A small advanced and left flank guard, under the command.fof Alajor Brooks, left %Warrington at nine a.m. to protect the march of Colonel X's advance force to Appleton Hall Park. Tbis force consisted of A, B and C Companies of the C.L.B. Cadets, and marched via Latchford, Lumb Brook, Appleton Diugle, Appleton Cross, on Mosswood Farm, where it. took up an outpost position, covering Colonel X's force bivouacking at , Appleton Hall. Major Brooks's force was covered by the Battalion Scouts, under Cadet-Corporal Hawthorne, and the cyclists, under Sergeant-Major Bottomley, who took the place of the independent Cavalry, and Christ Church Company, under Lieutenent Younger. The advanced guard cyclists and scouts aid their work very well, and tha communication kept up and the information sent back by the Scouts-cyclists and signallers was most creditable. The scouts had been trained by Lieutenant Seymour-Jones, 4th &Rita Lancashire Regiment, and their work spoke volumes for the careful way in which they had been trained. On arrival at Mosswood Hall Farm the Cadets were formed into No 2 Outpost Company, under Captain Henshall, with a front of about a mile, reaching from the east of Stretton Church to Appleton Cross, No 1 Company being on their right and No 3 on the left. All that wits knoAn of the Cneshires was that some of their advanced troops were reported in Northwich early on Easter Monday morning. Captaiii Henshall's outpost position commanded the probable line of approach of the enemy over Stretton Moss very well. A small section of a trench had been dug by two scouts in pouring rain on Saturday, and the position of the other fire trenches was shown by lines of red cloth on st!cks. A range chart of distances of •ohjects in view was placed in the trenches. captain 'lllenshall watched his front with three sentry groups and a standing cyclist guard. His picket was at Moss- wood Hall Farm, und.-r Captain Younger, and his support in the Brickfields in rear of the farm. Tne Artillery were in a position n-ar Hill Warren and the dressing station at Cann-lane Farm, with a collecting !atation in rear of the farm, where "casualties" were .40t1vt.3Pd in the wheeled errinulance and given first-aid. Major Green (commanding the troops at Warrington) came out on his horse in uniform at three o'clock, and was conducted round the outpost line by Cap Lain E'ankey. t h•-• adjutant. ,The enemy,- milich consisted of a few Territorial 'cNclists under Cap; ain Monks, at tacked the outpost line shortly after three o'clock, driving in the sentry groups who retired on the picket. The support then came tip and the picket lined the trenches. Operations ceased , at 3.50.

When the Cadets had fallen in et the farm, Major Green made a careful inspection of them and told them how pleased he was to finJ that they were learning bow to defend their country. It was quite possible that before long they might be wanted to do in earnest .41iat they were doing that day as a practice. He had been a soldier for 22 years. He had never regretted joining the Army, and he had always endeavoured to put the welfare of his country before everything else. fie trusted that the hatallion he saw before him would also always endeavour to do so. He would welcome any of them in the S alth Lancashire Regiment if they decided to adopt the career of a soldier, which he thought writi an excellent one,

Colonel B Fairclough (commanding the 4th Baqalion Prince of Wales's Volunteers) South Lancashire Regiment, paid a short visit to Stretton and watched the proceedings with great interest The Rev and Hon C F Cross vicar of Stretton, welcomed the lads to the village, and expressed the pleasure it had afforded him to see them act in such a gentlemanly manner. Mr Jacob Sankey, and his family, placed his farm and indeed, his house, at the disposal of the battalion, and it was almost entirely owing to his great kindness that the Cadets were able to spend such is pleasant and instructive day. Lieutenant F Bunch'and his staff were responsible for the provision of food and great credit is due to them tor the expeditious and skilful manner in which the work t. as done.
The battalion returned home at about 9 p.m., headed by St Paul's Bugle Band.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. ---- " The Man Tempted Me."
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. ---- " The Man Tempted Me."

This melodrama, which is sufficiently explained by its title, abounds in ultra-sensational incidents, the chief being the ingenious. methods of torture adopted to extort a confession from the heroine while wrong- fully immured in an asylum. The story is a curious compound of villainy, tragedy and broad humour, but it seems to appeal strongly to the popular parts of the house. Mr. James Usstier's company gives an effective representation, Miss Fay Garnet-Tayne being chief favourite as Lillian Wynter, the much•wronged heiress. Mr. Jesse Ablett also acts convincingly as the muscular p trson, while Mr. Juan D'Alberte, as his unscrupulous rival, Mark Wylde, succeeds in making the part sufficiently repellent. Mr Aubrey Norton and Mr F Marriott-Watson also do well iu the unpalatable roles of the shady lawyer and the German Jew respectively. Miss Hilda Gower supplies much or the humour as a London slavey and Miss Florence E Florence gives a sparkling performance as "La Jolie Diable."

div.head: "QUAKER GIRL" NEXT WEEK,
div.p: THE "QUAKER GIRL" NEXT WEEK,

It will be welcome news to Warrington theatre- goers that "The Quaker Girl" is corning to Warring ton again. She is due at the Royal Court Theatre next week. The company is Mr George Dance's and as usual with his shows the piece will be gorgeously dressed and beautifully staged,xvhile the company, it goes without sa3iog, will be a strong one. The play is bright and amusing; there are pretty and fascinating dances introduced at the most opportune moment. So far as the musical portion is concerned, there is a fascinating waltz song, end among other pleasing numbers are the duet, " The bad boy and the good girl," the songs " A Quaker Girl." "Just as father used to do," " Corue to the ball," " Take a step," and a concerted piece "tip-toe." Wherever she goes " The Quaker Girl " draws crowded houses. The comedy is a worthy sUadessor to "The Dollar Princess," "The Chinese Honeymoon," " The Arcadians," and other of Mr Dance's productions. The leading p3rt3 are all in very capable hands. Miss Elfigt—Vincent will play " Prudence," arid Mr Louis Wigley " Tony:"
