div.head: RATES.
div.p: THE RATES.
INCREASE NOT EXPECTED.

Next Tuesday will be "Budget night" in the Warrington Town Council and the Finance and Estates Committee met yester- day afternoon to make their final revision of I the estimates: The outcome of their delibera- tions is a carefully-guarded secret, members I and officials having been pledged riot to divulge information to the Press. We believe, however, that there is every reason to expect that there will be no advance in the rates this year. This, however, will be the utmost that the Council has to offer by way of comfort to the ratepayers, as, with the constant tendency to heavier expenditure in every department, the various committees will have a difficult task in avoiding the necessity for any increased call upon the rates The fact that the education rate has not risen this year, however, renders the position brighter than for some years past. The rates at present stand at Bs. in the L, the increase last year amounting to twopence.

div.head: ROYAL VISIT.
div.p: THE ROYAL VISIT.
GUARDIANS' CLAIM TO RECOGNITION.

At the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday, Mr W Brooks made reference to the approaching visit of their Majesties the King and Qaeeti of Warrington. He pointed out that Lord Derby had requested the Mayor to submit a list of twenty persons to be presented to their Majesties and those specially selected were ex-Mayors and freemen of the Borough. It would, however, be impossible to ccmpile a list of twenty from those gentlemen, as many of the ex-Mayors and freemen had passed away. The full twenty would therefore have to be made up from other sources and he suggested that the Board of Guardians had every claim to recognition on that occasion, as it was a public body doing a very useful work." He proposed that the Clerk be instructed to make application to the Mayor with a view to the Chairman of the Board being presented to their Majesties. Mrs COLLINGWOOD seconded.

The CLERK: You are certainly a public body— perhaps the Warrington Corporation would say the second in importance. Mr A Bitooks We are first, undoubtedly. Laughter.) The CLERK: You can have your own opinion about that, but I quite agree with you. Seeing that a list of twenty is required and that it seems to be a question of not having a sufficient number, I suggest that we should recommend more names than one. Mr W C BROOKS suggested that the names of the chairman and vice-chairman should be suggeeted. He knew other public bodies were approaching the Mayor, with the same object in view. The CHAIRMAN : I don't see why the outside Urban districts, as well AS those in Warrington area, should not be introduced.
Mr A BROOKS : That would be widening the thing too much.
It was decided that the Clerk should approach the Mayor and suggest the inclusion of the chairman and vice-chairman in the list.

div.head: ST. ANN'S CHURCH.
div.p: ST. ANN'S CHURCH.
Sale of Work for Renovation Fund.

For eighteen years St Ann's Church has enjoyed an immunity from tales of work,*lnt increasing expenditure on church renovation and a deficiency in the parochial fund has made it necessary to break that record this year A sale of wora was accordingly held in the schoolroom, Dannett-stieet, on Wednesday and Thursday, and so strikingly effective was the arrangement of the various stalls as to draw from the Mayor, who opened the sale. the comment that he had never attended a similar function at whizii the decorations had been more pleasing. Messrs Peter Walker and Sons Ltd. provided the stalls which were very artistically con- structed and the appearance of the room was improved by a display of tligs, bunting and plants. Lite stalls were in charge of the following worLers : Vicarage stall : Miss Davies, Mrs Corloett, Mrs Jolley, Mrs Thomas and Mrs 'l' Corbett.
- - Church stall : Miss Glover, Mrs Gorton, Miss Bunch, Miss Green, Miss Savage, Mrs Harrison, Miss Shaw, Miss Cooper. 6unday ctiool stall : Misses Evans, Misses Kenyon, Miss Barton and Mrs Ward.
Pound stall: Mrs Rigby. Sweet Stall : Miss L Glover and Miss V Corbett. Flower and fruit stall : Miss Bradshaw. Fret work stall : Mr A Catterall, Masters Sydney Catterall and A Gee.__
_ Advertisement stall : Messrs W Thomas, J Savage and F Lawton. _
Refreshment stall : Mrs Plunkett, Mrs Taylor, Misses Cuppage, Butterworth, Broadhurst, Taylor aud Hall.
---- Bran Tub : Misses D and I Smith.
Ice Cream Stall:
Master Harold Evans.

Presiding at the opening ceremony, the VICAR (Rev James Davies) explained that it was eighteen years since the church was decorated. When the wind was blowing in a certain direction, the building was enveloped in smoke which, ot c,nirse' tended to blacken it. At the same time they must trot find fault with the smoke, bc cause " no smoke" meant " no money," with poverty and its attendant evils. In addition to the expenditure on church renovation, tbey had to make up a deficiency occasioned by the missing of a grant to their puochial fund..Cloo was required for that purpose and, although that was the first sale of work for eighteen years, he hoped it was only the beginning of a series, unless someone would come forward to help them out of the difficulty occasioned by the loss of the grant. The Vicar mentioned that contributions of goods for the sale had been received from places so far distant as Ceylon and the extreme limit of Canada. Having thanked Messrs Peter Walker and Son Ltd, and particularly Mr Hutton end Mr Mercer, for their kindness in providing and erecting the stalls, the Vicar acknowledged donations amounting to £42. They included £25 from Lady Greenall, .£5 from Messrs Greenall, Whitley and Co, £5 5s from Mrs John Crosfield,Cl Is from the Hon Misses Wilson Patten, Ll Is front the Mayor, and 103 6d from Lord Wolmer. The MAYOR. said the Vicar and parishioners had been very forbearing to go for eighteen years without some function of that kiw4 to raise funds. With regard to the renovation of the church,he would point out that they all liked to have their own houses well decor-40d, clean, well-furnished and comforttble. How much more careful aid anxious should they be to have the House of God, in which they worshipped, in good order and condition. Touching upon the propriety of holding sales of work for the purpose of raising church funds, the Mayor said that only a comparatively short time ago he expressed the view that it was not right that the religion of God should, to use a common expression, go begging. By that he meant that he hardly thought it right that they should have to take extraordinary means to ask for aid, sometimes from reluctant or unwilling quarters. On the other hand, he regarded the title "sale of work "as a splendid one. The ability to work was n divine gift to human beings, almost as common as life itself. Carlyle, a rugged roan in his exterior and in his mode of expression, but withal a great philosopher and a man, whose writings well repaid study, had said there was a perennial nobleness and sacredness about work. The statement was quite true, for what would this world have been without work ? We should have had no houses to live in, no cities, no grand buildings no sales of work even—(laughter)—if it had not not been for our possession of the power to labour. Another feature of a sue of work was the encouragement it gave to those who could only con- tribute a little, for they had to remember that trifles made perfection,and perfection was no trifle. (Applause) A vote of thanks was accorded to the Mayor and Mayoress, who was also present at the sale, on the proposition of Mr T S JOLLEY (people's warden), seconded by Mr W THOMAS (lay reader). During the afternoon and evening, there were attrac- tive entertainments by pierrot parties, under the direc- tion of Mr W H Rigby. The sale was re-opened on Thursday by Mrs William Richardson, and it was announced that the first day's takings amounted to £B5 58 Qd. The total amount realized by the sale (including subscriptions) was £2ll —which is considered an excellent result.

div.head: Presentation to Mr. G. H. Dorton.
div.p: Presentation to Mr. G. H. Dorton.

On severing 14 years' connPction with Castle Rubber Company Mr G H Darton has been the recipient of a handsome case of cutlery from the staff. Mr Darton has won the esteem of aa the staff by his courtesy, and Mr A E Burdett (who made the presentation in the absence of Mr Peter Bate) spoke in felicitous terms of the recipient'H long association with the Castle Rubber Company. Mr Darton acknowledged the gift in suitable terms, remarking that the happiest days of his life had been spent with the firm. Mr Darton has received an appointment with the firm of Mr B Cunningham, brewer.

div.head: REV. A. J. BRATT'S DEPARTURE. Appreciation of His Work in Warrington.
div.p: REV. A. J. BRATT'S DEPARTURE. Appreciation of His Work in Warrington.
CURATES WHO ARE TREATED LIKE OFFICE BOYS.

Appreciation of the work done by the Rev A J Bratt, senior curate of the Parish Church, who is about to leave Warringtou to take up the duties of organizing secretary of the Church of England Waifs and Strays Society in the dioceses of Durham, New- castle and Carli..de, was cordially voiced at the annual vestry meeting in connection with the Warrington Parish Church on Thursday evening. The RECTOR said they were much indebted to Mr Bratt for his sermons and also for his instructions at the Bible class. They would miss him ye! y greatly when he had left the parish. (Applause). Councillor LocKna ptoposed a resolution expressing gratitude to Mr Bratt for his work in Warrirgton, and good wishes in his future undertaking. Be said Mr Bratt had endeared himself to all among whom he had laboured, and he fully deserved success in his new sphere. While regretting his departure, they recog- nised that they could never have hoped t 3 retain himn in Warrington for a long period, but they were proud to have had the privil,ge of his ministrations bra few years. Mr E IstfEnwoon seconded. They all regretted that Mr Bratt was severing his connection with the Parish Church, but they weze delighted that he was improving his position. The vote was passed with great enthusiasm. The Rev A J BRATT, ija responding, said he had been very happy in WarringEou. No-one could have had a better Rector than Canon \Willis, and it had been a delight to work with him. He never interfered with one, but gave one an absolutely free hand. In short, the Rector had treated hint as a colleague and not, as some Vicar's treated their curates, as an ofli as, bay. He trusted one implicitly and, of course, he hoped by that method his colleagues would do their best for the parish. That was a very wise and sane course to adopt. He (Mr Bratt) might have failed in many ways, but he had done his best for the Parish Church of Warrington. In order to keep abreast of the times and to give his congrega- tions something worth hearing every Sunday, one had to read and think also, but to prepare sermons and attend to the manifold duties of parochial work neces- sitated burning the candle at both ends. If a man had a message which went home to the people in their every-day lives he would always have an attentive hearing at the Warrington Parish Church. The con- gregation there was one of the finest he knew, from a preacher's point of view. (Applause.)

div.p: EASTER VESTRY MEETINGS.

SE'. HILDA'S MISSION. At a meeting in connection wit n the above, the Vicxr norLinated Mr Rathbone as his warden, and the people elected Mr J Cartwright as their warden. Mr Reynolds and Mr Livingstone were elected sidesmen.—Tbe accounts which were passed. showed a balance in baud of 4s 10d.

div.head: CHRIST CHURCH, PADGATE.
div.p: CHRIST CHURCH, PADGATE.

The annual vestry meeting was held in the Church House on Wednesday evening, the Vicar (Rev G W Dickenson) presiding over a fa,r attendance.—Mr Hernert Houghton was re-appointed Vicar's warden and the Vicar's sidesmen are :—Messrs Denham, Critchley, London, Muther, Hutchinson, Gorton and Hilditch. Mr Percy Royston is the new people's warden and the sidesmen elected by the vestry are : Messrs W Potter, Allen, Wright, T Autrohus, Howard, Jump and Houghton.—Meqsrs Mather and Jump were appointed lay representatives. ST. JAMES', LATCHFORD.

The annual Easter vestry meeting was held in St James' schoolroom, on Thursday evening. The Vicir, the ReY H B Firth, presided, and the itev El H Corsbie (assistant curate), and a number of parishioners were also present. Speaking of the importance of vestry meetings and the importance generally of church- wardens' work the Vicar thanked sincerely Mr W LE Storm&ld for his work as vicar's warden during the past three years. He had done his duty efficiently, devotedlY" and well. It was his, (the vicar's) custom to appoint a vicar's warden every three years end be had just cora- pleted his ninth year as vicar of that church. (Applause.) After reviewing the past nine years and stating the various improvements and alterations which, had been made, the vicar, said that whilst he had been with them the sum of £2,300 had been raised for various objects connected with the church,whools and mission. That amount was independent of money raised for i.be general working experases of the parish. He had pleasure in nominating Mr S Acton as his warden for the coming year. Mr Acton was a member of the choir in the Rev F Sister's time and all times he had shown his devotion and loyalty to the church. Mr Acton replied anti nominated Mr Harding as his sidesman. Mr W Eckersley was elected people's warden, on the pro- position of Mr J Grounds. -

At thecungregational meetitig the following sides- men were elected :—Messrs H Warburton, J (rounds, \Voodward, Hodge, Heath, Todd, Pargher, J Eckersley, Messrs W fi Stansfield and J Fargher were appointed lay representatives —The Vicar spoke of the importance of the office of lay representa- tives and said this year in the diocese of Chester scheme had been inaugurated for the raising of a large Central Diocesan Fund. The lay representatives would be consuhei a 3 to the amount of money each parish would be expected to contribute in connection with the Central Diocesan Fund. Each parish would be assessed. The churchwardens' accounts, which were passed. showed that the year had been commenced with a balance in hand of .£1 93 id. The general offertory was £9B 16s 10d, special offertory £5B 148, other receipts .£2. 53 9d, deficit on the year 14s 81. The Vicar said he , hoped this year that certain improvements would be made to the church. They needed a sounding board very much over the pulpit, a-t the acoustic properties at St. James' were admittedly exceedingly bad. The expense would be about £5O, and he appealed for help in that direction.

div.head: NEW INDUSTRY FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: NEW INDUSTRY FOR WARRINGTON.

Speaking yesterday at the annual meeting of the British Aluminium Co., Mr A W Taft, the chaizman. said that in order to cope with the increased demand for manufactures arrangements had been completed for the acquisition of laud and buildings at Warring- ton, the site providing for considerable future extension if necessary. The site had been obtained on favourable terms and contracts had been made for the supply of rolling plant. It was anticipated that the works would be in operation at the end of the present year or at the beginning of next, and as the demand increased further plant would be put in. We are informed that the works are to be erected at Bank Quay, in the neighbourhood of the t. Helen's Cable Company's works, and will provtde employment for several hundred men. The site is, of course, very advantageous from the standpoint of railway and river dccess.

div.head: STOMACH TROUBLES DUE TO ACIDITY.
div.p: STOMACH TROUBLES DUE TO ACIDITY.
SO SAYS EMINENT SPECIALIST.

So-called stomach troubles, such as indigestion wind, stomach-ache and inability to retain food,instead of indicating that the stomach is out of order, are in nine cases out of ten simply evidence that fermentation is taking place in the food contents of the stomach, causing the formation of gas and acids. Wind distends the stomach, and causes that full, oppressive feeling sometimes known as heartburn, while the acid irritates and inflames the delicate lining of the stomach. The stomach. however, is not at fault. The trouble lies entirely in the. fermenting food. Such fermentation is unnatural and acid formation is not only unnatural, but may involve the most serious consequences if not prevented. To prevent or stop fermentation of the food contents of the stomach and to neutralise the acid, and render it bland and harmless, half a teaspoonful of bisurated magnesia, probably the best and most effective antacid known, should be taken in a quarter of a glass of hot or cold water immediately after eating, or whenever wind or acidity is felt. This stops the fermentation, and neutralises the acidity in a few moments. Fermentation, wind and acidity are dangerous and unnecessary. Stop or prevent them by the use of a proper antacid, such as bisurated magnesia, which can be obtained from any chemist, and thus enable the stomach to do it 4 work properly without being hindered by poisonous gas and dangerous acids.--1.1.F.P

CYCiillg. Cairo-street Cycling Club enjoyed a delightful run on Easter Monday. to Alderley Edge, 'returning by Chelford and Knutsford. Glorious weather prevailed throughout the day. A record number turned out. To-day's run is to Acton Bridge and Frodsham.

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 29, 1913
[ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.

"We think," he said, "you ha.d better go to breakfast, and return as soon as possible, for you will be wanted to give evidence." "Thanks, I'll get a hansom and hurry off." The morning was damp, so Langdale put on his rain coat, then went out and caught a hansom. To his whistling no less than three had arrived, but he did not notice that Drew him- self sprang inside one of these. " Keep that cab in sight," the detective hurriedly told the Jehu, "but do nothing suspicious." The detective was at Langdale's door shortly after himself. But he waited for a time, then entered. "Anything fresh or new to tell me?" asked the cashier, in some surprise. "This coat belongs to you, I think?" He held up the Taincoat as he spoke. " Certainly, Mr. Drew." "Then, .Mr. Langdale, you must be mad if you robbed that bank, and thrust these notes and valuables so carelessly into the breast- pocket of your coat." Serious as the matter seemed Langdale could not repress a smile. " Certainly I should be mad," he said, "if, with my pro- spects in life, I either robbed a bank or placed the proceeds where you have found them." There was no smile about Drew's sternly- eet face. "You'll have an opportunity to ex- plain matters later on," he said. "Mean- while, under the circumstances, you cannot be surprised when I inform you that you are my prisoner." "No, I should be surprised at nothing new," returned the cashier. " Nor will I say anything except that there seems to have been a conspiracy of some kind, which I cannot un- derstand." It was not until the unhappy man heard the sounds of the prison keys turned in the awful door that the whole 'horror of the situation burst upon him. Then he sank upon the bench and buried his face in his hands. The knowledge of his own innocence did not comfort him in the least. Facts were black against him, and it was by circumstan- tial evidence he would be tried, and—horrible thought !—probably condemned. Evidence of this kind had doomed many an innocent man to penal servitude, ay, and the scaffold itself. In his cell next morning Langdale had a most painful interview with poor Nora, who came to his summons, accompanied by her old father.

She was convulsed with grief, stupefied by it, yet her eyes were dry; she was beyond the relief that tears bring. What was said at this interview Langdale never could remember. But he had one com- fort, one little consolation—Nora left the ter- rible apartment quite believing in her lover's innocence.
All the world might think him guilty, she could not, she would not. _
The trial came on after the usual months of law delays, and was probably, for so serious a case, one of the shortest on record. _ _
Even Langdale's counsel appeared. to be hopeless from the first. His Lordship's sum- ming up was brief, and the jury were absent but a few minutes.

Then came the stupefying sentence, of seven years' penal servitude, and Langdale left the dock walking mechanically beside the burly warders, who were really imbued with pity for the young fellow. And many more in the court were the same, though no one believed that the punishment was not merited.

mined desire and resolve—to kill the perfidi- ous scoundrel Morrison. He would not appear to heart-broken Nora, neither before nor after his fingers were wet with his enemy's blood. He would do that deed with his own naked hands, and, Heaven! how the tiger Langdale gloated over every detail of it—as he had planned it, and as it would be done. Heart-broken Nora indeed! To save her father from utter ruin caused by the machina- tions of the evil banker she had at last con- sented to marry him. She would leave the day as far off as possible, and at present, in- deed, she was laid upon a bed of lingering ill- ness. The doctor pronounced it to be rapid consumption. Langdale's plan succeeded, and at the risk of his liberty he even wandered down to the Broads, where he caught a glimpse of Nora. He had to 75e content. to gaze and long—then back to London to commit a deed that should thrill the whole city. It was the evening before the murder was to become an accomplished fact when Langdale sat in a coffee-house, an evening paper in his hand. Suddenly his eye fell upon a startling paragraph. Scotland Yard had received in- timation from Australia proving the inno- cence of Langdale, and that very morning Morrison himself had been arrested and thrown into prison.

For a long time Langdale sat with the paper iin his hand n a species of happy stupefaction. He could believe nothing, and hardly credited the fact that he was alive and in London. At last he beckoned the waiter. "Read that," he said; "do my eyes de- ceive me? "

The. waiter read, and glanced in a be- wildered way at the young man. " You are Langdale," he said. • "Oh, I know all your terrible story. But you'll come back to see me when the clouds roll by. I won't give you away." "I will," said Langdale, then wandered aimlessly away out into the street. But what • a dreadful calamity he had escaped ! He might have been a murderer, had things happened but a week or two sooner. Then a great happiness seemed to take up its abode deep down in his heart. He could see Nora now.

Little Jimmy Duccleish could hardly believe his luck when, months after this, •he found himself back on the links with Wallace by his side. The doctor who had condemned Nora to a lingering death admitted he had never before known so speedy a cure for consumption. Langdale was with her every day now, and would be till the wedding; and little Jimmy is still the caddie. [rnE END.]
Phi R 3 DOUI;Lb ATLEMPT AT SUICIDE

Frederick McCabe (30), a single man living in Leicester-ttreet, appeared before the Mayor and other magistrates at the Borough Police Court on Monday, on charges of drunkenness and attempted suicide. Prisoner was creating a disturbance in Marshhouse- kne and, as he refused to go home, he was locked up. Some six hours I.ter an officer, hearing a noise, went to prisoner's cell and found him lying on a form with a piece of string tied tightly round his throat. The officer cut the string and left the prisoner for a couple of minutes, soother officer being sent to watch him. Before he could get to the cell, however, prisoner had again attempted to strangle himself by means of a stocking. All night he kept saying he "wished he had dune it." _

The Chief Constable said prisoner had made two deliberate attempts to commit suicide. He suggested that he should Le sent, on a fourteen days' order, to the Workhouse, in order that his sanity might be tested, Prisoner, who now appeared in a penitent mood, attributed his conduct to the effects of drink.

The Ni ay° r : Instead of being here, you might have been deno, if you had bed your own way. What have you to say ai,out that? The Chief Constable pointed out that the attempts at suicide did not take place until six hours alter prisoner was locked up. He must therefore have got, perfectly sober. The Mayor : But in a very depressed state, though. (to prisoner.) The beat thing you can do in to keep off oriuk.

The mother of the prisoner, on being asked whether she was willing to take charge of him, replied : "Yes I am always taking charge of him and talking to him for his own good.' On prisoner promising to sign the pledge, the case was aajourned for a month. DRANK AMMONIA FOR POP.

"TOO DRUNK TO KNOW THE DIFFERENCE." At the Borough Police Court yesterday, before the Ma3or and other magistrates, Bernard lieddican, 14, Meiville-street, forgeman, wee charged with attempting to commit suicide. Prisoner stated that it was an accident. He drank some ammonia in mistake for pop As soon as the ammonia burnt him he dropped the bottle and called out. . .
The Chiet Constable said that version had originated that morning. Such CaSeS were never ptesbed but there should, he thought, be a reprimand when such state- ments as these were manufactured.

_ P.C. Cameron, who was called to the prisoner's houte and rendered first aid, produced the wattle Which was a blue poison bottle. On the way to the infirmary prisoner said he wished he had done the thing properly as there was nothing to live for. Prisoner (to the ruagistiates clerk) : I don't remem- ber saying that, sir. I was drunk. The officer stated that the bottle was still three parts full. PrisoLer had been using it to clean his clothes in the afternoon.

the Chit Constable : When charged this morning he replied "it was the drink." Prisoner's mother said he came home between twelve and one on Sunday morning and when she had let him in she returned to bed. He shouted "Is there a drink ?" and she said" There is a bottle of pop on the kitchen shelf." Soon atterwaras he called out." Oh, mother, mother, 1 got the wrong bottle; I m dying." The Magistrate's Clerk : Do you put pup in bottles like that? Witness: No ;it was on the same shelf and he must have mistaken it necause he was drunk. Pritoner intimated that he :would turn over a new leaf and sign toe pledge and his mother promised to look after Dim. The case was adjourned for a mouth, the Mayor inti- mating that if Mr Firth, the police court MlSsiOUttry, reported favourably at the end of that tune, prisoner would not he required to attend. SAD HUSBAND AND WIFE STORY. WOMAN'S VIOLENT ATTACK.

At the Borough Court yesterday before the Mayor and other magistrates Sarah Jane Allison, 370, Wilders- pool Causeway, was summontd for assaulting her husband, Fiederick Henry Allison, Spring Dale, tfair- fleld-road, Latchford Without, who appeared in the witness box with a badly bruised and bandaged eye. Mr Unsworth solicitor, who appeared for the com- plainant, stated that this was a case of incomnatability of temperament. They had agreed to a separation order before the Daresbury magistrates (when Mr Steel appeared for the womsn) the wife to have an allow- ance and the custody of the two children aged five and eight, and the husband to have the privilege of seeing the children. On going to see the children on the 26th he was invited into the house by his wite. She then locked the door rushed for a sties with some bright metal at it 3 end and endeavoured to strike him. He protected himself but the third blow caught him full on the eye, and inflicted a nasty wound which the doctor said would have destroyed the sight had it been an eighth of an inch nearer. His client had wished to do everything that was reasonable and only asked that his wile might be bound over tor his protection from this kind of thing. Defendant : lam sorry for what I have done but it upset me when he said be had been away to Blackpool with Mrs --

Defendant asked was it fair that he should come to her home when it preyed on her feelings to see him. Complainant stated that his vcile bad asked her to forgive her as she could not live without him and did not like seeing him in present conditions. He told her it was dishonourable to refuse to allow him to see the children after agreeing to allow him. Mr Unsworth suggested that complainant should be allowed to see the children at a neutral place, and defendant agreeing,

div.head: CUPID, THE CADDIE.
div.p: CUPID, THE CADDIE.
BY W. GORDON-STABLES, RN. Author of "Annie o' the Banks o' Dee," "Frank Hardinge," "In the Dashing Days of Old," "Every Inch a Sailor," &e.

It was nearing the close of what had been a bright, still day in the beginning of June. The spring tints still lingered on bush and shrub and tree, and yonder wide-beamed boat, NA ith her crimson cushions in stern- sheets and on thwarts, almost imperceptibly rose and fell on the waters of that Norfolk Broad. Her bows were well in through the sedges--the irises, blue, and mauve, and orange. And though all was calm there was a world of life and love everywhere. The rudder and oars were shipped, and on the thwarts facing each other sat a youthful couple, whose quiet and happy looks were quite in keeping with the scene around them. It had been an original sort of wooing that of young Langdale and the pretty Nora 0-Shane—if, indeed, there had been any wooing about it. He had never told her of his love, nor she confessed hers. But there it was all the same; it had just come flowing over their souls, as smooth waves -roll in from a placid sea and break drowsily on the shore. Little Jimmy Buccleish was T.ora's caddie and ghillie. In Glasgow the girl had done him a kindness that the lad would never for- get.. So he had come to England with her, and Scott's " Dugald craitur " could not have loved Helen McGregor more devotedly than Jimmy did Nora. He would risk his life any day to save her from the slightest pain. Langdale was chief cashier in Morrison's bank, City, and trusted in every sense of the word. • A tall, broad-shouldered Englishman, with a pleasant, smiling face. Nora looked but a child beside him—blue-eyed, petite, and with a wealth of chestnut hair, in which the amber rays of the morning sunshine loved to linger. She was as innocent and childish in her manners as in her looks. Yet this little Irish girl was capable of a love a Saxon could neither feel nor understand. The lovers' Walked to where Jimmy, "the Glesca chicken," and Wallace, the big New- foundland dog, were waiting. Wallace came bounding to meet them, and Jimmy shouldered his golf clubs and followed. Morrison, the head of the bank, often came down to Boyne House to dine and play whist with Mr. O'Shane.

He was here to-day. Elderly, somewhat grey, he was nevertheless as deeply in love with Nora as his selfish nature would permit. He looked upon the lovers as they came slowly up the avenue—looked upon them with feelings akin to jealousy. He Morri- son—meant to marry this sweet Irish girl. There is nothing, he told himself, that money cannot accqmplish. Langdale should not stand in his way. He would see to that. Determined and unscrupulous, he feared no rival. Kindness personified he always was towards Nora; condescending towards Lang- dale. Quietly he meant to fight his way to triumph and victory, as a great General con- ducts a campaign. He hardly knew his own plans as yet, bar the denofiernent, and, side by side, he and she should stand before the altar. Langdale did not trouble himself, and neither liked nor disliked his rival; but Jimmy hated the man, and some instinct told him he must look after his mistress. What is the good of a man, anyhow, who eannot play gowff? Jimmy spent his time 'twixt London and the ,Broads. He would wander down and wander back again. He loved the sweet cool country in summer; but, nevertheless, the City had great and manifold attractions for the boy. Especially at night, for there was al- ways adventure then. He cared but little where or how he lived, and would sleep in an entry, under a bridge, or at home in his own dingy bedroom, equally well and soundly. If the boy had an ambition—and he is a worthless lad who has not—it was to become a great detective some day. Hence the irre- sistible charm of being out all alone at night, though he took no heed of the ordinary street-arabs.

Strolling homewards late one night, and humming a song to himself, he stopped sud- denly with a whistle of surprise. He was near by Morrison's bank, and yon- der ahead of him was Mr. Morrison himself. Jimmy could spot him at a glance. The banker stopped at the door, and turned the lock, then something attracted his attention, and he went a few steps further tro the street. " I wonder," said the boy to himself, "what old grey-face is going to do? Hullo ! the door is open and in I pop." He suited the action to the words, slid in, and hid himself in a dark corner.
"Old grey - face" walked directly to his private room, Jimmy following in his wake as silent as a weasel.
What uncanny business was Morrison about to transact? He pored over ledgers for nearly an hour, and then opened a small safe with one of two identically shaped keys:. _ .

From the safe he'took- a bundle of notes and some gold, with a few legal-looking docu- ments. Then he switched off the light, and Jimmy had hardly time to stow himself away again before—electric lantern in hand— Morrison was once more in the hall,. The notes, the papers, and 'gold he thrust into the pocket of a light top coat that hung near by. Next minute Jimmy found himself seized by the collar, and hauled into the light. Hillo! a young burglar. Why, it is Miss O'Shane's caddie. Well, my lad, your career has come to a sudden stop, and it ends just here."
Was he going to be murdered? Jimmy won- dered. But lie spoke never a word, and suffered himself to be conducted below and locked up in a dark cellar.
There was very little else talked about next forenoon in financial circles save the great robbery at Morrison's bank, for evil news travels far and fast.
"Seems a bit of a mystery," said one man "on charge." "Ah ! my boy," said an older and wiser hand, "mysteries like these are speedily un- ravelled in these days."

Langdale was early at the bank that morn- ing, for there were some books to balance. With his private latch-key he let himself quietly in, and Was proceeding towards his own room when he noticed that the door of Mr. Morrison;s was slightly ajar. This was most unusual, and he entered, wondering. Some papers on the table were in con- siderable confusion, and some ledgers had been thrown on the floor. But, strangest of all, the strong box in the wall was open and apparently empty. Langdale knew there had been notes and valuable securities in it the day before, so he came at once to the conclu- sion that a most daring robbery had been perpetrated. The young man's duty was plain enough, so he at once crossed over to the telephone and rang up Scotland Yard. " Yes? "
" the cashier of Morrison's Bank, Blank-street. Robbery or burglary seems to have taken place. Please send me- assistance at once."

Half an hour after this an electric motor, driven by a plain - clothes policeman, drove up to the door, and two gentlemen stepped therefrom to the pavement. They were Inspector Walter and Detective Drew. Langdale himself had been watching for their arrival, and , conducted them inside. He was very pale and concerned - looking, but otherwise quiet in his manner. On his way to the room door Drew kicked something with his toe, and stooped and picked it up. It was a perfectly iw key, and it fitted the lock of the strong - r om. He smiled grimly as he remarked to Mr. Walter: " The robbery has not been .com• mitted by any professional burglar, but by someone belonging to the bank." Everything was examined and noted, then, after sealing the door, they proceeded to Langdale's own room. To all appearance it was precisely as the young man had left it on the previous evening. Drew took the inspector aside, and they held a brief consultation. Then the detective came towards Langdale.

Nothing seemed capable of cooling the courage of the " Gleska Chicken" Jimmy, nor daunt his spirits, else the treatment he now received would have done so. He had not been very long in the cellar before he heard the sound of stealthy footsteps, and next minute the door was opened wide, and he was half-blinded by the glare of an electric torch.
"Any show of resistance," he was told, in blood-curdling toncs, "means a bullet through your chump and a grave in the cellar here."

Jimmy meant to escape, if he got the chance, just the same. But the chance did not come, and his strange, and for the most part terrible, adventdres and experiences for the next many months would fill a book. He was bundled inside a motor-car, and very soon found himself at steps leading down to the river. Two rough-looking, sw art sailormen had the oars, and a third the tiller, and one of his captors took a seat by his side. Then, before he knew what was to happen, poor Jimmy found his head and arms en- veloped in a not over-clean sack. "Do you mean to drown me like a kitten in a bag?" he cried. " That is what we jolly well will do if there be any din." It was a long, long pull down the darksome river, and it was still night when they reached a large sailing barque at her moor- ings. He was led up the stair on to the greasy deck, and then down below, where he was locked up in a spare cabin, the sack .be- in taken off. 'Jimmy felt about, then threw himself into empty bunk, and with his left arm for a pillow was soon as sound asleep as ever he had been in his life.

Broad daylight was streaming in through the jalousies when he awoke hungry and faint. From the barque's motion Jimmy knew the Tartar, as she was called, was far away at sea. Then he was taken before the captain-4a more forbidding, looking fellow than any of his crew. "Anything to say, younker? " „.

" Only th-a-,t I'm 6tarving. sir." "Well, you'll have food and you'll have work to do; hut if there be the slightest at- tempt at insubordination you'll have four dozen lashes to begin with." " Sweet prospect," said Jimmy. The breakfast was but a whack of salt junk, biscuit, and bad coffee; but this was nectar to the lad.

Then Jimmy began to laugh and talk and sing, and was sent to work. They were a cut- throat crew; but, young as the lad was, there Was not a man among them he could not have knocked into the lee scuppers. His boxing and wrestling accomplishments, however, Jimmy kept to himself. He bore all species of ill-usage quietly, and even amused the mates and crew at night with his songs and antics.

But what a long and dreary voyage, in this leaky, wet, creaking, ill-found tub! Months and months, yet it never seemed to end. Storms that swept the decks with green seas, and blew the half-rotten sails into ribbons, and such personal ill-usage by day that often when he leant over the bulwarks at night he longed to sleep beneath the blue sea. But that he must not even think of. His time for escape would come; he felt sure of that. As soon as he landed in Sydney, which he heard was the first port of call, he mould swim to shore, and make a communication to the police; for Jimmy could see through the whole affair, and understood the plot. But alas for his schemes ! The skipper of the Tartar saw to it that Jimmy never landed at Sydney. And with a small bag of biscuits the poor lad was marooned on a semi-barren islund fully three hundred miles to the nor'ard and east of Australia.
do not believe that our terrible and absurd system of penal servitude, with its solitary confinement and horrors, ever re- formed a convict; but it has made tigers of many innocent men. -

MOnths and months ago Langdale was a dead man in all but name. His soul seemed dead within him, his body but a ma,ss of use- less muscle, his brain all but inert. He had about given up thinking by day, and at night he slept like a log, awaking every morning unrefreshed, and as if from hours of a living death.

But one portion of the brain was active enough and clear as noonday, and this he devoted in his waking moments to thinking out a scheme of revenge. Most Of the con- victs with whom he herded were men only in name, and probably no enlightened, practical scheme of escape had ever entered the brain of one of them. Many of them dreamt of free- dom, and some day these might make a dash for liberty, but it would be but like the stam- pede of bullocks, pointless, aimless; and they would speedily be recaptured. Langdale's was as well thought out as a game of chess by an expert. It was a certainty. And what should he do with his freedom? He must have been mad. for ho had hut. nne wish, one deter-

div.head: POOR MARY.
div.p: POOR MARY.
_ We will qUote only one other marriage- song, this time to call attention to the form of its concluding wish:

Poor Mary sits a crying A-crying, a crying Poor Mary sits a-crying Upon a summer's day. Pray Mary what's you cryirg for, etc. I'm crying for a sweetheart, etc. Pray Mary choose your lover, etc. When you're married I wish you: joy First a girl and seconi a boy Seven years after son and daughter Kiss her once, kiss her twice, Kiss her three times over. This game is almost exactly similar to "Pretty little girl of mine" and has an almost identical refrain. In few children's verses is the traditional aspect so clear. As was tpointed out in our discussion of "Sally iWaters," marriages were made among our remote ancestors not for life but for a provisional term of seven years. If a son and daughter had not been born within that period the union was dissolved. The patriarchal plan by which the wife could find a substitute is revealed in the story of Abraham, Sarah and Hagar, and provision is made for. a similar proceeding in the code of King Hammurabi which belongs to the same period.

FIRST A GIRL AND THEN A BOY. But whence the curious wish " First a girl and then a boy"? where one might have expected the re verse order. Here again is an echo of a remote idea— the belief that a man's life was not complete until he had a daughter, who herself had had a son. A woman's life was, however, according to the ancient conceit complete with the birth of a son. Curious traces of these old beliefs some- times show themselves in quiet corners of Britain. Thus a man pleaded for a separa- tion from his wife on the ground that she had sons and so completed het own life, but had no daughter and so left his life incom- plete. And not long ago a woman in Norfolk who had been deserted by her husband com- plained bitter!y to the magistrates making as her plea that they had not been seven years married and she had both a daughter and a son. ANOTHER WORD ON SALLY WATERS. We conclude with a further word upon the unique feature of "Sally Waters," the possible reference to water worship in the 'sprinkling " and" come out of the water." Among both Aryan and Non-Aryan Tribes water ceremonies are stlil practised at weddings. Among the Hindus who are, like us, of Aryan descent, the bride always casts offerings into a water vessel and then sprinkles the court of her new home by way of exorcism. She also sprinkles the bridegroom. The Esthonian brides, who belong to a Non-Aryan race, on the morning after the wedding are taken to make offerings to the water spirit. Offerings are thrown into a spring or vessel of water, a vessel of water is overturned in the house and the husband is sprinkled with it. Among the Teutons the bride always stepped over a vessel of water. These are all, doubtless, survivals of water worship, and it is well known that water worship was connected with the desire for children. With these scraps of custom before us it is not difficult to find a meaning for the " sprinkling " in the famous little rhyme of "Sally Waters." We have here, very possi- bly, a relic of the Pre-Celtic tribe which peopled our island in the dim and shadowy past. If we grant to the lines this high antiquity it becomes very interesting to note that the marriage is one in which there is no com- pulsion. Sally Waters " chooses" her young man, and the wedding is one without ceremony save that the witnesses give acknowledgment in the words "Those two's got married" and express the hope for " a son and daughter and a kiss and a smile." A. M.

div.head: HEALTH WEEK.
div.p: HEALTH WEEK.
NUMEROUS NORTHERN TOWNS ARRANGING PROGRAMMES.

Many towns in the Midlands and the North of England have heartily co-operated with the Health Week movement, organised by the Agenda Club, which will be celebrated from April 6th to 12th. Birmingham, Huddersfield, Darlington, Richmond, Scarborough, Warrington, Newcastle, Nottingham, Bolton, Doncaster,llkley, and Macclesfield are already arranging programmes, and the list is being added to daily. At Bolton three "health houses" have been rented in working-class districts, and these will be furnishen plainly and en economical lines, so that the artisan and his wife can see the standard of comfort they may attain for themselves and their families by the exercise of ordinary care and attention to the elementary principles of hygiene in their dcmestic arrangements. The Countess of Aberdeen, who is at the head of the movement in Ireland, has taken a warm personal interest in this branch of the work, and has made inquires at headquarters as t) the lines upon which to proceed in order to provide the Irish working classes with a similar obj-ct lesson in how to ensure a tidy home amid the most humble surroundings. In many towns there will be daily health talks and lectures, and from some hundreds of pulpits refer- ences to health subjects will be made by preachers of various denominations. Conferences have also been arranged on subjects closely allied with the health of the community, including housing problems and smoke abatement. The Health Week movement is not an addition to the already long list of institutions that seek to promote public health by new-fangled methods. What it aims at ard is successfully accomplishing is to bring forcibly home to the people the fact that health after all rests very much with the individual and not with the State or community, and that by the observance of ordinary conditions thousands of homes may be made , happier and the death-rate appreciably diminished.

SHAKESPEARE THEATRE, LIVERPOOL. Increasing interest is being taken in the return visit t 3 the Shakespeare Theatre next week of Mr Louis Me3er's chief company in "The Glad Eye." This famous play will be remembered by all playgoers as a bright, breezy, boisterous farce of sound material and ingenious surprises. It is the story of two light-hearted husbands intent upon furnishing their wises with a satisfactory excuse for their recurring absences from home. We know those husbands! they come from Paris. They hate played their part in endless farces. They have brought the art oi equivocation t 3 the pitch of perfection. A touch of" novelty is given to the picture by the fact that in the case of one of their wives they had met their match. The company that ' will appear next week will include many artistes of established reputation, viz :—Stanley Brett, Percy Marmont, Fred Eastman and W E Richardson, Miss Constance Hyem, Miss Enid Sass and Miss Billie Sinclair. " The Glad Eye" will be preceded each evening by a one-act play entitled "An Interrupted Divorce."

FRIENDLY SOCIETY FINED 10s. Councillor Higham, an unsuccessful candidate at the recent election of directors of the Blackburn Philan- thropic Friendly Collecting Society, which has 350,000 members, summoned the society oa Wedneschy under the Friendly Societies Act for refusing to allow him to inspect the books. A fine of 103 and costa was imposed,

div.head: MADNESS OF EUROPE
div.p: THE MADNESS OF EUROPE
[BY C. E. PARKER].

It is probable that the military expenses of the European and Eastern countries will after this year be permanently increased by nearly £100,000,000 per annum. It is well that we should clearly recognize what this means in connection with the world's economic advancement and its effect upon the workers. This amount will be spent upon forts, equipment, wages, which produce nothing and only consume the labour of others. You have this amount deflected from its present place in useful production and devoted to instruments of destruction, and the maintenance of the men to man them. In France an additional year is to be taken from the working life of the male population and employed in that which produces nothing useful. We want to realize what this misapplication of economic resources means to the world. It is very strange how, in this twentieth contury, there are still some (and they are not confined to Tariff Reformers) who think that money expended on unproductive work is good for trade, that making work is a good thing in itself. How absurd this is. If we would think of money in its true use as simply a medium of exchange and measure of values we would see the question in its true light. Let us eliminate money from our thought altogether for a moment. The things that minister to the comfort of life, such as food, clothing, houses etc., are the products of labour. If we divert millions of men into occupations which pro- duce nothing useful, we naturally throw on to the remainder the additional burden of providing the necessaries for such men. This means a considerable reduction in production of the world's wealth. This being so the pro- ducer gets less for his effort because he has to part with a considerable proportion of his produce to feed, clothe, and house others. Getting back to the money question and interpreting the produce in its money measure, it means that the worker has to produce more for the same remuneration. In other words it expresses self in a diminution of the wage factor. Turn this about any way you will and no sensible man can come to any other conclusion. The aggregation of production of wealth being lessened, a decreasing share comes to all interests engaged in its production. The immediate pinch is felt most and first by the worker. The Labour party has with a true instinct realized that wars, and preparations for wars, injure their class first and most,and from all countries protests are arising from the workers. Nor can it be logically contended that if in this country,we keep our heads and refuse to take part in this mad competition that we will benefit by the folly of our continental neighbours. There was a time when such a theory was in vogue ; all but the thoughtless have outgrown it. In the world-wide com- merce of nations if one suffers the whole suffer, if one is prosperous all share in this prosperity. Mr. A. J. Balfour in one of his illuminating speeches expressed this truth so well that although the quotation is long I Fould not have it spoiled by further contraction. The words were spoken in connection with industrial rivalry but it is true also in regard to the waste and misapplication of human resources.in war preparation. "I am one of those who profoundly distrust the current creed —or the creed which is largely current—that the prosperity of one nation is the adversity (.1 another; that he best serves the industrial prosper:ty of his own nation who attempts to depress the industrial prosperity or to snatch a share of the comm ,n work of industry from some other nation. I believe this to be utterly untrue. . . . . I would like here to give from one of the speeches of John Bright, delivered over fifty years ago, an extract which goes -0 confirm what I have said. It was stated that £2,000,000,000 had been spent by this country in connection with what were called "the liberties of Europe and the balance of power," John Bright said : " When I try to think of that sum of 5,2,000,000,090 there is a sort of vision passes before my mind's eya. I see your p ,asant labourer delve and plough, 807 f and reap, sweat beneath the summ-r s sun, or grow prematurely old before the winter's blast. I see your noble mechanic with his manly countenance and his matchless skill, toiling at his bench or his forge I 809 one of the workers in our factories an the North, a woman, a girl it may be, gentle and good, as many of them are, as your sisfers and daughters are,—l 80e her intent upon the spindle, whose reveutions are so rapid that the eye fails altogether to detect them, or to watch the alter- nating flight of the unresting shuttle. I turn again to another portion of your population, which, " plunged in mines, forgets a sun was made," and I see the man who brings up from the secret chambers of the earth Vie elements of the riches and greatness of his country. When I see all this I have before me a mass of produce and of wealth which I am no more able to comprehend than lam that ,4.:2,000,000,000 of which I have spoken, but I b hold in its full prcportion the hideous error of your governments, whose fatil policy consumes in some cases a half, never less than a third, of all the results of that industry which God intended should fertilize and bless every home in England. What the world wants irresp:ctive of class or nati nality, is a greater production of th things that mankind require; and the disputes as to the division of the results of this great indus- trial work are really insignificant compared with the interests that are involved in making the work of the world profitable and efficient. In the ordinary current controversies of the day it is supposed that what is good for one indu,trial country, let us say in a neutral market, is of necessity wholly had for what are called its trade rivals. There may be some truth in it ; but the truth is a petty and insignificant fraction of the whole truth; and the whole truth is that what we want is that methods of production should be improved, and that the improvement should be shared by every na,ion and people on the earth. The riches of one nation conduce, believe me, not to poverty, but to the weal,h of another nation, and if we could double or treble by the stroke of some fairy wand the wealth of eveiy other nation in the w, rld but our own, depend upon it our nation would greatly profit by the process." In the foregoing I have dealt purely with the economic side of war and preparations for war. The moral side may be the more important, but it is in the economic that there is the most loose thinking. If the electors in any country, formed largely of the toilers, could but realise that war and pre- parations for war are against their interests, a restraint would soon be put on those rulers and statemen who delight in war and who, in an increasing degree, desire to reverse the Biblical idea of race improvement and convert more plough-shares into swords, and more pruning hooks into spears.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.

WASTRELS. How perplexing is the problem presented by the case of the hopeless and incorrigible drunkard who is constantly falling into the hands of the police. As mentioned in a " Note 'S in last Saturday's issue, there were three of " them " before the Borough Court last week. I have found him (or her) in every town of which I have had excerience - a miserable burden to himself and an everlasting trouble to these who have to adminster the law, to say nothing of the expense entailed. One I knew who has been convicted con- siderably over 100 times, and I understood he is still " going strong " ; and I have a painfully keen recollection of similar wretched met elsewhere who were evidently "playing for the century." Surely, tremendous responsibility is incurred by those who supply intoxicants to these wileless creatures. BU UTER SUBSTITUTES. The story reprinted from a Manchester paper last week reminded me of the desperate and persistent plunges of an unscrupulous and would-be-rich-quick tradesman wh ) I knew into the teens of years ago. He became noted for a special " line " in the way of what he retailed as, and appeared to be genuine butter. He sold it at a little less per lb. than his rivals, and consequently managed to " collar " a big share of the trade. Eventually it si as remarked that he had very large and frequent deliveries of margarine. Then an inspector took a sample of his "best but.er," and as it proved on analysis to be margarine, the offander was summoned and lined 3:10 aid costs. The profits on suet' trans- actions as he had been engaged in were evidently too great for temptation to be resisted, and the convicted shopkeeper actually went on selling margarine as butter. He was again summoned, and once more fined Xilo and the expenses. That ruined him, for after au ineffectual struggle of a few months, during which his place of business remained practically deserted, he clozed the establishment aid disappsarea. MY DOUBLE. Councillor Henshall's story as Co how be hid been mistaken for Alderman Pierpoint reminded me that I had a double in one town in which I formerly resided. Once a stranger drew me aside and informed me that he had received my postcard and it was " all right." I expressed by gratification at the assurance that nothing was amiss, but m..destly disclaimed all knowledge of the post card. It turned out that my double was the author. On another Occasion an income tax collector stopped me in the street and challenged the accuracy of certain returns which I was alleged to have made a few days previously. My bewilderment la, ing apparent, he asked if I would mind just stepping round to his place which was nigh at hand. I did so, and he selected one from a bundle of official parers and triumphantly p)inted out what he was convinced was an error. I said no doubt it was all very interesting, but confessed that I was unable to make out what it had to do with me at the same time pointing t ) the the name on the form. "Well" snapped the tax-gatherer, "it's your name, isn't it? " "No, incited," I mildly protested, handing in the card. My double again, of course. And for once in a life time the tax-collector apologised —he did positively, in fact, he was ever so nice about it. Just fancy! lam rather given to bragging of the unique experience. NEVER-TO-BE-FORGOTTEN. The concluding sentence of the foregoing paragraph brought to mind an exploit of an angling friend of mine who msny years ago had the good fortune to I ok a 311 b. trout. He not only called his neighbours together to rejoice with him, but he also summoned an artist, and, not content with sardines in oil, had the counterfeit presentment of the precious trout permam ntly done on canvas—ia generous proportions, too, you may be sure —and, duly framed in substantial gilt, it now has pride of place in the best room, and serves as text for an oft-repeated et my. The record thus constituted has never been beaten by my friend, and assuredly never will be—for with his best cipture he laid his rod aside for ever, having no hope of any- thing better to swank with than that ugly (the adjective is mine) little oil painting. ESPERANTO. What I read in my" Examiner" last Saturday tic t me thinking of the international language and the test which I set rrtyseif some time ago. Since then a member of my family has taken it up, and now regularly corresponds in esperanto with fellow students in various parts of the won 11, including not only places like Rotterdam, but a remote corner of the Russian empire. It is now a simple matter to pay a pop visit to the Continent, for in every port and city there are Esperantists who will welcome and guide and help in every po Bible way the English visitors—who of course will at any Ono be ready to return the com- pliment. Truly someone has put it, the ideal of a univei sal, language—an international language which would exist side by side with the national languages is a noble one. Nationalism, untempered by faith in the brotherhood of man, is in tiatiger of becoming a narrow and lifeless creed, just as an intarna- ti malisna which refuses to be interested in the free- ing of the varied individualities of the nations is a mere barren reaction against the wr )ng sort of pataio- tism. True nation ilisrn and internationalism are the same thing appi-oaelied from different sides Both of them aim at a brotherhood of man, which shall be a brolerhood of groat individuals great individual men and %TOMEI., and great individual nations. I( is for nationalism of the better sort that Esperanto stands with its wiser advoca'es. PROFI P-SH ARING. I have had opportunities of studying at close quarters at least two co-operative productive concerns based on this principle, and one of them, commenced in a humble way by a handful of working men, received the benediction of men of such eminence as the late Marquis of Ripon, Judge Hughes, author of "Tom Brown's school days," &e. I was present on different occasions when these gave their blessing to the enter- prize, and it certainly has been amazingly successful. Lord Robert Cecil declares that co-partnership is not only good business for empleyers and employed but good morals as well. Mr. A. Williams, hon. sec. of the Labour Co-partnership Association, puts the claim thus:— 'that the manual worker should have, besides his interest in a high wage and short hours and good conditions of work, a direct interest in the amount of wealth produced by his labour; that he should have a share in the capital with which he works; and that, taking as part owner of the capital part of the responsibility of the enterprise, he should obtain, eventually at any rate, a shareholder's voice in the control of his own industry. These conditions obtain in the Co-operative Manufacturing S.;cieties of Warrington ? I have brit. fly written from personal knowledge, and there are no dis- putes. As to this point, Mr Williams xplains " We do not desire to takeaway the worker's incentive to demand a higher wage, reasonable hours, arid good conditions, and to combine with his fellow-workers in trade unions to attain these. Quite the contrary. But. we desire that he should have more than mere wages can ever give him, and that the oruel harshness of the industrial conflict should be softened by some measure of common interest." Suppose the railways and the mines were worked on the pi inciple hero advocated. It seems to me the possibility of a strike in either of thetee great national concerns would be exceedingly iemote. At present,as the authority whom I have already cited says, it would seem that these conflicts are inherent in an organization of industry based upen mere wage-se-vice' because it divides the necessary agents in the production of wealth into two great armies : those who provide the capital, enterprise, and controlling po aer, and those who provide the muscular force and manual skill, but have no interest in the capital, and, save through their trade unions, no voice in the control of their industry.

div.head: CHEAPER STEEL
div.p: CHEAPER STEEL
No Blast Furnace Required.

It, is reported that what might easily prove an epoch- nmking invention in the steel trade has been evolved. This is nothing less than the discovery of a process for converting iron ore of any grade (even the hitherto quite useless iron sands, of which hundreds of millions of tons exist ready for working) into steel of excellent quality without the aid of the blast furnace, the steel being produced direct in a single operation. Tests have been made (says the " Standard "I of the steel so produced at an experimental plant, the result obtained being something quite n markable. By the new process the saving will be enormou; In the first pi cc n 1 blast furnace is required, and there- fore, no coke. This means an enormous saving of capital expenditur,,, as well ag econotioy in production, while ores can he used which at the present time have no market value whatever. The ore is reduced by the heat obtained from gas, which in its turn is produced from slack. It is claimed that steel can be made at out-third of the preteut cost.

div.head: DROWNED IN THE CANAL.
div.p: DROWNED IN THE CANAL.
Lire-Saving Appliances Wanted
at Peaketh.

The question of insufficient life-saving appliances was raised at an inquest which was held at the Red Lion lon, Penketh, on Tuesday, by Mr F A Jones (deputy coroner) into the circumstances attendiag the death of Wm. Murdock (65), of 7, Gatewarth-street, who was drowred in the St. Helots and Sankey Canal on Good Friday. The evidence was to the effect that the,deceased left home at 6 a.m. on Good Friday morning to visit friends at Widnes. At 8.30 in the evening he called at the Ferry Inn, Fiddler's Ferry, was served with a pint of beer and remained 20 minutes. He was in a sober con- dition. About half an hour atter deceased left the house, Mr Henry Burthem,licensee, was told that a man was in the canal near Fiddler's Ferry Wharf. He and several others ran there and saw Murdock floating in the water. Ile was drawn to the side with a boat hook, but showed no signs of life. Artificial respiration was tried, but without success, A manure barge was moored at the wharf, and some of the mooring ropes were across the towing path in a slanting direction about six inches from the ground. Deceased was in the canal opposite to where the rope crossed the path. Robert Scott, mate on board the barge, said about 855 p.m. he was in his cabin when be heard a cry for help. He raw a man in the middle of the canal, about twenty lards from his boat. He could not reach him with his boat hook, and ran for assistance. P.C. Houghton said the mooring rope to the manure barge was passed under a rail at a gateway on the tow- ing path, and it crossed the path about six inches front the ground. It would be dangerous to people walking on the path, because if they tripped they would easily fall into the canal. A verdict of " Accidental death" was returned, and the jury added a r.der to the effect that the Penketh Parish Council be asked to provide some life-saving appliances near the place where Murdock fell into the water.

div.head: HOW LONG DOES THE STAG LIVE?
div.p: HOW LONG DOES THE STAG LIVE?

"The hart, as also the hind, are very long lived. being said to live about one hundred years. They are bred in most countries, but England is said to he the best." Thus says Mr Richard Biome, writing in the year 1600 or thereabouts ; and a little further he continues, in his account of the halt, which we to-day call the stag : "At one year old they have no horns, but )nly bunches; at the age of two years they appear more perfect, but straight and simple ; at thee years they grow into two speers ; at four, into three, and so increasing every year in their branches until they be tix ; and above that time their age is not known by their heads." _ _
To this testimony to the longevity of the red deer stag we may add that which is implied in the Gaelic prcverb :

Thrice the age of a dog is the age of a horse, lhrice the age of a horse is the age of a man, Thrice the al.'s of a man is the age of a stag, Thrice the age of a stag is thh ago of an eagle, Thrice the ago of an eagle is the age of an oak.
That is to say, presuming man occasionally to attain the century, that the stag might go to three hundred, an eagle to nine hundred, and an oak to two thousand seven hundred.

About the rest of the patriarchs we have no present concern, but it is rather interesting to try to discover on what, if any foundation, rests the idea of els great age attained by the stag. We may dismi,s the three hundred years theory as a freak of the imagination captivated by the arithmetical charm which has always seemed to linger about the magic number three ; tut it is certain that there has been in the past a very widespread faith in the stag's often reaching the age of a hundred pars, or theteabouts. We thcught it might be of some further interest to make enquiry of a number of owners and tenants of deer forests and others who have have had opprtunity of learning much about the life-story of the red deer, in order to see whether the experience cf any of them gave any ground what- ever for the ancient faith in the longevity of the stag. It may be added that it is by no means a wholly lost faith. Then.) are some conservatives who hold still to the belief in the existence of occasional centenarians among stags. We hardly find them, however, among those whose opportunities for knowing their subject have been the most extensive. Of all who have been goad enough to give us the benefit of their experience only one put the limit of age reached by the red deer stag at higher than thirty years.—" Courtly Life."

div.head: MR. URE AND TIIE OPPOSITION.
div.p: MR. URE AND TIIE OPPOSITION.

Speaking at the Scottish Liberal Club, Edinburgh, on Saturday night, the Lord Advocate svid that to-day the Liberal party found itself with its fortunes higher and its prospects brighter than ever since they took office in 1906. Ile did not attribute that entirely to their own virtues ; they owed a debt of priceless value to their political opponents and their twin leade-s. Tariff " Reform " had become a long and fl eiting array of incoherencies and imtecilities. The insanity of the latest phase of this policy was obvious It was not merely insane, it w.:s impossible, for the proposed Colcnial Conference would never meet and the pro- posed sec nd general election would never be held. Every sane political partiain knew that the policy would he all or nothing.

The death has occurred at Northwich, of Mr John Little, aged seventy-two, who ranked as the oldest Mid. Cheshire Volunteer. Joining the first Northwich Company over fifty years ago, he was also the first to join the Cheshire National Reserve, in which be waa keenly iuterested. The deceased man was a native of Northwich, his father being a salt proprietor. For some years he was in business as a painter, sabsequently becoming Northwich agent for an insurance company, retiring a few years ago after over thirty 3 oars' service. He WAS probably the most familiar figure in Northwicb. He was an ardent Liberal and Free Churchman.

div.head: VISITOR.
div.p: THE VISITOR.

"Has anyone been here to-day, mother, while I was away ? " Effie had been away all day since breakfast and now it was supper-time, and daylight had faded out of the sky, and the moon's silver sickle was hanging 'Above their heads. "Lot me see," said mother, putting on her thinking cap. " Yes,l have had one visitor" "Oh ! have you, mother? Who was it ?" "She did not tell me her name," said mother, with a little smile. "Did not tell you her name? How very queer! Where did she come from ? " "She did not say." " What did she come to our house for ?"_

"Ah ! for several reasons. For one thing she cured my headache; she brought me a letter from a dear friend ; she gave me a new book to read; she put a rose on my table, she finished a piece of sewing for me, and gave me some swee.t new thoughts." "What a strange visitor!" murmured Effie. " Was that all ? " "No, she wanted me to do many things for her. She asked me to make broth for a sick girl, to write two letters offering to help two people to pay a visit, to make a pudding and several other things." " And did you do them for her ?" " I did some of them, and some I left I undone. I wish now that I had done them

all." " [would give anything to see her, mother. Will she ever come again?" "No," said mother, "she cannot come again , because she died at sunset." "Died, mother? How dreadful! And yet . you are smiling. I think you are joking somehow. Are you ? " " Not joking exactly, Effie dear, but I am talking in a little parable, which I think you can guess when I tell you that her sister is coming to-morrow at sunrise—her twin sister, so like my visitor that no one could tell them apart, though Fome of her gifts and some of her wishes will be different from those of to-day's guest." "You say you don't know her name, mother?' " I didn't say that. I said she did not tell me her name. But I do know it; it is Thursday." "Thursday ! 'Cried Effie, laughing. "You just mean to-day, then ! " " Yes' to-day." And then your visitor to-morrow will be named—"

"Friday, of course." Effke was very much amused .at the idea of the Thursday visitor and the Friday visitor ; but when she woke up in her little bed the next morning, she said softly : " How do you do, Miss Friday? I wonder what you have brought me to-day? At any rate I am going to do all the things you ask me, 'cause you have to die at sunset, you know." And right away, Miss Friday asked the little girl to get up and dress and go smiling downstairs.

But when I'm at my Grandpa's house, He hands me out a book, And let's me choose a place to read; And then he'll sit and look At me, and listen, just as pleased— I know it from his face; And when I read a great long word, He'll say ' Why, little Grace, Ycu'll have to teach our biggest school, Some cne o' these bright days! Mother, you come and hear this child V That's what my Grandpa says.

Bowes had a good appointment at Newton as registrar RN- htia and relieving officer. He (Mr Knowles) did not know what the Warrington Guardians thought. At one time if they were purchasing anything from baby linen to coffins, and selected an outside firm, they heard a shout of "Give your orders at home."
