The Rev T R MATTHEWS said the law and the Gospel sometimes appeared at variance, and on that occasion he begged to point out that Mr Knowles, representing the law, was not correct in his statement. They were not going out of Warrington for this officer. The CHAIRMAN: You must remember that Mr Bowes is ai veryNoloEffis : I see allceroafours. Mr K L that. The Rev A M MorcuEn also took exception to the objection that they were going outside Warrington. They had to deal with the Union and not with Warrington only. As to the suggestion that a man was too old at fifty, Mr Mitchell remarked : "Well, lam over fifty and I don't think lam too old for another post yet." Mr Klsowees : Those people (presumably the electors of Winwick Division), thought you were too old, you know. The Rev A M Mnrostees, strongly disaent,ed from the view that because a man who had done good service was over fifty years of age, he was not eligible for another appointment which would bring him more emoluments and be a little easier for him. He supported Mr Bowes' appointment because he was an old servant of the Board and because he would be all the better for a little easier position. Mr Bowes had not been well for some little time, but he was better now. There was, however, little doubt that relief from the duties of relieving officer would be -of great benefit to him. They all respected Mr Sutton who was a very nice, genial young man of considerable ability, but he bad the advantage of being young and ha could afford to wait. If Mr Bowes was to receive anything in the way of easement and betterment, he should receive it now. With all his heart, concluded Mr Mitchell, he cordially supported the appointment of Mr Bowes. Mr HOUGHTON said both the can lidatrs were excel- lent man, but he supported Mr Sutton as a young man who had already proved his ability to do the work satis- factorily. Mr FURNESS also supported the appointment of Mr Sutton. He had a thorough knowledge of the work and enjoyed the confidence, not only of tbat Board but of the Registrar-General. It would be a very great hard- ship to place him entirely out of the running for the more important position. The system of promoting deputies to vacant appointments was a well-known one in the procedure of public bodies. Dealing with the question of age, Mr Furness pointed cut that the reason of Mr Harrison's resignation "was that the state of his he-.lth had not allowed him to give csnstant personal attention to the duties. If they appointed Mr Bowes they had no guarantee that his health would withstand even the mild and easy strain of the effi.ea of registrar. In appointing Mr Sutton they woald be doing what was right and jest. Mrs COLLING WOOD pointed out that Mr Bowes had performed the duties of relieving Meer and registrar for twenty-one years and lisd therefore had experience, far in excess of that of Mr Sutton, of registration work. lie had nothing to learn in that respect. The Board would certainly be doing what was right and just in appoint- ing an old official who had served them faithfully to an easier post. Mr Be urea was at present in goad health and if he only held the position for ten years, would it not he some reward for his long services to the Board ? The Rev T R MATTHEWS : Who has any gusrantee of future good health ? Mr B ACK HOUSE asked what Mr Bowes' present nen uneration amounted to? The CLERK said that as relieving officer Mr Bowes received £lOO per annum, and the registrarship would be worth about £lBO gross. After paying rent and other expenses, the combined positions would be worth about £250 or £260. Mr JOLLEY supported Mr Bowes' appointment. As a public body exercising the right of patronage, they ought to be guided by pubic rather than personal consideratk as To put the matter at its lowest, from the £ s. d. point of view tha line of action foreshadowed by Mr Mather would be the most economical to the ratepeyers. Any modification of it would involve a substantial addition to the Union expenditure. He would, however, put the matter on somewhat higher ground and he strongly desired to ass ,ciate himself with all that had been said in commendation of Mr Bowes' work. They had an opp )rtunity of paying a well-decerved tribute of good- will and respect to an officer who had served the Union faithfully for over twenty- years and be for one would not hesitate for a moment as to the course to be adopted. On a vote being taken the Beard decided, by 13 vote to 9, in favour of the appointment of Mr Bowes. Mr Bowes was called into the room and acquainted with the decision of the Board. In returning thanks he said the offiaers of the B )ard were delighted that the Guardians were considering old servanas and that they had something to look forward to. Mr JOLLEY gave notioe that at the next meeting he would move the appoin'ment of Mr F H Aukland to the post rendered vacant by the promotion of Mr Bowes. Mr MATHER gave notice that he would propose Mr F Gidman as Mr Aukland's successor. The CLERK to the Haydock Urban District Council wrote suggesting that representations should be made to the Registrar General with a view to Ilayd ,ck being made into a separate registration area, with a resident registrar of birth, death, <Sae It was pointed out that the Urban Dlatrict of Ilaydock had an estimeted population of 9,750 inhabitants, a rateable value of £30,815 and an area of 2,408 acres. Gmeiderable incon- venience arose under the present arrangements for registration, as owing to the awkward hours of attend- ance at Haydock,dwellers in that district were in many cases compelled to journey to Earlestown, three miles away, to register. The Board decided to reply to the effect that the Registrar General would not, in their opinion, enter- tain the proposal to create a separate district. In appointing a new registrar they would, however, endeavour to arrange more convenient hours for the residents of Haydock.

Criticisms of the system of dealing with contracts were made by the Rev A M Mitchell at the fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday. Mr E L Bent presided and there were also present :—Mr A J Jolley (deputy-chairman), Mrs Collingwood, Mrs Simpson, Miss Broadbent, Revs T it Matthews and A M Mitchell, Messrs J W Knowles, J Billinge, W Gill, A Brooks, W Fureess, G Allen, R Lee, J A Rushwortb, J Evans, W Flanagan, J A Hughes, J Backhouse, U Mather, J Cook, W Houghton, M W Seton, T Ritchie, A Bottomley (clerk), It I Partridge (assistant clerk), W J Brown (master), C E Lowrance (superintendent of Cottage Homes). During the consideration of the contracts for the coming half-year, the Rev A M MITCHELL asked how It was that the envelopes containing the tenders had been opened before the meeting. The CLERK replied that, in accordance with the usual procedure, the tenders were opened at the last meeting of the Board. The envelopes containing the name of the person tendering were, however, left closed. 'the Rev AM IdITdHILL remarked that he did not think sufficient precautions were taken in connection with the tenders. Mr A BROOKS: I dont% think that is a fair statement. The Rev A M MITCHELL : Was not a complaint made by the auditor a short time ago ? Mr A BROOKS: Yes, but the auditor knew nothing about what he was talking about. This Board has been most particular in trying to avoid every semblance of favouritism and unfairaess and we have achieved it, too. Mr MATHER said that he, along with Mr A Brooks and several other members, had sat there hour after hour to devise some schemo which would provide no ground for criticism, and he thought that at last they had got one. It had worked very well for a few years —so much so that he knew other public bodies had copied their method of dealing with tenders. Miss BROADBENT : The auditor never said the names were divulged. Mr A Bsoofts : The very tenders wlich he thought could be divided were those in, which division was impracticable. Mr Manisa suggested that in future, when tenders were invited, it should be intimated that in any case where the name of the person tendering was left exposed the tender would be disqualified. The CLERK said the instructions sent out by the Board when a person asked for a form of tender were so explicit that he was surprised that any firm could make a mistake. They really deserved to be disqualified, Mr A BROOKS : The fact is, I suppose, that the post- ing of the tenders is left to the office boy. The CLERK : Contractors have brought in forms themselves and they have been wrong. I have told them : "The name is exposed and you will be disqualified." Contracts; for the half-year were placed as follows For the Workhonse.—Wines and spirits, It Rowson and Sons ; tobocco and snuff, T Sudlow ; male officers' uniforms, E A Jones (twelve months) ; dressings, &c., A Brown, Ltd., Leicester ; men's suits, E A Jones ; leather, T Samuel, Liverpool ; drugs, Corbyn Stacey and Co, London ; paints, Davis and Co; tailors' goods, Lee and Clark ; brushes, Peers and Morton ; drapery, Lee and Clark ; groceries and provisions, E Richardson end Son boots &c, Porter and Co, Liverpool ; beer and stout, P Leigh ; thirds, &c, J Hallwood ; coffins, H Hough ; fish and ice, H Porter ; oatmeal and flour, J Hsllwood ; soda water, II 111 Ashton ; tea (inmates), J J Meakin, Mar chester (officers), Tetley and Sons, London ; coke, W Westwell; coal and steam coal, Pearson and Knowles, Coal and Iron Co, Ltd; meat, H Singleton; crockery, R Bailey ; e/ectrical fittings, etc., II Bibby ; ironmongery, S Green ; milk, A Broome (12 months.) div.head: SCALDING FATALITY,
div.p: SCALDING FATALITY,
UNSATISFACTORY STATE OF BOILER LIDS.

A Warrington jury recommended that the attention of the Corporation should be drawn to the lack of proper boiler lids in dwelling houses, after returning a verdict of accidental ci(ath in the case of a child which sustained fatal soalds by falling with one foot in a boiler.

At the Coroners Court on Tuesday Mr FA Jones, Deputy Coroner conducted an inquest on the body of Jessie Kirk, aged three years, daughter of John Kirk, general labourer, 3.38, Knutsford-road. The mother said that after lighting the boiler fire in the back kitchen she went to clean the front room. At 430, hearing a scream, she ran into the back kitchen and saw her daughter standing on the boiler with her right foot in the hot water. Her foot was badly scalded and she was taken to the Infirmary, where she died on Sun- day. Witness continued that her daughter had evidently gone to the water tap over the slopstone to get a drink, as she (witness) found an old chair near the sink with a cup on it. Having got on the chair she must have climbed on to the slopstone, which was only two feet and eight inches from-the floor, and from there to the boiler. There was no proper boiler lid, but she wed two pieces of wood as a substitute. Her daughter must have slipped on one of these and put her foot into the water.—A verdict of " Accidental death " was returned, and the jury recommended that the attention of the Corporation should bp drawn to the want of proper boiler lids in the hinges.

div.head: MR. W. H. HARRISON RETIRES AFTER THIRTY-FOUR YEARS' SERVICE.
div.p: MR. W. H. HARRISON RETIRES AFTER THIRTY-FOUR YEARS' SERVICE.
GUARDIANS AND THE NEW APPOINTMENT.

After thirty-four years' service Mr. W. H. Harrison has resigned the office of registrar of births, marriages and deaths for the Warrington sub-district, and on Wednesday the Warrington Board of Cluarc,ians recommended the appointment of Mr, Thomas Bowes (relieving officer and registrar for the Newton district) as his successor. The promotion of Mr Bowes will necessitate some re-arrangement of the staff of relieving

officers. The CLERK stated that he had received the following letter from the Secretary, Somerset House, London : I am directed by the Registrar General to state for the information of the Guardians that he has accepted the resignation of Mr W H Harrison, registrar of Births and Deaths for the Warrington sub-district, to take effect as from the 31st inst. With reference to the impending vacancy I am to say that the Registrar General observes that the population of this sub- district far exceeds that of any other in the registra- tion aistrict, and, while he has no desire to intei fere with the Guardians in the full exercise of their statutory right of appointment, I am to suggest that they consider the claims of other registrars in the Idistrict to promotion to the vacancy in preference to those of inexperienced strangers. The emoluments are undoubtedly sufficient to secure the services of a first-rate man. The CLERK also announced that he had received applications for the position of registrar from Mr E J Sutton (deputy registrar) and Mr Thomas Bowes. Letters withdrawing their applications for the appoint- ment bad been forwarded by Mr H Aukland (relieving officer in the principal Warrington District) and Mr R I Partridge (assistant clerk to the Board). Mr KNOWLES : You haven't advertised the post? The CLERK: No, sir. The Rev A M MITCHELL: Could you tell us what the emoluments amount to ? The CLERK: I could not. The Rev A M MITCHELL : You have no idea ? The CLERK : Oae can form some idea of what the position would be worth. Mr Knowles : £5OO a year ? The CLERK : I shall not asy that. Mr KNoWLES : Thera will be very little change out of £5OO, I understand. The CLERK : Well of course, if you know-- The CHAIRMAN (Mr E L Bent): I think this question is really out cf order. The Rev A M MITCHELL: I asked a question and I should like the Clerk to answer it. The CLERK : I am N% Ming to answer it, but there are other people asking questions as well. I say, as far as I am able to judge, that the position is worth between £350 and £4OO a year net. The Registrar has to find his own (files and pay the rental and everything concerning the upkeep. I am unable to get at the exact amount of the fees but, from my own knowledge, I should say from £350 to £4OO net. Mr W C BRoOKE3 : What is our position? When has the vacancy to be filled and what status have we as a Board? The CLERK said the appointment of registrar was vested in the Guardians to this extent—that when a vacancy occurred the Guardians must make the appoint- ment within fourteen days ; otherwise it reverted to the Registrar General. If, for some particular reason, the Guardians desired an extension of the period, they would have to write the Registrar. General, laying their case before him, and it would rest with him to give or refuse permission. Mr KNOWLES said he took it tint if the Board made a reasonable application for extension—say, with a view to advertising the eppointivent—the Registrar General would be bound to f.ill in with their wishes. The filliug of such an important post ought not te be rushed. People outside did not know that the job was to let and, if an advertisement were issued, the salary was sufficiently large to attract some very good applica- tions. Only their own officers could have had information of the vaaancy. Mr MATHER said that, in view of what the Registrar General had stated, he thought the Board might now take into consideration the filling of the vacancy. Ever since he knew there was going to be a vacancy, he had hnd in mind the fact that the Board hid many good officers who had served them faithfully for a long number of years. Mr LEE: And been well paid. The CHAIRMAN : If you don't mind, the resignation of Mr Harrison has not yet been laid before you. The CLERK than read the fc Bowing letter from Mr Harrison :—I regret that after a period of 34 years I have bad the honour of occupying the position of Registrar of Births,and Deaths for the Warrington sub- district. I have been requested by the Registrar General to tender my resignation in consequence of illness which has at times unfortunately prevented mel from personally attending to my duties which, ' however, have been satisfactorily carried cut by my deputy, Mr E .1 Sutton. I may say that I have now practically recovered from a long and serious illness, and am fully conlpetent (as per my doctor's certificate to carry out duties which have been so long entrusted to me. These I have faithfully carried out to the best of my ability. My resignation takes effect on the 31st ice. Mr MATHER went on to eulogise the work done by officers of the Bard in "an admirable, straight and honest manner." Some of them were well up in regis- tration work. Mr Bowes had served ths Board well for twenty-one years as relieving officer and registrar. The work in connection with the former position in the Earlestown district had been done at considerably below the price they would have to pay if the two offices were not combined. By promoting Mr Bowes to the registrarship for Warrington, to which he (Mr Mather) considered he was strongly entitled, they could put in his place at Earlestown Mr Frank H Aukland, who had acted as his deputy for m-.ny years and had also had charge of the principal district in Warrington for relief purposes. Mr Aukland was a young end strong man who was fully capable of carrying out the duties of the combined offices. He would also be willing to undertake the relief work from house to house, as required by the Local Government Board. In the event of the Board approving of Mr Aukland's promotion, they had a grand young officer in Mr F Gidnaan who was in every respect fitted to succeed him. The Board would thus be able to give a substantial advence to three good servants without costing the rat. mere an extra penny or causing the work to deteriorate in any deper tment. The only step then left for them to take would be to appoint a new officer in Mr Gidman's place. He formally moved that Mr Bowes be recommended to the Registrar General for appoint- ment to the registrarship. Mr BILLING,: said the emoluments of the registrar- ship were statutory fees and there was no necessity to advertise the vacancy. The Board was justified in con- ferring h.onorar upon one to elren honour was due and for that reascp he scpcnded the appointment of Mr Bowes who had enjoyed ttae supreme confidence of all the members of his committee. Mr HoueitTow : Do I understand the Clerk to ray that the Local Government Board would fill up this vacancy fourteen days from the receipt of the notice or from the date when it takes effect ? The CLERK: The Local Government Board have nothing to do with it. It is a Somerset House appoint- ment, by the Registrar General. The registration of Mr Harrison has been accepted to take effect from the 31st inst. If you make the appointment this morning it will be quite in order and will come into force on April Ist. Mr HOUGHTON questioned whether valid notice of the intention to make the appointment had been given. The agenda did not actually state that the appointment was to be made that morning, but only considered. The CLERK : It is for you to decide. ?,Irs SIMPSON : If Mr Bowes gets the appointment, what will be the position of Mr E J Sutton who has been doing ata work ? Mr FURNESS : We have fcurteen days in which to make the appointment. Does that date from the expiration of Mr Harrison's appointment, or from the date of the rceeipt of the notice. The CLERK ; I theuld say from the expiration of the appointrr ant. Mr FURNESS : That means that at the end of th's month we have fourteen days in which to make the appointment. .Mr W C BrtooKs, referring to the sugges'ed promo- tion of Messrs Aukland and Gidmen, said different Opinions had been expressed on several ocaasions as to whether the two offices held by Mr Bowes should in future he given to a single officer. Mr KNoWLES : They ought not to be. Mr BROOKS: If the two offices are not combined there will be no promotion for Mr Aukland or Mr Gidman. The CHAIRMAN: We are not really considering that question, Mr MATHER ; Jtls a very important question to my mind. The Rev T R MATTHEWS : Does the appointment of 'Nfi Bowes involve the appoiutrnent of other officers to any other position? Is it not a single appointment about which we are met to-day? (Hear, hear.) The CLERK (replying to Mrs Simpson) said Mr Sutton's position would be vacated, as far as the deputy-registrarebip lies concerned, unless Mr Bowes or whoever might be appointed registrar, could arrange to appoint him as deputy, The question of deputy was entirely in the bands of the registrar, Subject •to his (the Clereg) approval, Mr KNoWLES : Is it a fact that Mr Button has done the work for twelve months? The effAIRMAN ; He has done it practically for that time. Mr KNOWLES Without complaint? The CHAIRMAN: Yea. Mr KNoWLES said that in view of that fact and of the recommendation of the Registrar General that someone esperienced in the work should be selected, he proposed that Mr glutton should have the appoint-

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Court Mourning.—The death of King George of Greece has placed most of the Royal Families of Europe in mourning, which will be worn at our owe Court for four weeks, changing to half-mourning on April 9, and going out of mourning on April 16th. This will not serioualy affect the social world of London, but it has greatly upset the arrangements for the Dublin Castle season, which Las been unfortunate in this respect for the past three or four years. Last year it was affected by the death of the Duke of Fife, the previous year the period of mourning of Ring Edward had not expired, and the year before that Lord and Lady Aberdeen were in mourning. The late Kiri; of Denmark died on May 16th last year, and that more affected the London season, which does not commence until the end of April. During a period of Court mourning no member of the Royal Family or their representatives can be present at a dance but in half mourning they may attend race meetings, dinner parties and other functions. St Patrick's ball which was to have been held in Dublin on March 28th, has conse- quently been pcstponed Had no Drawing Room or official dinners can take place in the Irish Capital until after April 9,11. The King will be unable to pay his project° I visit to Lord and Lady Derby at Knowsley for the Liverpool races the first week in April, but later on in that month, their Majesties will go to Crewe Hall on their promised tour in the district of the potteries.

Law --Prescribed Faihions- —ln several countries where the Legislature takes a fatherly interest in the population under its care, laws are already in force concerning women's dress. Long skirts which raise the bacilli laden dust, the wearing of plumage birds in millinery, high heels, and dangerously projecting hat pins, are some of the things which have been forbidden, but in Ohio, in the United States, a Bill has been intro- duced in the Legislature to prescribe the fashions to be worn by women, and to set up a State oensorshiP oi ifi edgraels st. T h e wueiairmi nega measure if passedpifenw ork n t blouses, law wouldtransp amr kn et stockings, and practically prohibit the dkollete gowns. The censorship empowered to forbid anything of an impudent or far-tetched nature in fashion; would consist of a commission of three members one being an ordaineU minister of religion. It remains to be seen what the Ohio leaders will think of this proposal, but it has been promptly answered by the women of Chicago, who consider, that if men are to dictate to women in the matter of fashions, women should have the same authority concerning masculine attire. They object to bald heads, and wigs for all men thus afflicted with nature's mistakes are one of the things demanded by the National Bureau of Correct Dress for Men. Daring Modes. —The Ohio Legislature may possibly frame laws concerning women's insufficient attire, but it would be another thing to carry them out. At the same time there are a goad many people both in America and Europe, who ate wondering how far the craze for scanty clothing is to be allowed to go. It can not be denied that the tendency of the present day is to go from one daring mode to another not only in ballroom fashions but in every day wear. Some evidence of this is afforded by the attempt to push the vogue for the" slashed" skirt. The "hobble became the "trouser" skirt, and Paris is now sending to London the skirt divided on one side. At first it began with only a small slit to enable the wetorer to walk more freely, but in the later models, the skirt is " slashed as far as the knee and one sometimes wonders where the quest for bizarre, or sensational effects will end. The War on Flies.—The British Museum has recently Issued a penny booklet on "The housefly as a danger to health." It is by Mr Austin of the Department of Entomology and is an authoritative work on a subject which has been much before the public in recent years. No one knows what the summer may bring forth, but the housefly certainly appears to be less of a nuisance than it used to be. Whether or not it is due to the campaign against it, or to partible dustbins and other modern sanitary improvements, it behoves everybody to keep the house as free from the pest as possible. That the fly is a disease carrier is beyond all question, and in this timely issued booklet we are told that it is "a dangerotis enemy whiph should te destroyed and kept in check by every possible means." Sunshades for the Summer.—The shops windows are full of summer attire of all descriptions, although bitter winds have beat blowing and snow and hail storms have been passing over. Among the harbingers of summer, to be found in the West End windows, are sunshades of the lightest possible description. Judging from their diversity, they follow this year the lead of fashion in everything, and are made of every likely and unlikely material, and in every shape that strikes the designer's fancy. Those now on show are covered with the most delicately painted chiffon plain or spotted net with broderie Anglaise lace, figured silk, moire, brocaded and plain velvet and plain silk. And as the summer advances even more fanciful materials are to be employed, so it is said. Furthermore any combination of two or three of these materials is to be observed on one sunshade. A Diversity of Shape and Size.—ln shape and size there is just as much diversity—some are circular, others oblong, pyramidal, dome-shaped or flat like the Japanese. These gosamer sunshades, of bizarre shape are not for every day use, but intended as a finish to a dainty toilette which they complete, or to which they give a note of c, ntrast. For protection from the rays of the sun there are many new and useful, and at the same time charming designs in a variety of materials, and a bewildering diversity of colours. To buy these beautiful and expensive accessories so early in the season, shows no small amount of faith in the belief that a warm summer is in store for us. Last year'll experience appears not to have daunted the many who purchased early in order to be prepared for the hot . weather that never came. This year, however, may . prove kinder, and the charming frippiness that are so tempting may have a chacce of being worn in bright sunshine under cloudless skies. The New Coiffure.—The coiffure to suit the small bat is necessarily of the simplest, and gradually the fashion for elaborately puffed and waved hair, bas given place to the smoothest and flattest arrangement of tresses. These must however he or appear to be, abundant, of a glossy and satin smoothness. The front hair is brought low on the brow, and over the ears, then it is spread out towards the back, where it is rolled and held in place by means of a fancy comb. The hat fits on the roll which often comes quite low in the neck. When the hair is waved it is almost imperceptibly undulating—a mere ripple in fact—and this is in keeping with the ()reek style which has inspired the change.

MANAGER AND HIS FIRM. At Widncri Police Court on Monday morning the case of Henry Stewart Dunn, who was charged with embezzlement, was mentioned by Mr Madden, barrister, who appeared on his behalf. Dunn was employed se manager of the Widnes branch of Messrs Barker Bed Compat 37. of Widnes and Blackpool, and the alleged defnloations are said to amount to £l6O. Mr Madden applied for a remand fora week and said that there was the prospect of the arrangements being come to between the defendant and his employers hi which the money would be refunded. The application was granted.

game" and prove that they were, in more than name, true citizens of no mean village. (Applause.) Their congratulations were also due to Captain Kershaw for haviug formed a company of the National Reserve. There was one thing that Lymm was all right in, and that waa the martial spirit. In one respect, however, it was sadly lacking, and that was in not having a GOOD. ACTIVE RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION. During the last twelve years the Tradesmen's Associa- tion had taken up and safely carried through matters ehich properly belonged to a ratepayers' organization, had one existed. It as during c,ises such as they were passing through at the present time, that a favour- able opportunity presented itself for the forma- ticn of such a body. The could not all be councillors, ,but they could try to do some little thing to further the i nterests of the place in which they lived, and such an organization would serve to keep alive interest which at present only seemed to crop up when an election was taking place. It would also be a help rather than a hindrance to the gentlemen who gave their time and experience to public affairs, and would form an excellent school for prospective candidates for Council honours. He threw the sugges- tion out for what it was worth. With regard to the trade of Lymm, the " Daily Mail " a few weeks ago published a long article in which it was stated that the trade of Lyn= was booming. He thought be was speak- ing for all the tradesmen of Lymm when he said they would like it to boom a little louder. (Hear, hear.) With Lymm Hall, Oughtrington Hall, and Beechwood lying empty—and he believed those three residences reprtsented something like a two penny rate— it could not do otherwise than mike a great differ- ence to the trade of the villace. They welcomed the advent of the Vice-Chancellor, Mr Stewart-Smith— (applause)—end sincerely hoped that he would never have occasion to regret the °holm) he had made (Applause.) They hoped the taking of Lymm Hall might be the foreshadowing of the occupation of Beechwood and Ooghtrington Hall in the near future. (Applause). In conclusion Mr Evans appealed to the members to _ _ _ _

Ignore allrelfish ends and interests of thine own, For he lives for little good who lives for self alone." (Applause). The Rev G B Thurston, in responding, expressed his appreciation of the kindness of the association in inviting him. The clergyman's life was one that required very much sympathy from the parishioners. He was appointed to perform certain duties which were not always very acceptable to the people and it was necessary that,in spite of what might be said,he should go straight forward without fear or favour. Therefore one needed very much the sympathy of one's brother mem- bers of the community. A clergyma often did things which he knew were bound to be unpopular and make him sometimes, more .than one ought to be, a butt for a simple and cheap jest. It was therefore a great pleasure to him, whether at the Church Inn, the Spread Eagle, or the Fleece Hotel; to meet such a representa- tive gathering as that, knowing that most of them had b3eo very good friends to him and had helped him in many a difficult situation. He was one of the newest- corners to Lymm, which spoke much for the attractive- ness of the place, for he bad been there fifteen years. (Applause.) To anybody who had eyes to see and who could go about witn his nose a little above the ground and his thoughts above worldly things, there was very great inspiration in a place like Lymm. There was not only the charm and beauty of its surroundings, but, having studied tbe archteology and history of I..iymrn, he could never pass along its streets without being accompanied on his way by the many thoughts which the place provided. The room in which they were assembled that night had 120 years ago a very close and sad connection with tbe Rectory in which he lived. It was the old Coroner's Court, and he bad at home the notes of the Coroner's inquiry held there into a great tragedy which happened at the Rectory. He did not want to go into the story, because perhaps it would not he very edifying, but it presented a very interesting picture of the Lymm of those days. "I am supposed to sleep in the room winch the ghost inhabits' added the Rector. " Many people have told me they would not sleep there for hundreds of pounds, but I have slept tbere for fifteen years and I have not grown very much thinner." (Laughter.) If they had minds to catch the inspiration of historic scesies, they need never be dull or find Cymm uninteresting. They hoped i always to make progress n the future. They always placed before their minds' eve some great: and noblecity on the site on which their charming little village dwelt. That vision might or might not materialise but, speaking to gentlemen who were very much interested in the commercial side of Lymm, he would say that those who had had some experience in life and who could judge of a place thought they could see a

HAPPY AND BRIGHT PROSPECT FOR. LYMINI. ,Applause). Perhaps it was not quite the thing for a clergyman to say, but be was a great believer in luck. He thought that in one's life there were waves of fortune and misfortune. There were some lives which fortune seemed to smile upon, and others which mis- fortune seemed to dog, but most of us bad our ups and downs. All the indications at present pointed to the fact that Lymm was on the up-grade. It was generally the case, when great changes such as bad been made in Lymm during the last two years happened, that they gave the dice a kind of jump-up, so that it came down on sixes instead of ones. it looked very much as if that were the case at Lymm. Just when many of them were regretting the departure of a valued and generous friend of Lymm—Mr W Peter Rylands—and were expecting to find another "to let" board displayed, they bad the intimation that,following the letting of Lymm Hall, a very good tenant had been found for Dingle Rank. (Applause.) With the making of new roads and the can) uag out of other improve- ments, he hoped they would soon have all the large residences in occupation and that they would not to continue to lose that two pence which they wanted so much for their district rate. Most of those who had hearts in the right place, continued the Rector, had a very warm place in those hearts for the tradesmen of Lyinm. It was a great grief to see them as they often did—struggling against adverse ciroumstaoces. They bore up bravely and put a bold face on the situation but those who knew the inside of things realized that much sympathy was needed by those who had sunk their capital and were getting their living in Lymm. If he could speak without impertinence, he believed the tradesmen of Lymm, as a class, stood extremely high compared with tradesmen in other places. He did what little business he could with them, and be To sorry, on their account, he had not a ;vile an ten children. (Laughter). Congratulat- ing the association on the secretaries who • had served it so faithfully, the Rector spoke of the clean, straight tight which Mr F E Evans put up for Counql honours and said that if he would consent to stand when next a vacancy arose, they need have no fear of his return. (Applause.) In a few graceful and humorous phrases the Rector spoke of Mr Daniels as a poet and a prophet, and added that he cast a kind of higher light over such a dull thing as a trading association. In conclusion he appealed to the members, to what- ever denomination they belonged, to take to heart what Mr Daniels seid in his report as to the association consisting of relieious men. Religion was the secret of all life,and of all inspiration, decency and niceness iu intercourse, social or otherwise, and to have such a lesson taught them in the annual report of a 'trades- man's association was something for which Lymm had cause to be thankful. (Applause.) Mr DANIELS proposed' Our guests." He said they were proud of the members of the Council,and honoured them as men of standing and sound common-sense. To prove that the public thought well of them, they had only to take the result of the recent poll on the water- works question. It showed that the public appreciated the work done on their behalf by their elected representa- tives. The members of the association were proud of the fact that they had a citizen of Lymm who bad been counted worthy to be called upon to occupy the important office of High Sheriff of Cheshire. (Applause.) They felt it to be no small honour to Lymm. (Applause.) Lymm was proud of Mr Watkin and he only wished they could see him oftener in public assemblies, for his character commanded respect and admiration. They would bear in mind his promise of what he woild do for them on Citizen Sunday., (Applause). Mr 0 G Smith responded. He said the members of the Urban District Council. who for the moment enjoyed the confidence of the ratepayers, did not always find it smooth ssilinit, but public life had its compensa- tions and the kindly feeling shown to them by the tradesmen's association was one of them. (Applause) Mr W G Groves, in proposing "The entertainers, " said the District CounoiLlika the Tradesmen's Associa- tion, bad had a prosperous year. They had, however, gone through very hard work—in fact some of them bad been working almost night and day. They had done it for the benefit of the ratepayers of Lymm and did not begrudge it. As to the advisability of young men joining the Territorials, he did not believe in con- scription, hut there was no pne in that room who took a greater interest in the Territorial force. He joined the Volunteers before be was seventeen years of age, and he remained in that force until they turned him out (Laughter.) To-day he was happy to say he was a mem- ber of the National Reserve. (Applause.) He thought it was the duty of every young man to join the Territorialsit would do them far moregood than devot- ing all their Saturday afternoons to football. Mr W Cooke responded. Mr Watkin proposed the health of "The President." Referring to the compliments which had been paid to him, he said he was not the first High Sheriff who had lived in Lymm. They all remembered with a great amount of affection Mr Lyttleton Dewhurst who was taken away from them at far too early a stage of his life, but who did a great deal for Lymm. His (the speaker's) only wish was that when his year of office was over it would be said of him, as it was of Mr Dewhurst, that" he did his best." (Applause). A most enjoyable musical programme was submitted, the accompaniments being played with taste and skill by Mr William Cooke, A.R.C.0., organist of the Parish Church, who also gave a pianoforte solo in finished style. Songs were pleasingly rendered by Messrs H E Odber, J W Gibbon, Levi Thomason, G H Parker and E Creasey. Humorous ditties by Mr J Bircball and Mr T Warburton met with great acceptance.

The musical items were given by the following : Mr R Wallington pianoforte solo, and song by Miss Alice Lawton. Miss Dutton gave two abort recitations and a humorous sketch was given by Misses ttuth and Edith Tanner. At this stage refreshments were banded round: At the last social it was arranged to bold a " Shilling competition" in aid of the forthcoming Wesleyan bazaar. div.head: Urban Council and the Provision of Workingclass Dwellings.
div.p: Urban Council and the Provision of Workingclass Dwellings.

"It is beyond dispute that we have in Lymm a very great scarcity of cottages for working people. In tact, I think it is understood that a good cottage cannot be obtained for a lot of money." Those were the opening sentences in a speech made by Mr It H Gotobed at the Urban District Council meeting on Thursday, when he proposed the following resolution : "That it be an instruction to the Housing and Town Planning Committee to conisder the desirability and practicability of this Council adopting a Housing Scheme for the provision of workmen's dwellings and to report to the May monthly meeting of the Council." Mr Gotobed continued that the shortage of cottages was one of the main causes of overcrowding. They had undoubtedly numerous cases of overcrowding, some very gross cases indeed, where conditions obtained which violated every sense of decency and broke the elementary rules of health. From that point of view he thought the matter ought to be considered at the earliest possible moment. As a public health authority they, in common with other bodies, were endeavouring to stamp out consumption and yet they had people living together in those bedrooms in the small cottages, producing a vitiated atmosphere and encouraging that disease which they were studying to avoid. They lied cases of two families living together in one cAtage and numerous cases of young people (iesirous of getting married unable to find a home for themselves. teor those reasons he thought they ought to press for- ward with the question. He thought they were suffer- ing from a policy of exclusion which bad been exercised in the past on certain estates in the district. The erection of cottages was discouraged on certain estates and the result was that they could not meet the demand of the growing population. With the impending indus- trial expansions, the demand would become more and more insistent and it would have to be met in some way. There were two ways of meeting the situation, one was by private enterprise and the other by municipal action. He would much prefer private enterprise, but person- ally he could not see that private enterprise was going to meet that pressing need. As the health authority and the authority responsible for the housing and general welfare ox the people of the district, it became imperative that they should consider fairly, in the interests of the ratepayers, that question, and

FIND SOME SOLUTION whiLh would obviate the pressing needs Which were manliest throughout the district. Tney could get a type of cheap cottage with three bedrooms. He thought if they took the whole of the cottages in the d strict, they would find that less than 10 per cent. had three bedrooms, and that 00 per cent, had what welts known as "two up and two down." No cottage ought to be built with less than three bedrooms... Of course,

if they passed that resolution, those details would be thrashed out in committee. He was absolutely opposed to anything in the nature of subsidy. If tbey found that they could not build cottages at a fair figure which would meet all outgoings, he would be opposed to the Council taking action. Ile would be opposed to the rates being charged with any portion of the necessary payment for the loan incurred by the building of cottages. They ought to do everything in their power to enable the cottagers of the district to obtain whole- , some and decent condition's. (Hear, hear.) Mr Locker seconded. Mr liolt said there was no question about there being a scarcity of cottages at the present moment, but it was as well to examine the causes of the scarcity. Mr Gotobed had said that the estates were to blame but he (the speaker) thought they could scarcely put the blame on their shoulders. Land could bo got in the neigh- bourhood and he had had some offered to him that week Mr Gotobed : My remark referred to years gone by and tot to the present time. Mr Holt: I wanted to make that clear. What is the reason for this scarcity ?—The Government are responsible, for the chief reason that they have put a second income tax on the builders in the form of incre- ment duty which is a most unjust tax. Continuing, he argued that until that tax could be removed building c.ievelopments would be kept back in all the districts. All the profit was taken from the enterprise. Until that unjust tax was removed there would still be a scarcity of cottages, for people would not invest their money in building. If they, as a Council, could do any- thing he did not object to it. The game was not worth the candle to builders because of the second income tax —the increment duty. It was most, unjust and he thought— _.

Mr Smith: We are not expressing any opinion 013 the controversial point raised by Mr, Holt. I don't think that explains the matter. The increment duty is only 20 per cent on the value. Mr Welford said they were not there to enter into a political discussion. He was opposed to Mr Gotobed's resolution,not on principle—be was quite a supporter of municipal authorities taking over those enteprises where the need for such elite:prises was fully and amply shown—but there was a time for all things and whatever one's opinion might be on the principle involved in Mr Gotobed's resolution, he thought the time for such a resolution was at present most inoppontune. They were a small Urban Council and were at the moment engaged in two very large enterprises, one of which was to carry out a new sewerage scheme which that Council never sought but which had been imposed on it and which would involve the district in a considerable addition to the rates in the coming year. That in itself should give them pause and make them investigate a matter of that kind very searchingly. Then they had the purchase of the waterworks and the possibility of large additions and alterations in connection with the gas works. 'nose would mean a large expenditure of money and,although tbat Council had been unanimous in the view that the purchase of the waterworks would add hardly anything to the rates of the district, yet that development of the waterworks was in the future and just what might happen, if tbey had those impend- ing industrial developments at the Heatley end of the district, no-one coul d foretell. The Council should be very slow in embarking on anything which might com- mit it to an expenditure, the magnitude of uhich it was impossible to foresee. He had no knowledge of any cases where the building of cottages bad been a financial success. He did not say there were no cases where the enterprise had ever been a success but he bad never come across one. lie knew of several incidents where there had been a substantial financial loss to the district which had bad to be met out of the rates. H e was not even open to " consider " the desirability at the present time. Very much as he sympathised vath the objects he thought they as a council DARE NOT UNDERTAKE

anything of that kind at the moment. Mr S Davies said Mr Welford had just expressed his views entirely. He suggested the matter should stand over until the Council got better off. If they were not very careful they were going to laud themselves with a large rate in the district. The Chairman (Mr W G Groves) would not say he was opposed to the scheme. If they accepted the suggestion of Mr Gotobed they could appoint a small committee to go into the question and that would not put the Council to any expense, if they found out that they were not going to get any return, then the thing would be off. It was appalling to think of the number of persons who were asking for cottages. They would never have an increased population if they had not houses for them to live in and for that reason he supported the resolution. Mr Warburton said it seemed to him that from which side they looked at the matter they were viewing it in I a right way. Cottages were needed. They would have an increased population and the developments at the Heatley end of tbe village, and es a mult cottage property would go up. (Hear, hear). Mr 0 G Smith said that if Mr Gotobed's resolution involved any immediate expenditure he would certainly oppose it at the present time, bee ruse he thought the arguments that Mr Welford put forward were unanswer- able. They should take the resolution simply as an instruction that they consider and investigate the matter. If they did that it would advertise the whole community and that might result in bringing some enterprising firm in the field to do something to meet the pressing need. Mr Gotobed deserved their heartiest thanks for bringing the matter forward The shortage of cottages was a most insistent and recognised evil. If the resolution was only to investigate the matter and report, he eartily supported it. it Mr Gotobed prefaced his reply with tbe remark: "Sympathy without relief is like mustard without beef." He was, however, grateful for the sympathy that had been extended to him. He did not attach so mech importance to the expenditure the Council was com- pelled to undertake, as he did to the health, comfort and housing of the people. There was a question far greater and more important than sd, and that was the health and well-being of the people, which to him was paramount. (Applause). The resolution was carried.

div.head: URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Lymm Urban District Council was bola on Thursday evening in the Council Chamber, Mr NV G Groves presiding. There were also present :—Messrs T H Warburton (vice-chairman), G L Welford, 0 a Smith, J H Holt, S Davies, W Gould, H H Gotobed and F Lockyer, W Ariullard (clerk and collector), D Mort (surveyor), and W L Donaldson (gas manager). APPOINTMENT OF OVERSEERS.
On the proposition of Mr Welford seconded by Mr Warburton, Messrs W G Groves and S Gould were re-appointed overseers of the parish.
SCHOOL RKPRESKNTATIVES.

Mr Groves was appointed the representative of the Council for the next three years on the board of managers of Lymm Elementary Parochial schools and Statham schools, and Mr Warburton will represent the Council on the management of Ougbtrington school.

THE PARLIAMENTARY BILL. The Clerk said the Lymm Parliamentary Bin might come before the House of Commons for the third reading at any moment and evidence might have to be given. Unless a general resolution was passed, no member had power to attend. He wanted the Council to pass a resolution that any member of the Parlia- mentary Committee, including any offichls, whom the solicitor desired to attend, should be eppowered to do so. The Council agreed to this course.

THANKS To THE CHAIRMAN. Mr S Davies proposed a vote of thanks to the Chair- man for his services during the past year which he said would always be remembered in gratitude. Mr 0 G Smith seconded and said Mr Groves had been the right man in the right place during the strenuous times of the past 12 months. He had worked hard for the Council and the good of the community, (Hear, hear.) Tee resolution was carried and the chairman in reply thanked the members for the way they bad supported him in his work. The year had been a hard one but the work bad been shared among them. It was intimated that the annual meeting of the Council will be held on April 17th at 5.30.

LECTURE AT THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL —At the Grammar School, on Wednesday night, a public lantern lecture on the work of the Arethusa, and Chichester Training Ships was given by Mr II G Copeland (secretary). There was a large attendance to hear the lecture and witness the splendid views that were shown by Mr W Moss, jun. NEW CONGREGATIONAL MINISTER.—We understand that the Lyirnra Congregational Church has given an uminimons and vary cordial invitation to the Rev Arthur Penaliggon, minister of the Bucklow Hill Con- gregational Church, to become pastor of the Lymm Church conjointly with that of Bucklow Hill. Mr Penaliggon has accepted the call, and will commence his pastorate on the first Sunday in April. BANK HOLIDAY. —Besides the wreck of the "Solway Prince," reported elsewhere in this issue other attrac- tions in Lynim on Easter Monday were the whist drives at Mr W Brookes's Pleasure Gardens, and the dance organised by the Lymm Sunscription Band which was head in the Tennis Court, Oughtringtou. In addition to the usual bank holiday visitors there was a large number of the members of the Friar's Green Independent Methodist Church and Sunday schools present in the village, being well catered for at Mr P Warburton's farm.

OUGHTRINGTON ST. PETER'S.—For the observance of Holy Week, Gr,od Friday, and Easter Services at the Ouehtrington St. Peter's Church, the Vicar, the Rev E P Wethered, M.A., has had the co-operation of Father Millard, of the Community of the Ressurrection, Mirfield. Pesiles the usual observances there were two special services on Good Friday. One, devotions on the Pt ssion, wa4 held from 12 to 3 p.m., that is during the isist ihree hours our Saviour hung on the Cross, in uhich various hymns, prayers, and addresses were given, the other being a lantern service in the evening, showing scenes from the Passion, with hymns and a iciresit s.

REV E PARKER'S WEDDING ADVENTURE.—The Rey Edward Parker, late of Lymm, who some months ago accepted the pastorate of the Baptist Church,Leicester was married at Wisbecti. Cambridgeshire, on Thursday the 20th inst. After the reception he with his wits left by motor for Peterborough, and London. When, about two miles out of Wisbech, as Mrs Parker was leaning forward shaking the confetti from her dress,the car collided with a lurry and she was thrown forward through the glass front of the car. Her lip and face were cut, and Mr Parker had his hand and wrist cut in the endeavour to save his wife, in addition to which both bride and bridegroom were suffering from shock. The car was disabled but they eventually arrived at Wished] where they stayed until Tuesday last, when, we are glad to say, the bridal pair were sufficiently recovered to resume their delayed journey to Bourne- mouth. AT THE PARISH CHURCH.—At the Lymm Parish Church during the Holy Week and Easter cervices, which have been well attended,the Rector, the Rev G B Thurston, M.A.. has bad the assistance of the Rev R A Cochrane. On Good Friday evening a lantern address on " Our Lord's Passion" was given by the Rev R A Cochrane. The life of our Lord during Passion week, terminating with the Divine tragedy of the Cross, was vividly portrayed by the speaker. Beautifully hand. painted slides were shown by Messrs W Moss, sen. and jun. The offertories on Good Friday were given to the Chester House of Mercy, and those on Easter Day, amounting to nearly £32, as an Easter offering to the Rector. TEMPERANCE MEETING.—On Thursday night the Lymm Branch of the National British Women's Temperance Association held a public meeting in the Primitive Methodist schoolroom, when th.e president Mrs G L Weltord occupied the chair. The speaker was Mrs S J Hodgett, national organiser of the association, who gave an address on the society's working methods. On the proposition of Mrs Welford, seconded by Mrs Edwards, the following resolution was sent to the Prime Minister :—" That the Lymm Branch of the N.B.W.T.A. urges the Prime Minister to delay HO longer the fulfilment of his pledge that he would place the 1908 Licepsing Bill on the Statute Book as soon as the Parliament Act set the House of Commons free to carry out the legislation demanded by the people. and prays him to introduce the long promised temperance measure in the session of 1913." A vote of thanks to Mrs Hodgett was also recorded.

FREE CHURCH SERVICE.—The Lymm Free Churches held a united service on Good Friday morning in the Zion Chapel, Cherry-lane, when there was a good repre- sentation of all the nonconformist churches present. The preacher was the Rev it W B Whiteway who chose as his text 1 Cor. i., 18 ; speaking chiefly on the power of the Cross of Christ. All that is noblest and best in every country finds its centre round the Cross. Its story being the force behind all the finest art, music, poetry, devotion, Sco. The preacher said that the story of the Cross inspired people with the same spirit that dwelt In His own heart- "AU the works of regeneration centre round the force of the Cross of Calvary for it is the power unto Salvation." He told his hearers that if they had this power in their own lives they would be a blessing to others,who would thank God for their lives. Appropriate hymns, prayers, and Bible reading also formed part of the service. Miss Greenman presided at the organ. LOCAL WEDDING.—On Saturday afternoon last, at the 143 mrn Primitive Methodist Chapel, and in the presence of a large assemblage of friends, the marriage between Bert ram Wellington, son of Mr and Mrs Drink- water, of Sandy-lane, I.yrnm, and Esther, second daughter of Mrs Appleton. widow of the late Mr James Appleton, of "Thorne Cottage," Statham, was solemnized. The bride, who was charmingly attired, in a dove coloured cashmere ere's, with black hat and white plume was given away by Mr W T Moss. The bridesmaids were Miss M J Appleton, Miss M Appleton (sisters of the bride), and Miss M A Clare ; whist the duties of best man were performed by Mr Drinkwater (brother of the bridegroom. The Rev RW B Whiteway was the officiating minister. During the service the hymns " The voice that breathed o'er Eden," and "Since Jesus freely did appear," were sung ; wedding music also being played by Miss Welford who presided at the organ. A reception, largely attended,was subsequently held. The happy couple were the recipients of a large number of useful arid pretty presents. CHAPEL TEA AT BROOM EDGE.—Tbis year the annual Good teridav tea at the Broom Edge Primitive Methodist Chapel was as successful Ili ever. The efforts of a capable force of caterers in the persons of Meedames H Champ, G W Cross, Ford, Lawson, Reid, Scott, Whiteway ; the Misses Champ, Cro.s, Perrin, Priest net. ; and Messrs Cross, Perrin, and Reid,delighted the" two sittings" necessitated by the attendance of a large number of L3mcu and Altrincham friends. After tea a miscellaneous concert was pro- vided by the Al tr incham Primitive Methodist choir, %hose efforts during the past three years at various Lancashire contests have secured them several first prizes. They gave delightful Interpretations of the part songs "How calmly the evening,"" A request," "Moonlight," " As the moon's soft splendour," " Come to me, gentle sleep," "God sends the night " ; and the anthems" Holy, art Thou" (Handers celebrated Largo), and "0, clap your bands," the latter, one of their test pieces we believe, being very finely rendered. The rest of the programme con- sisted of a duet "0 Jesus T have promised " by the Misses Mabel and Doris Evans, and solos by Mrs Norwood, •"The lost chord " ; Mrs Barber," I think" ; Mrs Thomas," Lead kindly light," the charming singing of which brought requests for an enco-e which was responded to by that nopropriate song "There is a green hill" ; Mias Wardlow, " The King of love " ; Mr G Smith, " Saviour Divine " ; Mr Biddulph, whose bass voice was beard to such advantage in `• Curfew " that he bad to be recalled, giving "Within these sacred bowers " as an encore ; Mr H R "'['he Good Shepherd." In his opening address the cbaliman, Mr GL Welford, offered the choir a hearty welcome. He congratulated both the choirmaster (Mr J A Hills and the choir members on their successes and hoped the? would continue their victories. At the close of the entertainment the Rev R W B Whiteway in proposing g vote of thanks to the Altrincham choir expressed his appreciation of their performance. This was seconded by Mr J Perrin, supported by Mr G L Welford, and heartily carried. Mr Hill in responding, said tbat the choir members were enthusiasts, and thanked the audience for their appreciation.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

WESLEYAN CHURCH.—To-morrow (Sunday), Rev Edward Davidson will commence an Evangelistic cam- paign in Padgett, Wesleyan Church. A young people's service will beheld on the afternoon of the first Sunday and a service for men only on the afternoon of the second Sunday. A Bible reading will be held on the Thursday afternoon at 3. A meeting will begin each evening at 7.30. Mr Davidson entered the ministry in 1886 and stands in the front rank of missioners. His addresses are powerful and convincing. WESLICY G CILD.—The usual weekly meeting was held on Monday evening. The Rev E Morgan presided, and a paper was read by Mr Ward on " Victor Hugo, his work and ideals." Extracts from the poetic and prose work of the great French writer were read. In pro- posing a vote of thanks to the lecturer Mr Plinston took occasion to criticise the exhibition of films at the Picturedrome protesEing to illustrate "Les Miserables." Mr Newton seconded the proposal of a vote of thanks and it was therefore accorded. The Lecturer replied in suitable terms. PARISH COUNCIL—The concluding meeting of the old Council was held on Tuesday night. Mr R Denham presided and there were also present Messrs Critchley, Howard, Potter and F Wright (clerk). Among the ordinary routine businets the following resolution was unanimously adopted. Proposed by Mr Howard, seconded by Mr Critchley, " That. t,his Council desires to place on record its appreciation of the many years of service of Messrs Dr Bennett and James Houghton as members of this Council."

div.head: ORFORD.
div.p: ORFORD.

-- EASTER SERVICES.—Two services were held in thel church of St Margaret and All Hallows, Orford, on ' Good Friday—matins at 10.30 a.m. and evensong with a musical service at 6.30 p.m. Both services were con- ducted by the vicar, the Rev 0 Vale-Owen. Solos were sung by Miss E Brownbill," The Gate of moray," Mr J Gibson, 'The Guardian Angel," Mr W Knowles, "City Glorious," and Master A Hackett, "Angels ever bright and fair." The Easter Day services were com- menced by members of the choir singing hymns from the top of the church tower at 7.30 a.m. Holy Com- munion was celebrated at 8 o'clock. Matins and Holy Communion followed at 10 30, children's service at 3 o'clock, and evensong and sermon at 6.30. Solos were sung by Mr W Knowles, "But thou didst not , leave," (Handel's Messiah) and Master A Hackett, "I know that my Redeemer liveth " (Handel's Messiah), and the choir sang the anthem "I will arise," and a chorus from tbe Messiah, "And the glory of the , Lord." All the services were conducted by the Vies r

div.head: MR. B. S. TOWNROE AND LIBERAL FOOD TAXES.
div.p: MR. B. S. TOWNROE AND LIBERAL FOOD TAXES.

Sir,—Under the above heading, in your local contemporary, appears the follovring :—Addressing the Newhey Habitation of the Primrose League on Saturday last, Mr Townroe said "Since the Liberals came into power, however, they had actually imposed something like .1:66,000,000 ot taxes on food. The Unionist party intended, if possible (the italics are mine) to take some of the taxes off food, that were at present imposed by this Free Trade Government. " Now, Sir, if Mr Townroe is an educated man, and I think a 'Varsity man, I want to ask him a question. What does he mean by saying that the Liberals have imposed ;4:66,00000 of taxes on food and further, what did he intend his bearers to under- stand by this statement? Mr. Townroe, and quite a number of other ambitious but very superficial students of politics, posing up and down the country as "Prospective Unionist Candi- dates," are trying to foster an impression that the Liberal Government have created new or additional food taxes, whereas these young and inexperienced politicians know, or ought to know, that the very opposite is the truth. Food taxes for revenue purposes only levied on articles not produced in this country (and not protective) have been collected every year from the time of the abolition of the Corn Laws until .now, and the great and only difference between the Tory and the Liberal policies has been that every change in the amount ot these taxes collected annually which the Tries have made (with rare exception) has been by way of increasing them, while the alterations made by the Liberals have invariably and substantially lessened them. _ _

Mr Townroe's promise that the Tories will—"if possible"—take " some of the "Taxes off, Food," is- -well really, too qualificative to deceive a child. Neither Mr Townroe nor any of the more experienced Tory candidates has given the slightest hint'as yet, as to how they are going to replace the present revenue from customs duties on tea, coffee and the like,without resorting to protective duties on corn and meat. Kendal has just shown us what the northern folks think about Food Taxes. Is Mr Townrce a bupporte r of Imperial Preference? If be is, let me advise him to study "fiscal " plitics a little more seriously and conviction will be forced upon him that Tariff Reform in all its phases, is theoretically, financially and fundamentally rotten, that such a policy as it involves can only add to the fierceness of the struggle for decent living amongst so many of our workers, 'Which even now is almost too grey ions to be borne, and then when the scales have fallen from his eyes and he sees and feels the light of better knowledge,
let him apply his admitted -abilities on sounder and more enduring lines to the eocial, material and spiritual betterment of his pocrer brethren.—Yours, FREE TRADER. March 21st.

div.head: CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY AND POVERTY.
div.p: THE CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY AND POVERTY.

Sir,—Some few of us have exerted ourselves lately to draw attention to the "War against povetty campaign that has been going on in the country. We thought that locally the working class organisations *ere very much behind other towns in this respect. In nearly all towns of any importance the Trade -Union, Socialist and Co-operative Societies have joined hands in holning conferences, meetings, etc., to discuss and protest against this great crime against nature and reason. Our efforts here, however, have been met with the wintry blast of indifference and absolute opposition instead of the warm summer breeze of encouragement. The controlling fbction of the local Co-operative Society have been especially energetic in stemming every source that sought to bring the poverty question into publicity. Personally I sent a letter to the " Wheataheaf " (which I would be glad if the Editor of the " Examiner " would print) giving my reasons for believing why the Co-operative Socuity should take a hand in dealing with this question. But a brief acknowledgment was never so much as tendered. Courtesy and good manners are ever so cheap. I also understand that attempts were made at the quarterly meeting to bring the matter before the members, but the autocratic manner in which certain members of the committee dealt with the promoters certainly makes one believe that the local Co-operative. Society is under the domination of an oligarchy, and not, as boasted, under the direction of all its mea,bers One ineident will serve to prove this statement. The chairman ruled the movers of a resolution, asking

the Co-operative S, ciety to take the poverty question up, out of order. When challenged to quote the rule which put the mover of the resolution out of order, the reply was given that--in the rule book it was stated that "the chairman's decision shall be final."
I hope you will give this matter the publicity I think it deserves, and let us hope that it will bring something of a tangible character.—Youre truly, LABOR OUNIA VINCIT.

div.head: To THE EDITOR OF THE " WHEATSHEAF."
div.p: To THE EDITOR OF THE " WHEATSHEAF."

Dear Sir,—As a young man who has interested oneself in all appertaining to the advancement of the working class from poverty end ignorance to msterial'welfare and enlightenment, I have been much interested In the progress and furthet develop- ment of the Co-operative movement. I can only express my appreciation feebly of the part the Co-operative movement has taken in the advance of the workers, but it is whole-hearted. But I often ask myself if the Co-operative move- ment has done as much as it ought to do for the working class. IVe know that it provides a dividend, a good quality of goods and a certain number of educational lectures' not to forget a good amount of amusement. These things are excellent in their way, but somehow I have come to the conclu- sion that the movement hardly expresses itself in the manner in which the founders of the movement intended.

We know tbat,at lenst,9o per cent of its members are "in the stores" for the " divi." There is an amazing amount of ignorance of the fact that the founders of the Co-operative movement started the Co-operative idea as a means of tackling the poverty question. Now it is my opinion that a working class organisation like the Co-operative Society ought to be in the vanguard of the army that is working to abolish poverty, and that they ought to use every means to remedy this great contradiction of life. For poverty is absolutely unnecessary. Science has so far advanced that economists are agreed that we can produce, at least, ten times more than we can consume of food, clothing etc. But whilst I believe that the movement is developing along lines that are correct, what is it doing to allievate the present great dis- tress ? Locally, we are not even considering the question. What I want to know is why is not the local society falling into line with large num- bers of co-operative societies that are now joining hands with Trade Union and Socialist Societies in the " war against poverty" campaign. These orgaoiastiona jointly are working hard up and down the country in working up public opinion so as to Wing pressure upon Parliament nest session to do something with the poverty problem. The agita- tion takes the form of conferences to consider what is hest to do to reduce the great evil, and also publio demonstrations addressed by leading men and women in the country. What I should suggest is that locally something similar should be done. I feel that if nothing resulted of a tangible character the members themselves would be greatly benefited edricationallv.—Your (Ste. LABOR 01INIA VINCRNT.

div.head: Zxarainer, Saturday, March 29.1913.
div.p: The Zxarainer, Saturday, March 29.1913.
THE WRECK ON THE SHIP CANAL.
THE RAISING OF THE

A vessel was sunk in the Manchester Ship Canal, within two miles of Latchford Locks, on Saturday afternoon, as the result of an accident remarkable alike in its suddenness and in its immediately disastrous effects. A coasting steamer named the Solway Prince, belonging to Messrs. Clark and Grounds, of Runcorn, left Partington Basin with a. cargo of 220 tons of coal for North Wales. She had reached Statham, which is on the straight course to Latchford Locks, when she swung broadside across the canal, owing, it is said, to a jamming of the steering gear. At the moment when the Solway Prince thus fouled , the course the steamship Rossmore, of about 280 tons light, owned by a Glasgow company, was proceeding in the opposite direction and she was so close upon the seaward-bound vessel that a collision could not be avoided. The Solway Prince was struck near the bows and several of her plates were rent. Water poured in and the crew, numbering about ten had only just time to make their escape in a small boat before the Solway Prince sank. In five minutes she was almost totally submerged. With the Solway Prince lying at right angles to the ,Lancashire bank of the canal, it was feared that the waterway would be impassable. As a matter of fact there was a complete stoppage of traffic on Saturday, while soundings were taken to ascertain the ; exact extent of the interference with safe navigation. Early on Sunday morn-
SOLWAY PRINCE IN THE SHIP CANA

ing it was found possible to allow coastwise traffic to proceed as usual, as there was a channel 40 feet wide and 28 feet deep still open. Practically all vessels of 1,000 tons net register and under were able to get through in safety, but most of them were towed past the wreck by tugs which were kept continually in attendance. The canal, however, remained blocked to ocean liners for four days,and eight big vessels were held up. Throughout Sunday and Monday thousands of people from Warring- ton and district gathered to witness the salvage operations, and the little village of Thelwail, which has the nearest railway station to the scene of the accident, was as thronged as its neighbour Lymm which is •a favourite resort on a fine Bank Holiday. The masts and funnel of the Solway Prince were visible above the surface •of the water. Divers, cranes and lighters were kept busily at work, the 'first operation —a lengthy and tedious one—being to remove the coal from the hold of the sub- merged vessel. In order that direct com- munication with the various locks might be established, an emergency telephone station was erected on the Lancashire bank, and progress was coutinually reported. The Rossmore, which was only slightly. damaged about the bows, left for Eastham at ten o'clock on Sunday morning. _ _
It is recalled that this is the first accident of any moment that has happened on the

div.head: MR. PARKER ON PROFIT SHARING.
div.p: MR. PARKER ON PROFIT SHARING.

Sir,— Seeing that Mr. Parker is anxious that his main cointention should not be side-racked, might I suggest that he leave out such subjects as temperance, Tariff Reform &c., and treat the suoject as an economic problem. lam exceedingly sorry that his coeteuu- plation should have been obscured to the possibilities of the cudgels being .taken up by an industrial Socialist (whatever that may mean). Pet haps Mr. Parker thought that his subject should pass unchallenged by any except those who are equally desirous of obscuring the real issue. In fact he says he confined his remarks to the workers generally. He therefore did not expect any particular worker would trouble to air his views. Fortunately the correspondence columns of the press do not lend themselves to any such exclusiveness. Mr Parker says the points I raise are fit subjects for academic debate, but do not come inside the scope of the present subject. Of course academic reason- ing presupposes scientific perception, which is not good for superfical economics. Take the conclusions of Mr Parker in relation to labour displacement by machinery. Be takes up ..my point that a higher intensity of labour displaces men, and immediately concludes that I agree to machine smashing lice the Luddites. Or, in other words, all who start from the same point must inevitably arrive at the same destination. Now the Luddites were certainly correct in tracing their poverty to the macbine, but they were as far from the solution of the problem in machine smashing as Mr Parker is when he advocates profit- sharing or co-partnership. Let it be understood I have never opposed the application of labour saving devices. My grumble is in the workers' failure to obtain the benefits. It can be proved that co-partner- ship is unsound economically, that is to those who do require a solution of the poverty problem. Mr Parker says that interest is the reward of they who work the business and take the risk. Now who does work the business? Does the cap,talist, or does he buy the brains of men of ability who are just as much wages slaves as any other workers? With regard to interest on stored labour, it would clear the air somewhat if Mr Parker told us whose labour is stored and how the accummulation of the said labour is brought about. This might be academic reasoning, but it is essential to a clear understanding of the process. When Mr Parker quite sympathetically accuses me of looking on work as an end instead of only a means of producing wealth, I can only say that I look upon work as a regrettable necessity ; a burden which should be borne by all alike; a task which has been forced upon the workers by they who store their labour for them and claim a reward for risking that which is not their own. We are informed that the demand for labour depends primarily upon our wants. I have never known our wants to be satisfied, but I have seen labour unemployed. Why this contra- diction? How is it that the worker is always wanting and yet they who could supply his wants are pariodi cally unemployed? Thousands of children in Lancashire are ragged and bootless at the very moment that we are trying to dispose of the goods they want at the other end of the world, and in the face of this we are informed that want is the basis of labour, without a statement why that want is not supplied. Again Mr Parker sacs that where there is competition, a higher efficiency results in the cheapening of the article. That is true, but it is only part of the s ory. The workers also compete for jobs, with what result? Wages tend to a bare existence level. The cheaper the goods, the less the worker can live upon. Adulterated foods produce cheaper wage slaves. The modern house wife knows only too well that many of the cheap food stuffs are little more than garbage. Two women in every three are always attempting the impossible, i.e. trying to make the Li go to 2.55. They are always grumbling about prices instead of wages. This craze for cheapness, this short-sighted economy is a curse. A system is to he judged by ita effect upon men and not by the pelf it produces. " What shall it profit a man if he become a co-partner and lose his souL? "

--There are two ways of allying the poverty problem. One way is by men organising to control their own destiny ; the other is by allowing capitalists to do it for them. Co-partnership is necessary to the latter course ; it lays the foundation for the factory cast system. You may have a well-fed, well-dressed, well- groomed and well-boased slave, and he is still a slave. You may pander to his tastes and grant him little privileges, but you cannot make him free. Freedom comes by the way of self-assertion.—Yours etc., CHAS. DUKES (Secretary, Trades and Labour Council).
