div.head: SANATORIUM QUESTION
div.p: THE SANATORIUM QUESTION

At a meeting of the Health Committee, the Town Clerk reported on the Conference recently held in Liverpool on the suguestion for the provision of a Joint Sanatorium, and the Committee, after hearing his report, adhered to their previous decision that it is undesirable for Warrington to join with any other authority in view of the fact that tbey are in a posi- tion to carry out their own arrangements.

div.head: COUNCILLOR LASIIFORD'S ALLEGATIONS.
div.p: COUNCILLOR LASIIFORD'S ALLEGATIONS.
The following correspondence has passed, between the Town Clerk and Councillor LasHord :
Town Clerk's Office, Warrington,llarch 703, 1913

Dear ir,—At the meeting of the Health Committee held on Wednesday last the statements made by you at the Conned meeting on the previous evening, with reference to the acceptance of tenders by this Coin- mittee, were referred to, and the Committee pqssed a resolution instructing me to invite you to attend their next meeting, and tie they are anxious to investigate the whole m tter thoroughly they will be glad if you will give them the information in your possession. I shall also be glad if you will let me know as _ _
early as you can the names and addresokes of the individuals to whom you refer, so that their tenders may be looked up—Yours faithfully,
J. LYON WHITTLE
59, Ohorlerstreet, Warrington, March 17th, 1913
. „ . , Dear air,—ln reply to yours of the 7th inst , I absolutely decline to give the information in my possession to the Health Committee implicated in my htatements in the Council Chamber.

I do not consider that they have any right to sit in judgment on this ease. if they are anxious to have this matter investigated I must insist upory the matter being investigated in open Council, or in public.—Youra faithfully,
FREDERICK T. LASHFORD.

The Committee expressed their- regret that Mr Councillor Lashford had refused to give them the information to enable his allegations to be th Toughly investigated, and expressed the hope that Mr Laslaford would give the Council, at their next meeting, ate information which he states he has in his possession.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

The special Easter holiday programme has attracted a large number of patrons to the Hippodrome daring the week and the vaundeville menu provided has I proved palatable to numerous tastes. Fiiend and Downing, the popular Hebrew comedians, are well placed at the head of the bill and are delightfully• funny as cross-talkers with an abundance of up-to-date gags, which are witty, breezy and clever. Something new is introduced in the way of parodies on rag-time songs, a most popular number being the one on " Alexandars rag time band," We should have to. travel far to find the equal. to the Pasquali Bros., a, really clever tri ) of tumblers, acrobats and equilibrists. There is a neatness and smartness about the turn which at once impresses the on-lookers. With astonish- ing rapidity and dexterity, these daring performers go through the most intricate of evolutions, to be rewarded with unstinted applause. A special feature is the neat band to hand and head to head balancing on the part of two of the troup. A recent pantomime favourite, Mr Arthur White, who played the part of Sammy Blenkinsopp in the "Pride of Byzantia " presents a screaming comedy spasm. The New Detective." Mr White is ably supported by a charm- ing comedienne and a clever comedian and be is to he congratulated on submitting such a mirthful, racy sketch. There is one long laugh from beginning to end and although the theme is somewhat gost.amer- like, one cannot suppress laughter at the utter absurdities introduced by the Yorkshire dialect comedian. Winifred Ray is welcomed for her smart songs and stories which she gives in a piquant manner. Georges Bass is a comedian who pleases, his make-up being especially good, worked somewhat on the lines of that popularised by George Formby. His patter and songs were well received. Frank Maura, the Mexican Wonder, gives a novel and pleas- ing turn. Lying on a stand with his feet in the air, Maura controls and manipulates a light barrel and table in a moat dexterous manner. Rolando Martin, described as a comedian and patterer, also appears to the delight of the "god." "The Fisher Girl's Romance" is a romantic picture stoly shown on the cinema.

div.head: L NEAR LATCHFORD.
div.p: L NEAR LATCHFORD.
canal in the Warrington district since the disaster in the early days of the undertaking, when one of the gates of Latchford locks was carried away by a vessel. THE VESSEL RAISED.

It was not until noon on Wednesday that the operations for the raising of the sunken vessel were carried to a successful conclu- sion. Over 100 men were engaged, under the direction of the chief engineer of the company And scenes of remarkable activity were witnessed before the waterway was cleared for all traffic. On each side of the Solway Prince NVLS a "camel. "—a specially con- structed type of flat boat—to which wire ropes were attached after having been passed ;under the wreck. When everything was in readiness the " camels " were sunk by means of water which was subsequently pumped out, causing them to rise and so to lift •the ship. The Solway. Prince was then swung close up to ' the north bank, pending further measures to remove it altogether. No accident of any kind occurred throughout the operations. The removal of the obstruction opened the waterway to an almost continuous stream of traffic, and between the hours of twelve and five nearly forty vessels, sufficiently large to necessitate the opening of the swing bridge, in addition to a multitude of smaller cra'.'t passed through Latchford. The largest was the Median which carries 10,000 tons and is of 4,000 tons net register.

div.head: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.
div.p: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.

INTERNATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP. ENGLAND WINS. At Juvisy, near Paris, on Easter Monday, there was a large concourse of spectators to witness the representa- tives of England, France, Scotland and Wales taking psrt in what proved to be quite the fastest and best class 'ace of the series. England maintained her unbeaten record, but only after a fiplendid exhibition of team racing, at the Frenchmen shewed clearly that they intend to be topsswyers at the game. The course con- sisted of about 1,800 metres on the Aerodrome, about 150 metres of easy plough, and abut 3,400 metres of " upend down "forest land ; three laps were necessary to complete the distance-16 kilometres (10 miles). The going was very fast with the top on the bard side— too hard, in fact, for men who follow a winter sport in flarep climate—and was considered favourable to all the Frenchmen. The race aroused a wonderful degree of excitement among the French spectators, and the strong running of Bonin was greatly admired. All along he seemed a certain winner for the third year in succession. The French team was out-pointed in the later stages and were eventvally beaten by 23 points by the all round excellence or the English team. div.head: GREATER WARRINGTON.
div.p: GREATER WARRINGTON.
WILL STOCKTON HEATH COME IN?
A REPORTED CHANGE OF VIEW.

The one topic of discussion at Stockton Heath is the proposal that overtures should be made with the object of securing amalga- mation,on favourable terms,with the borough of Warrington. It is expected that all the oratorical big guns of the village will be brought into the firing line at the parish meet- ing which is to be held on Monday evening to discuss the question which everyone admits is fraught with great possibilites to• the future develpments of the suburb. On ,Wed- nesday evening the Parish Council met, apparently with the object of traversing some of the ground in advance, but when the important business was reached the members promptly resolved themselves into committee and what transpired we are unable to state. Yesterday Mr. James Whitley, the chair- man of the Parish Council, was interviewed by a representative of the " Examiner" and indicated that opinion was not quite so gener- ally in favour of amalgamation as appeared to be the case at the annual parish meeting held last week.

"There are signs" said Mr. Whitley "of a distinct reversion of feeling in many quarters. Ratepayers who were at first very favourabry disposed towards amalgamation are now becoming sceptical, if not actually opposed to the project. A great many people would be sorry to see Wallington absorb Stockton Heath, and contend that we should receive no tangible advantages in the long run. They are NI favour either of remaining as we are or of seeking to establish an Urban district." _

Questioned as to the reason for the opposition to amalgamation, Mr Whitley pointed out that differential rating for a period of fifteen years—as was allowed on the occasion of the last extension of the borough boundaries—had been generally spoken of. Fifteen years, however, was only a short term in the life of a community and on the expiration of that period, Stockton Heath would undoubtedly be liable to a tremendously higher rate. It was not inconceivable that they would have to pay lOs in the X whereas he considered that there was little likelihood of the rates of Stockton Heath advancing beyond 6s. 6d. in a like period. By remaining under the present regime a saving of 4s in the X might therefore be effected." _ _

Our representative reminded Mr. Whitley that concessions in the prices of gas and water might reasonably be anticipated as an immediate consequence of amalgamation. Mr. Whitley, however, said some of the inhabitants of Stockton Heath were doubtful whether the advantages to be gained under those heads would be sufficient to justify the amalgamation, in view of the certainty of an ultimate serious advance in the rates. With regard to the introduction of electricity which the Warrington Corporation might also take in hand, he pointed out that gas production, particularly, with regard to incandescent lighting, had reached such a stage of perfection, that it was no mean rival to electricity and moreover it did not cost as much.
On the question of the rating of property, Mr. Whitley said the overseers of Stockton Heath were in the habit of making consider- able deductions which caused the assess-

ments, from the house owner's point of view, to compare very favourably with those of Warrington,. Another aspect of the question'on which Mr. Whitley laid some stress was that the roads in Stockton Heath had been practically re-Made, with good, solid foundations, and were therefore likely to stand the strain of traffic for years to come. He admitted that the sanitary arrangements were not altogether adequate for a parish of the import- ance of Stockton Heath, but the authorities had adopted a progressive policy and considerable additional improvements would no doubt be made in a short time. Already the water carriage system had been largely adopted and every effort was being put forth to improve the sewerage system. • "Then you don't think Warrington would be able to do this work for you any better than you yourselves can carry it out 2" asked the reporter.

Mr -Whitley expressed some doubt on the point and added that in time Stockton Heath might have a destructor of its own. Notwithstanding his frank statement of the objectors' point of view, Mr Whitley is, however, disposed to give sympathetic con- sideration to the amalgamation proposals if the advantages can be convincingly demon- strated.
There appears to be every prospect that the parish meeting on Monday will appoint a representative committee to enter upon preliminary negotiations with the Corpora- tion.

div.head: TERRIBLE DEATH OF A CHILD. Former Warrington Man's Crime.
div.p: TERRIBLE DEATH OF A CHILD. Former Warrington Man's Crime.

A terrible affair occurred in Darlington late on Satur day night, the seven-year-old girl of a wireworKer nailed Walter Scott (formerly of Warrington) being killed by the smashing of her skull with the butt-end of a gun. Scott returned from work on Saturday morning and remained indoors for the rest of the day. He retired to bed at the same time as his daughter, who was named Lottie, at ten o'clock, his wife following an hour later. Scott, who had complained of severe pains in the head, went downstairs soon after his wife entered the bedwom, and she, knowing he was unwell, went after him. On reaching the kitchen she found him with a razor in his hand about to make an attempt to cut his thlost. She closed with him and secured the razor, but in the struggle he is alleged to have attempt el to strangle her. She got the better of him, and took the razor upstairs, secreting it in the child's bed. When she returned downstairs with the child, her husband continued to complain bitterly of pains in the kead. She decided to go to the doctor, and had hardly got into the street when the thought occurred to her that her husband might do the child injury in her absence. She hurriedly returned to the house, just its time to see him striking the child vith the butt-end of a gun, the blow smashing one side of the child's head and lace. Tha woman ran into the street, and neigh- bours attracted by her cries went into the house. Scott rushed into the street and exclaimed "1 have killed my child. I have killed my child. God gave me strength to do it. Take me away." He was seized by two men and banded over to the police. Scott is a native of Warrington, and prior to going to Darlington in July he worked for three years in Sheffield.
On being brought before the magistrates Scott, who pleaded guilty, was remanded with a view to committal for trial.

Mr Norman Peter Christie, of Hoddesden, a director of Messrs Christie and Company, tha well-known brewers, was killed while hunting at Hayford Bury, Herts. His horse shied aud Mr Christie was unseated, falling violently on his head. He sustained concussion of the brain, and died on Wednesday morning without baying regained consciousness.

DUCKS HATCHED BY HENS. Give ducklings the opportunity of nestling under d hen for the first week or two, especially when hatchea early in the year or when cooped as they should be later in the season in the open air. At a fortnight old they can be placed three or four broods together with one hen, and will do much better than if allowed to remain by themselves. Ducklings which are intended for market will make more satisfactory progress if kept in an enclosure by themselves, and not allowed their liberty at all. When they are allowed to wander wherever they like they spend the greater part of their time in the neighly,urhood of a stream or pond, and require more food. This does not mean that the ducklings should be confined entirely in small tuns ; they should be placed in a small enclosure fenced off in a corner cf some field if no other opportunity offers, and not be allowed access to stream or pool. If it can be managed they may be allowed out in the grass field in early morning and late at night on a slug-hunting expedition. They generally return from such ramble with their crops filled with (to them) very dainty food. If, however, during this ramble they find their way into some pool it is best to deprive them of it, for a visit to the water only makes them unsettled afterwards.

Result Great Sankey, two; Muspratt'sA.F.C., one. • ANGLING. WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ANGLING ASSOCIATION. (N.A. CENTRE). This year the Easter Holidays are conspicuous by their early arrival, and the weather not being settled during Friday and Saturday, together with the coarse fishing only finishing the week previous, were the joint cause of many anglers not turning out to try for the jack and trout. All these things coming close on top of one another seemed to damp the ardour of the local angler. We have not bad such a poor turnout at Easter for years, and those who braved the elements put up no new records in trout and pike,in fact we only heard of one trout being put over the scales at the Bay Horse, its weight being about 7oz. However, the specials both at the Bay Horse and the Cooper's Arms are enough to lure anglers out almost under any conditions and it will be no surprise to see members out in full force about a week hence at the Gowy, as this is the favourite place during the close time Chester may take a few for the flounder special. The next item of interest during the close time is the Rambling match and it is predicted to be a big thing. We are almost sure a medal will be put up for the let prize, as the Centre Club has already got the same number of medals to be competed for as last year, that is, one for each matcn, so members need not worry about the Centre's specials. The list will be just as good as last season's, to say the least. We hear from the Bay Horse secretary that this up- to-date society is putting up a challenge shield and gold medal for a match during the season. The match is not yet decided, it may possibly be the annual match, but particulars will appear later as to the value of the prizes, and when they will be competed for. Will members please note that contributions must be kept up during close season, and to be in benefit for weighing in for close season specials, contributions must be paid at the rate of 6d. per month. A.S. • ONTARIO'S INDUSTRIAL GROWTH. Though agriculture in all its branches is the most important industry of Ontario, and the one which offers the greatest advantage to British immigrants, the province leads all the rest of Canada in the extent of its manufacturing industries; indeed it is the opportunities and attractions which the sons and daughters of the successful native-born Ontario farmer find in the grow- ing cities which are largely responsible for the scarcity of labour that exists. Moreover, the very fact that the manufacturing industries of Ontario are growing so rapiply is an additional security to the old countryman who takes up land that he will always find markets close at hand to use all the farm, gardening and dairy produce that he can supply. The Ontario farmer has an advantage over the man in less settled areas who has to pay heavier freight and transportation charges to reach the consumer. Recent statistics show that Ontario is practically the manufacturing province for the whole Dominion. It has over 8,000 factories, whereas the other provinces except Quebec do not exceed 2,000 factories. This is to a great extent due to the fact that Ontario is centrally situated and can reach markets both to the east and west more economically than can be done from the other provinces.

LABOURER'S INSURANCE FRAUD. At Crewe, on Tuesday, Thomas Hind, labourer, was charged with falsely obtaining unemployment benefit under the National Insurance Act. Mr F H Cooke, on behalf of the Board of Trade, said the case was the first in Lancashire and Cheshire. The defendant signed the unemployment register for nearly one month, and received unemployment pay. It then transpired that he was working for the Crewe Corporation. When challenged he suddenly left the labour exchange. He was fined five shillings and costs.

It was decided to act in accordance with the Clerk's suggestion. RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICr CDUNCIL. The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Dis- trict was held at Dutton on Tueidss, Mr C E Linaker presiding. MEETINGS NOT PUBLIC. The Clerk to the Helsby Parish Council wrote stating that the following resolution had been passed at the annual parish meeting—" That, the Rural District Council of Runcorn be asked if they can see their way to allow the public to attend the Parochial Committee meetings. This was allowed up to a year ago." The Clerk said public uttenclance had never been officially allowed. The Chairman : lam strongly of the opinion that it is not advisable for the people to attend. The request was not acceded to. WESTON IMPROVEMENTS. The Local Government Board wrote sanctionine, the borrowing of £765 for private attest improvements at Weston. ESTIMATES. The estimate for the Rural District Council was sub- mitted. The probable expenditure was given as £6691, less a probable balance at 31st March, 1913. of £586. The net expenditure to he provided was £5,105. The assessable value in the district was £84,506, and a rate ot 611. in the £ produces £5,100. It was therefore pro- posed to cali upon the various overseers for sums in accordance with the rates. The Clerk atated that the call was the same as that for the previtrus sear. HALTON-ROAD ROUSF.S. The Housing au' Town Planning Committee reported that the surveyor bad submitted plans of proposed alterations to houses in Halton-road Halton, by Messrs. G Davies and Co. It was recommended that subject to sufficient air space being provided at the rear ot each house and to the work b sing done to tiie satisfaction of the surveyor, the proposals be approved. Toe Chairman reported as to the remuneration to be paid to the Puolic Health Surveyors for their services during the year ended December 31 1912. and recom- mended that Messrs Wright and Hamlyn be paid £205. A question arose as to the apportionment of the cost on the various parishes and it was decided that the question as to the portion to be paid be left until the next meeting. The Chairman's reoommendation was acted upon. . No INFECTIOUS DISEASES. The Medical Officer repotted three tuberculos cases but there were no infectious disease cases te report. TENDERS ACCEPTED. WORKHOUSE NURSE BECOMES INMATE. Bertram Herbert Foster. described as a canvasser and advertising agent, was charged at Widnes Police Court on Monday, with deserting hie wife and two children and leaving them chargeable to the funds of the Prescot Union. Mr Ratcliffe said that Foster deserted his wife on January 28. Tne wife applied for outdoor relief. Foster Wok no notice of the official warning. The wife was compelled afterwards to go into the workhouse with her cLildren' and had cost the guardians about £4 ss. The most distressful part of the affair was that the wife was formerly a nurse at the institution of which she is now an inmate. Prisoner pleaded guilty to failing to maintain his wife,but attributed the cause to being out of work. A month's bard labour was the penalty imposed. OVERCROWDED RUNCORN HOUSE. At Runcorn Sessions, on Tuesday, James Clarke, Cambridge-street, was summoned for not abating a nuisance caused by overcrowding at his house. James Psrcival,sanitary inspector, said when he served the notice on February sth, there were eight adults and seven children in the house, which contained only two bedrooms. There resided in the house the defendant and his wife, ton unmarried children from twenty-two years of age to one year, and a son-in-law, daughter,and their baby. The only remedy was to get another house, and he bad recommended one, but they would not leave that district. Defendant's wife said they were all her own family. She had reared thirteen children and had never bad any sickness. Her son-in-law and daughter had since gone into a house of their own. He had not been able to get another house. Mr Percival said there was still a nuisance, as the number of inmates was still too high. There was from £4 to £6 a week coming into the house. The Chairman said be understood there was some difficulty in getting houses in Runcorn and they would adjourn the case for a month to enable them to get a hsuse.

THEFT OF COPPER. Martin Burke (57), a native of St. Helens, was charged at Widnes, on Monday, with stealing 20Ibs weight of copper, the property of the Liverpool Silver and Copper Company. Superintendent Foster said the prisoner was engaged as a slater at works in Widnes, and he admitted the offerce when charged, saying that he had taken the metal home in pieces, and triei to dispose of the mWerial to a marine store dealer at St Helens, who informed the police. Prisoner said he had been a ratepayer for thirty- seven years at St Helens, and he threw himself on the mercy of the court. The prisoner was bound over for six months.
